concepts.title: Read the physical, group and logical layers
concepts.text: A physical volume contributes space to a volume group; logical volumes receive whole extents from that group. Run pvs, vgs and lvs, then compare the separate filesystem-capacity table. Displaying reports changes no allocation.

concepts.title: Count free extents before growing
concepts.text: The supplied device profile reserves 1 MiB, then uses whole extents; a partial tail cannot be allocated. -L 16M requests an absolute 16 MiB, while -L +8M adds 8 MiB; supported M/G units are binary and requests round upward to extents. -l +100%FREE assigns all current free extents to one LV, so plan both targets in a handover.

concepts.title: Grow the filesystem after its backing LV
concepts.text: lvextend changes LV backing, not the filesystem. resize2fs /dev/VG/LV grows the modeled ext4 filesystem to that boundary. Growing the filesystem first cannot create backing space. If the LV is already large enough, grow only the filesystem.

concepts.title: Add only a required blank supplied device
concepts.text: pvcreate /dev/NAME initializes a supplied blank device; vgextend VG /dev/NAME adds it to the group. Direct vgextend can initialize it too. Neither operation creates an LV/filesystem. Keep foreign devices, neighbor allocations and existing files untouched.

concepts.title: Two resources, not one
concepts.text: Blocks hold file data. An inode is the filesystem’s record for a file. A new file needs an inode even when its logical length is zero.

concepts.title: Diagnose the exhausted resource
concepts.text: The supplied filesystem still has available blocks, but no free inodes. Making an empty file smaller cannot help: it already uses zero data blocks. Removing an expendable file releases its inode.

concepts.title: Count whole blocks for each file
concepts.text: A file that crosses a block boundary needs another whole block. In the sample, blocks are 1024 bytes: 1025 bytes uses 2 blocks, while 8193 bytes uses 9. Round each file separately.

concepts.title: Free is not all available
concepts.text: Reserved blocks are free space withheld from ordinary allocation in this model. Available = free minus the supplied reserve, with a minimum of zero. Use Available to plan ordinary writes.

concepts.title: Budget beyond the new file
concepts.text: First allow for the new file’s rounded blocks, then retain the required headroom. Shrinking an expendable cache can be as valid as removing it.

concepts.text: Preview removal shows what a selected cleanup would do to the current virtual files. It does not remove anything. The projection belongs to that exact snapshot.

concepts.title: Another write changes the plan

concepts.text: The independent task checks the final active file, manifest and headroom. A safe order that avoids a stale preview is also valid; you do not need to deliberately trigger an error.

concepts.title: Choose what the application needs to recover
concepts.text: A backup needs the settings that describe how an application runs and the lasting records it cannot rebuild. The separate Willow example needs both kinds of information; read its source manifests before choosing what to save. The application is already paused consistently. This activity teaches file selection, not how to stop a database or back up an entire operating system.

concepts.title: Distinguish lasting records from disposable working files
concepts.text: The filesystem layout gives useful clues: /etc holds system settings, /var/lib holds application state that survives restarts, /var/cache holds data an application can rebuild, and /run holds information for the current boot. This fictional application explicitly rebuilds its cache and runtime files. Real backup choices also need application documentation and recovery requirements; a pathname alone is not a universal exclusion rule.

concepts.title: Keep the two sources separate
concepts.text: The Willow example folders have the same top-level name and member names, but different text and ownership. The full parent path tells tar which folder to save. Give configuration and record archives different names and restore into separate parents so one kind of information cannot overwrite the other. Apply that reasoning to the independent assignment.

concepts.text: Only the two requested full archives belong in the delivery folder. Do not create incremental tracking files for this task. Listing archive names proves neither their source nor their contents: read a trial restore and compare its modes and owners. A full restore overlays stored files and retains unrelated destination files. Independent checks repeat recovery with their own empty and nonempty sample destinations.

goal: Diagnose a partially successful client test and repair a dynamic range while retaining a held binding.
context: Builds on Linux host IPv4 addresses, routes and resolver settings. The editor and all client exchanges here are simulated; no real server preparation is needed.

concepts.title: An address and the settings a client needs
concepts.text: DHCP can give a computer an address plus settings such as its router and DNS server. A lease is permission to use an address for a limited time, not permanent ownership. The subnet declaration identifies the network; range identifies the inclusive first and last addresses offered dynamically. Edit the configuration text here; Run client tests evaluates virtual clients only.

concepts.title: A range is not the whole subnet
concepts.text: In the worked workshop, subnet 10.60.0.0 netmask 255.255.255.0 selects 10.60.0.0/24. Its range .100 through .103 contains four addresses. The network, broadcast, supplied interface addresses and occupied addresses cannot be handed out as fresh leases.

concepts.title: Count available addresses, not just range endpoints
concepts.text: The busy workshop case already occupies .100 and .101. The four-address worked range still leaves .102 and .103 for two new clients. A three-address range ending at .102 works when empty but runs out in the busy case; a successful first case is not enough.

concepts.title: Existing leases are separate from new configuration
concepts.text: The supplied management client already holds .10. Loading a different dynamic range does not rewrite that held client lease. This task tests new requests while preserving that existing binding. Use braces for a subnet block, semicolons after parameters and # for a comment. Put shared parameters before subnet blocks and local parameters before range.

worked.label: Select a network
worked.explanation: The declared network and mask select the client subnet; they do not themselves allocate an address.

worked.label: Offer an inclusive range
worked.explanation: Four potential addresses; after .100 and .101 are occupied, two remain.

worked.label: Client options
worked.explanation: The router forwards off-subnet traffic; DNS resolves names. The requested exercise grant is 600 virtual seconds.

worked.label: Held client
worked.explanation: An already-held binding is not replaced just because new clients use a different range.

requirements: Keep one dynamic range entirely within 10.50.0.100–10.50.0.110 on 10.50.0.0/24; serve no additional subnet.
Both new clients need distinct usable leases in both supplied cases, including the case with .100 and .101 occupied.
Supply router 10.50.0.1, DNS 203.0.113.53 and a 600-second grant to each new client.

practice.observe: One case can pass while another runs out of addresses. Read the failed exchange and the client without a lease.

practice.observe: The busy case has two usable free addresses. Compare the actual new leases with the supplied management binding.

practice.observe: Address exhaustion is a client-result failure, not a syntax error. A retry replaces the previous result only after all current tests finish.

goal: Diagnose option inheritance across two networks and distinguish new, renewing and untouched client settings.
context: Builds on Linux host IPv4 addresses, routes and resolver settings. The editor and all client exchanges here are simulated; no real server preparation is needed.

concepts.title: A shared default saves repetition
concepts.text: A parameter before the subnet declarations supplies a default. In the worked example, option domain-name-servers 203.0.113.53 applies to alpha because alpha has no local DNS option. Values inside one subnet override only that option for that subnet.

concepts.title: Each subnet still needs its own router
concepts.text: A router must make sense for the client network. The workshop alpha router is 10.61.0.1; beta’s is 10.61.1.1. Put these local numeric router options in the matching subnet blocks. A wrong but well-formed address is a configuration mistake, not a syntax error.

concepts.title: Override only the different setting
concepts.text: The worked beta block specifies DNS 203.0.113.54. It still inherits the global 600-second default and 3600-second maximum. Removing beta’s DNS option makes beta inherit .53 instead; inheritance is not a second independent copy of the same configuration.

concepts.title: Saving configuration does not contact every client
concepts.text: The supplied management client initially holds old DNS .10. Tests load your configuration, advance 300 virtual seconds to its renewal window and renew that client. It then receives the current alpha settings. The untouched beta client sends nothing and retains its old binding. This is a logical renewal exercise, not a real daemon/cache or wire-protocol model.

worked.label: Shared parameters
worked.explanation: Global parameters come before the subnet declarations. No requested lifetime is modeled; the default is capped by the maximum.

worked.label: Alpha local setting
worked.explanation: Alpha inherits global DNS .53 and duration 600.

worked.label: Beta local override
worked.explanation: Beta overrides DNS, while retaining the inherited lease duration.

worked.label: Actual observation
worked.value: Load; advance 300 virtual seconds; renew management; request new clients
worked.explanation: The renewed alpha client gets .53. An untouched held client does not silently change.

requirements: Alpha clients need router 10.51.0.1 and DNS 203.0.113.53; beta clients need router 10.51.1.1 and DNS 203.0.113.54.
Every new or renewed client needs a 600-second grant; evaluate both supplied occupancy cases.
Keep alpha’s dynamic range inside .10–.20 and beta’s inside .50–.60 in their respective supplied /24 networks. Serve no other dynamic subnet.
The management client renews at 300 virtual seconds and must receive the corrected alpha settings.
Keep the untouched beta client’s supplied address, options and lease timing exactly unchanged.

practice.observe: Well-formed wrong DNS values parse, but client outcomes fail. Management changes only at the scheduled virtual renewal.

practice.observe: Both cases should pass; routers and durations remain separate checks. The untouched beta binding retains its supplied timing.

practice.action: Remove beta’s local DNS option and run again. Read the beta client’s actual DNS, then restore the option and retry.
practice.observe: Beta now inherits global .53 and fails its .54 requirement; the alpha cases can remain correct.

goal: Add a manually chosen IPv6 address alongside an existing IPv4 connection.
requirements: Give ens3 one unused IPv6 primary address in 2001:db8:110::/64, with the correct /64 prefix. Do not use a supplied peer or router address, or the subnet-router anycast address.

concepts.title: Two address families can share an interface
concepts.text: IPv4 uses dotted-decimal addresses, such as 192.0.2.40. IPv6 uses hexadecimal groups separated by colons. Adding an IPv6 address does not replace the IPv4 address: the same interface can have both.

concepts.title: Read the address and prefix
concepts.text: IPv6 has 128 bits, written as eight groups of hexadecimal digits. Each group uses 0–9 and a–f (hexadecimal). Leading zeros can be left out; one :: abbreviates a run of zero groups. In 2001:db8:310::77/64, the /64 says the first 64 bits (four groups) identify this link’s prefix; the remaining 64 identify the interface. You do not need to expand every group for this task.

concepts.title: Choose an unused address in the supplied link
concepts.text: The example LAN is 2001:db8:310::/64. Choose a primary address in that prefix, different from supplied peers. IPv6 has no broadcast address; do not apply IPv4’s subtract-two rule. Subnet-router anycast and /127–/128 primary assignments are outside this activity.

concepts.title: Inspect, then add without disturbing IPv4
concepts.text: Run ip -6 address show to inspect IPv6; ip -4 address show inspects IPv4. The supplied link-local address starts with fe80:: and is scoped to its interface. Here you add only a manual global primary with ip -6 address add ADDRESS/PREFIX dev NAME. Keep the shared interface Up state and all existing IPv4 settings.

concepts.title: Check the prefix as well as one working path
concepts.text: A nearby IPv6 peer may still be reachable with a prefix that is too broad. Check network compares the requested /64 and unused address separately from path availability. The native path test uses supplied facts; it sends no packets and does not model duplicate-address detection.

context: Builds on Linux interface and route practice. IPv6 notation, separate address-family routing and device scope are taught here; no prior CCNA course is required.

concepts.title: IPv4 success does not prove IPv6 routing
concepts.text: The two address families have separate route tables. A server can reach an application with IPv4 while its IPv6 packets choose the wrong interface. Inspect ip -6 route show rather than changing an already-working IPv4 default.

concepts.title: A link-local next hop needs a device
concepts.text: fe80::1 is meaningful only on a particular link. In this example both ens3 and ens4 have a router with that address. The dev field identifies which router receives traffic; the application router and management router have different onward paths.

concepts.title: A specific route wins before a default
concepts.text: A default ::/0 matches any IPv6 destination. A 2001:db8:590::80/128 route matches only that address and wins first, even with a higher numeric metric. Compare metrics only between equally specific routes.

concepts.title: Repair the matching entries
concepts.text: This subset uses explicit positive metrics for IPv6 route changes. route replace changes the entry with the given destination prefix and metric; it does not erase every other matching route. You can remove an exact bad /128 or repair it with the correct scoped next hop.

concepts.title: Verify more than one application path
concepts.text: Test both supplied application destinations and keep the existing management route. One can work through a repaired default while the other still follows a bad /128. Check network identifies which current paths and preservation requirements pass.

concepts.text: This finite activity requires removing an interface’s IPv6 gateway routes before deleting its primary address. concepts.title: Separate preference, specificity and next-hop scope
concepts.text: A /128 entry wins over a default. A syntactically valid fe80::2 is not necessarily a supplied router. Inspect the selected prefix, dev and known onward path; do not guess that changing a metric repairs an unknown next hop.

goal: Create a raw harbor/staging LV of 24 MiB in the existing harbor group.
context: Builds on the existing LVM growth unit: you can read PV, VG and LV reports. New-volume creation, explicit names, whole-extent allocation and raw-storage limits are taught here before the assignment.

concepts.title: A new LV is a new allocation, not more space in an old LV
concepts.text: A physical volume supplies pieces of storage called extents. A volume group pools them. lvcreate reserves some of that pool under a new logical-volume name; lvextend instead grows a volume that already exists. Inspect pvs, vgs and lvs before changing the allocation.

concepts.title: Plan with whole pieces and leave the reserve
concepts.text: With 4 MiB extents, a 12 MiB new volume needs three extents. A 9 MiB request also consumes three because it rounds up. Keep the required free extents for later work; 100%FREE uses everything currently free, not the total group size.

concepts.title: Raw storage is not a filesystem
concepts.text: A new LV in this unit has no filesystem, files or mount. lvs proves its allocation, not that it can hold ordinary files yet. Formatting and mounting are separate skills; neither happens automatically here.

concepts.title: Recover only the new raw allocation
concepts.text: If you allocated a new raw LV incorrectly, this subset supports lvremove -y VG/LV and then a corrected lvcreate. The -y option explicitly skips confirmation. Real lvremove can destroy data. This exercise refuses removal of filesystem-bearing LVs; do not treat that refusal as a safety feature of real Linux.

concepts.title: Remove the intended allocation, preserve the data
concepts.text: A logical volume reserves pieces of its group. concepts.title: Retire storage from the inside out
concepts.text: An LV belongs to a volume group; a PV supplies storage to that group. First remove only the unused raw LVs named in the plan. Then vgremove NAME can remove the empty group in this subset. A nonempty group is refused here; real vgremove can remove contained volumes after confirmation and has broader destructive behavior.

concepts.title: An absent group does not mean an absent PV label
concepts.text: After vgremove, its devices are still labeled physical volumes, now without a group. Read pvs: pvremove /dev/NAME... clears only the specified unowned PV labels. Do not clear an unrelated orphan PV merely because it has no group. No force, vgreduce or filesystem-bearing removal is modeled.

concepts.title: No label is not secure erasure
concepts.text: Clearing an LVM label stops that device being recognized as a PV. Its size does not change, and this does not format a filesystem, wipe every byte or securely erase data. The inventory reports no modeled PV label; it makes no claim about recoverable media contents.

concepts.title: Inspect before making a destructive change
concepts.text: Read lvs and the supplied inventory before choosing a name. Here lvremove -y VG/LV explicitly confirms removal of one raw LV; /dev/VG/LV and --yes are supported alternatives. goal: Make every LV in reports active so the simulated application reader can read reports/ledger and its original /keep.txt contents.
context: Builds on LVM allocation and raw retirement. This unit adds LV availability and supplied open-consumer facts. It teaches the supported activation commands before the full assignment; mounting, boot policy and real kernel behavior remain separate.

concepts.title: Stored data can exist while its LV is unavailable
concepts.text: An inactive logical volume still has its allocation, filesystem metadata and saved contents. It is not currently available as an LV device for use. Recreating or growing the storage does not fix that availability problem and can damage data. Inspect the current state before choosing a change.

concepts.title: Activate the intended group, not every pool
concepts.text: vgchange -a y NAME makes all LVs in that named group available; -a n makes them inactive. --activate y|n and the common -ay/-an forms are supported alternatives. This lab requires one explicit supplied group name. Read the simulator’s ModelActive column in lvs: it reports each LV, so a group may initially contain a mixture.

concepts.title: Availability is separate from mounting and boot policy
concepts.text: Making an LV active does not create a filesystem, mount it or configure automatic startup. The file inspection here is a simulated application reader over the supplied filesystem; it is not cat on a raw device and does not model a Linux mount. After activation, it can read the retained sample contents.

concepts.title: Keep the supplied consumer facts in view
concepts.text: Some supplied LVs may be marked open by an application. This bounded subset refuses group deactivation when any of its LVs is marked open, before changing anything. Real LVM can have partial effects and requires broader use/mount checks. No consumer discovery, force, process stop or host kernel operation is simulated.

goal: Rename the original team/draft LV to team/reports while preserving its data, neighbor and availability.
context: First complete LVM availability. You should be able to read the VG/LV columns, distinguish allocation from filesystem capacity, and recognize Active, Inactive and Marked open. This lesson introduces names without changing any of those properties.

concepts.title: Names identify a route to existing storage
concepts.text: A volume group (VG) is a pool of storage; a logical volume (LV) is an allocation inside that pool. A path such as studio/notes names one LV. Renaming changes that route, not its size, data or filesystem. Inspect vgs and lvs first so you can name the intended original object.

concepts.title: Rename rather than remove and recreate
concepts.text: lvrename studio notes journal changes the existing LV name. lvrename studio/notes journal and lvrename /dev/studio/notes journal are equivalent supported forms. Afterward, studio/journal is the current path and studio/notes no longer resolves. Removing and creating another allocation is a different operation: a matching name does not recover the original data.

concepts.title: A collision is a useful refusal
concepts.text: A destination name must be unused in its group. An existing neighbor is not overwritten or merged. Read the error, inspect current names and retry the intended rename. Avoid force options: they are outside this supported subset.

concepts.title: Verify more than the spelling
concepts.text: Use lvs to check the current path, capacity and ModelActive state. Open Inspect retained files and exact byte capacities to compare original data through the simulated application reader. Preserve inactive allocations and supplied open consumers; renaming does not require rebuilding them. Real application, mount and boot references can still need separate updates; this exercise does not edit those references.

goal: Rename a group and its existing data LV while preserving mixed availability and a live neighbor.
context: Complete the volume-renaming lesson first. This handover combines a VG rename and an LV rename while preserving a mixed active/inactive pool and an unrelated live application.

concepts.title: A group rename changes every member path
concepts.text: A VG name is the first part of VG/LV. vgrename workshop atelier renames that same group, so workshop/notes becomes atelier/notes and workshop/buffer becomes atelier/buffer. Their PV membership and allocations stay intact; the devices are not copied or relabeled as a different pool.

concepts.title: Use the current name for the next command

concepts.title: Preserve the individual availability states

goal: Recognize an already-enlarged PV, then grow the intended LV and filesystem while protecting a neighbor and another pool.
context: Complete LVM growth and storage names first. You should recognize VG/LV paths, binary MiB, whole extents and the difference between LV and filesystem capacity. This lesson adds the PV’s recognized end inside an already-enlarged supplied device.

concepts.title: A larger device can still have a smaller recognized PV
concepts.text: A physical device supplies bytes. LVM records how far its physical volume (PV) extends inside those bytes; its volume group allocates whole physical extents (PEs) from that recognized area. Enlarging the supplied device does not itself give an LV or filesystem more capacity. Read Supplied device facts and pvs before choosing which layer needs a change.

concepts.title: Compare device, PV, LV and filesystem separately
concepts.text: In the worked example, /dev/aspena is 49 MiB but its PV still recognizes 17 MiB. This exercise reserves 1 MiB before data: (17 − 1) ÷ 4 = 4 physical extents, all already allocated. After recognizing 49 MiB, (49 − 1) ÷ 4 = 12 extents are available to the group. pvs reports the whole-extent data capacity, so its size is 16 MiB before and 48 MiB afterward. Real metadata arrangements can differ.

concepts.title: Refresh the PV, then grow the intended allocation
concepts.text: pvresize /dev/aspena recognizes the already-supplied device size; it does not edit a partition or change an LV. After that, lvextend -L 16M aspen/sample allocates enough extents for a 16 MiB LV. M is binary MiB here. Keep the neighbor and bench pool unchanged; adding replacement storage does not repair the intended PV metadata.

concepts.title: Grow the filesystem and verify the retained data
concepts.text: resize2fs /dev/aspen/sample grows the separate modeled filesystem to the current LV size. Inspect all four layers, then open Inspect retained files and exact byte capacities to read the original record. PV, LV and filesystem size changes are different operations; a successful command in one layer does not prove the others meet the task. Actual disk/partition, mount and kernel operations are outside this simulation.

goal: Set a smaller recognized PV end while preserving separated physical allocations and every existing capacity layer.
context: Complete the capacity-layer lesson first. You should know how PV metadata differs from the supplied physical device, and how to keep LV and filesystem sizes separate. This lesson adds physical placement and a smaller recognized PV end.

concepts.title: Free capacity does not describe physical placement
concepts.text: An LV’s logical extents can occupy separated physical positions. The worked cedar/sample uses physical extents 0 and 5; neighbor uses 1. There are only three allocated extents, but the PV must still include position 5. Read the derived highest allocated PE in Supplied device facts; numbering begins at 0.

concepts.title: Check which numbered extents the new end retains
concepts.text: This exercise reserves 1 MiB before data and uses 4 MiB PEs. A 33 MiB recognized PV gives (33 − 1) ÷ 4 = 8 PEs, numbered 0 through 7; physical extent 5 still fits. A 17 MiB end gives only 4 PEs, numbered 0 through 3, so it would exclude an allocation even though three total allocations sound small. The simulator refuses that end without moving data.

concepts.title: Change the PV metadata without shrinking other layers
concepts.text: pvresize --setphysicalvolumesize 33M /dev/cedara records the smaller recognized PV end. M means binary MiB; automatic pvresize without this option would recognize the full supplied 41 MiB device again. Neither form shrinks the device, LV or filesystem. No relocation, real partition editing or LV/filesystem reduction is implemented here.

concepts.title: Verify the end and unchanged data independently
concepts.text: After the change, pvs reports 32 MiB of whole-extent data in this example; the device remains 41 MiB. Check that the original LV allocation, filesystem capacity, files and unrelated pool stay exactly as supplied. Inspect retained files through the simulated reader. This bounded metadata exercise does not establish that shrinking a real disk, partition or filesystem would be safe.

concepts.title: Identify the data before choosing a target
concepts.text: An array is one logical device built from component devices. A UUID is the array identity stored with those components. mdadm --examine reads that existing metadata. concepts.title: Assemble existing members; do not create a new array

context: After persistent Ethernet profile editing and conventional IPv4 addressing. No prior VLAN configuration is assumed; the parent, software interface and switch tag plan are introduced here.

concepts.title: Separate the address from the tag
concepts.text: Reports uses one software interface, reports0, carried by a physical parent such as enp1s0. The IPv4 address identifies the host in its IP network; the VLAN ID selects the switch broadcast domain. ID30 does not follow from an IP octet. The supplied switch plan places Reports peers in VLAN30 and Audit peers in VLAN40.

concepts.title: Read the saved keyfile
concepts.text: In [connection], type=vlan creates a VLAN profile and interface-name names its software interface. In [vlan], parent names its physical NIC and id is the numeric VLAN tag. The supplied flags=1 retains header reordering; protocol=802.1Q uses one conventional tag. Keep those supplied settings. In [ipv4], address1 is the host address/prefix; method=manual keeps it static.

concepts.title: Read the switch path in both directions
concepts.text: A trunk can carry several VLANs. Its allowed list admits tags and its native VLAN normally leaves untagged. The primary trunk has native99 and carries Reports30 and Audit40 as tags. A Reports VLAN interface sends tag30 and accepts a return tagged30; an untagged native return is not that interface.

On a real machine, editing a keyfile alone does not reload or activate NetworkManager.

goal: One active-backup bond carries two VLANs. Repair its saved controller/member dependencies and prove that either NIC can carry both networks after startup.
context: After Linux VLAN profiles and the native-return handover. The IP/tag plan is already supplied; this capstone teaches how controller and port profiles make both physical NICs available to that plan.

concepts.title: One virtual uplink, two physical members
concepts.text: A bond is one software interface built from physical NICs. In active-backup mode, only one member carries traffic at a time; the other provides a backup, rather than adding bandwidth to the first. reports0 and audit0 are separate VLAN interfaces above bond0. bond0 uses enp1s0 or enp2s0 underneath.

concepts.title: A controller starts ports that are actually bound to it
concepts.text: The bond profile uses type=bond. Each participating NIC uses an Ethernet port profile with controller=bond0 and port-type=bond. Without those two binding keys, the NIC profile is an unbound Ethernet candidate. On the controller, autoconnect-ports=1 starts matching bound ports when that controller starts;0 leaves ports untouched.

concepts.title: Keep automatic startup separate from forced port activation
concepts.text: autoconnect=true makes the controller eligible for automatic startup. The supplied port profiles use autoconnect=false, so they do not start on their own. The controller can still start them explicitly through autoconnect-ports=1. Changing a port to true is not a substitute for binding it to the bond; independent port-driven startup is outside this exercise.

concepts.title: Verify carrier, tags and current versus future settings
concepts.text: miimon=100 is a real 100ms carrier-monitor interval; this simulator uses settled physical cases rather than running that clock. primary=enp1s0 prefers that member when it is attached and has carrier. Otherwise an attached available backup can carry traffic. MII does not check IP addresses or VLAN reachability, so both tags must still work outward and back. Editing saved files does not replace the supplied current settings or membership.

goal: Connect two untagged LAN segments with a Linux bridge, keep the host address on the bridge, and explain which paths remain when one port is unavailable.
context: After saved profiles and bonded VLAN handover. Reuse controller/port roles, then learn why forwarding between segments differs from selecting one backup NIC.

concepts.title: A bridge joins segments; a bond chooses a physical member
concepts.text: The two workstations use the same IPv4 LAN but sit on separate Ethernet segments. A software bridge forwards between its attached ports so those segments can communicate. Both ports can forward at once. An active-backup bond, by contrast, selects one member for a common uplink.

concepts.title: Put the host address on the bridge controller
concepts.text: br0 is the host-facing logical interface. Its manual address and prefix must identify the supplied LAN without duplicating a workstation. The physical port profiles only attach enp1s0 and enp2s0 to that bridge; they do not hold separate host addresses here.

concepts.title: The controller starts ports that are bound to it
concepts.text: A participating Ethernet profile uses both controller=br0 and port-type=bridge. autoconnect-ports=1 on the bridge starts matching bound profiles even when their own autoconnect is false. Without both binding keys, a candidate is still a separate unbound Ethernet profile.

concepts.title: A down port isolates its segment
concepts.text: A bridge does not move a disconnected left workstation onto the right NIC. Test both ports available, left unavailable and right unavailable. Success means the available paths work and the disconnected paths stay isolated. This simulator uses a settled tree; it does not run STP timers, learn MAC tables or change real networking.

worked.label: Separate practice LAN
worked.explanation: A bridge host can use another conventional address in this LAN. For the worked example, use 10.250.0.20/24 on br0.

worked.label: Controller settings
worked.explanation: The section names identify where each key belongs. Repairing this file makes one physical case pass; the missing right-port binding still matters.

worked.label: Attach the right port
worked.explanation: Put both keys in [connection]. Keep the supplied false autoconnect; forced controller startup includes bound ports. Omit the port IP groups or retain disabled methods.

worked.label: Predict each physical case
worked.value:
Both available:both segments joined
Left unavailable:right remains usable
Right unavailable:left remains usable
worked.explanation: Expected blocked paths are part of these tests. Actual current/future membership and path feedback appear after Test startup profiles; current selections are preserved.

requirements: Prepare the four saved virtual profiles for the next simulated startup: put a usable address with the supplied LAN prefix on br0, distinct from the two workstations, and attach both intended physical NICs as bridge ports.

With both ports available, br0 must reach both workstations and the workstations must have a two-way untagged path through the bridge. When a physical port is unavailable, retain the reachable segment and keep the two segments isolated; do not invent bond-style failover.

Keep the current bridge IP settings, controller configuration and attached membership unchanged while re-reading saved files. Keep audit.nmconnection unchanged, keep Audit reachable on mgmt0 and add no default route there.
Retain all four supplied filenames and UUIDs. Choose Test startup profiles and inspect all three physical cases.

goal: Diagnose an early authentication bypass, repair the rule controls, and verify acceptance as well as rejection using supplied module results.
context: After local account and group administration. No prior PAM knowledge is assumed: learn the three rule fields and the control words before editing.

concepts.title: An application asks ordered checks to decide
concepts.text: PAM connects an application to a list of identity checks. In a pam.d file, a rule has three parts: auth selects the authentication stage, the control word says how its result affects the decision, and the module names the check. Read rules from top to bottom. A module result and the final stack decision can differ.

concepts.title: Password results are supplied in this activity
concepts.text: Each sample tells you what pam_unix.so returns: success, incorrect password, unknown user, unavailable service or no decision (PAM_IGNORE). You do not type a password. pam_permit.so supplies success here; pam_deny.so supplies authentication error. Neither one checks a password.

concepts.title: Required remembers; requisite stops
concepts.text: If a required check fails, PAM remembers that failure but continues through later rules. A later success cannot erase it. Requisite also requires success, but a failure returns immediately. The first remembered failure determines the returned error.

concepts.title: Sufficient can return early; optional can ignore a failure
concepts.text: A sufficient success returns immediately if no earlier required check has failed. Its failure is ignored. An optional success contributes, while an optional failure is ignored. If every result is ignored, there is no success: this model returns permission denied. Do not treat an ignored password result as verification.

concepts.title: Check both legitimate and rejected attempts
concepts.text: A repair must allow the supplied successful password check and reject the other four samples. Accepting everyone hides a bypass; rejecting everyone locks out legitimate users. Use the visited-rule trace to explain a surprising decision.

worked.label: Read the faulty practice rule
worked.explanation: auth is the stage, optional is the control and pam_unix.so is the module. A bad supplied password result is ignored by this control.

worked.label: Why the faulty practice accepts everyone
worked.explanation: The next rule contributes success without checking a password. The final result can therefore accept the incorrect-password sample.

worked.label: A worked repair
worked.value:
# example-login: repaired
auth required pam_unix.so
auth optional pam_deny.so
worked.explanation: Required password checking remembers failures. The optional deny does not lock out the successful sample. If the password module supplies no decision, nothing contributes success.

worked.label: Predict a different valid approach
worked.value:
auth sufficient pam_unix.so
auth required pam_deny.so
worked.explanation: Password success returns early. Other supplied results reach the denying fallback. Try it in practice and compare the visited rules.

practice.title: Run the faulty example and inspect a rejection that was accepted
practice.action: Choose Test stack. Under Actual results, open the incorrect-password sample under Visited rules. Compare its supplied module result with the final Accepted decision.
practice.observe: The password failure is ignored; the later permit supplies success. Expected and actual decisions are labeled separately.

practice.title: Repair the practice control
practice.action: Change optional to required on the pam_unix.so line and remove the required pam_permit.so line. Test again. Fill worked example offers the separate practice repair on request.
practice.observe: All five samples should pass their expected decisions. Rejected samples are successful tests when rejection is expected, not failed grading cases.

practice.title: Compare an early-return repair
practice.action: Try the two-line sufficient-password/required-deny approach from the Introduction, then Test stack. Change sufficient to required and test once more.
practice.observe: The sufficient version returns before the deny for a good password. The required version continues into the required deny and locks out the successful sample. Inspect the trace and repair it.

requirements: Repair the virtual lab-login auth stack.
Accept the supplied successful password check; reject an incorrect password, unknown user, unavailable password service and an ignored password check.
Test every sample and inspect why each decision occurs.
Do not solve the task by accepting everyone or rejecting everyone.
Use only the supported auth rules; no real credentials or host configuration are involved.

goal: Separate a directory URI, a search base and a search scope while repairing a client lookup.
context: Builds on service/DNS client recovery and Linux command basics. No previous directory-service knowledge is assumed.

concepts.title: A directory name identifies a branch or an entry
concepts.text: LDAP stores entries in a tree. Read uid=ava,ou=People,dc=workshop,dc=test from the specific entry at the left toward its containing branches at the right. uid is a login-name attribute, ou an organizational unit, and dc a domain component. A DN is a directory name, not a file path.

concepts.title: Client defaults and command overrides are different
concepts.text: URI chooses the supplied virtual directory. BASE is the distinguished name where a search begins. Write each setting as an option followed by its unquoted value. Apply configuration stores those defaults. -H and -b change one command; they do not repair the displayed defaults.

concepts.title: Scope chooses which part of the tree to visit
concepts.text: -s base considers the named entry itself; -s one considers its immediate children; -s sub includes the base and all descendants. A People branch can contain a Remote branch whose users are missed by one-level search. Subtree is the default in this supported command subset.

concepts.title: The filter chooses entries; the final names choose attributes
concepts.text: Use ldapsearch -x -LLL '(objectClass=person)' uid cn. Quote the parenthesized filter so it stays one literal argument. The filter selects person entries; uid cn asks which attributes to return. -x selects simple instead of SASL authentication; this exercise performs anonymous virtual reads. -LLL shows plain LDIF without comments or a version header. No real connection is opened.

worked.label: Sample defaults
worked.explanation: URI selects the supplied workshop directory; BASE starts in People rather than Archive.

worked.label: Sample tree
worked.value:

  ou=People
    uid=ava
    uid=noah
    ou=Remote → uid=zoe
  ou=Archive → uid=ava
worked.explanation: The repeated ava name has different DNs; the base and scope decide which can be visited.

worked.label: Worked search

One level: ava, noah

practice.observe: Run search uses the applied defaults. A -b override changes only one command; an edited but unapplied BASE is reported.

practice.title: Write and run the sample search
practice.action: In Search command, enter the worked person query selecting uid/cn and choose Run search. Add -s one and run again; remove it or use -s sub to include Remote.
practice.observe: Actual search result should include zoe with subtree scope and exclude that nested user with one-level scope.

goal: Select entries by role and available contact data, then request only the needed attributes.
context: After Linux client configuration and directory-query foundations.

concepts.title: A directory name identifies a branch or an entry
concepts.text: LDAP stores entries in a tree. Read uid=ava,ou=People,dc=workshop,dc=test from the specific entry at the left toward its containing branches at the right. uid is a login-name attribute, ou an organizational unit, and dc a domain component. A DN is a directory name, not a file path.

concepts.title: Build a condition from smaller filters
concepts.text: An equality filter such as (description=on-call) tests one attribute value. A presence filter such as (mail=*) asks whether an attribute exists. AND uses (&(condition1)(condition2)); OR uses | and NOT uses !. These characters belong inside the quoted filter, not separate shell commands.

concepts.title: A selected person may still lack a contact address
concepts.text: A person marked on-call without mail cannot be included in a usable email contact list. Combine the role and presence conditions. The uid/mail words after the filter choose returned fields; they do not restrict which entries match.

concepts.title: Test the same query against changing inputs
concepts.text: Changed directory inputs has different people on call. No matching on-call contacts has no qualifying entries, which is a successful empty search. A hardcoded user may work once and fail the next roster. Unknown filter attributes are not ordinary false conditions: negating an unknown name does not select everyone.

goal: Import a small contact roster safely and verify the resulting directory.
context: Prerequisites: directory names, search scope and attribute selection from LDAP clients. LDIF data editing is taught here before the full assignment.

concepts.title: An entry is a named collection of fields
concepts.text: A directory person has a distinguished name (dn), not a file path. uid=iris identifies the person within the People branch; cn is a display name, sn is a surname, and mail is a contact address. You already practiced searching entries in the preceding unit.

concepts.title: Describe new people with LDIF
concepts.text: LDIF (LDAP Data Interchange Format) is text data for entries or changes. Start with version: 1, then a blank line. Each entry begins with dn: followed by attribute: value lines. Put a blank line between people. objectClass: inetOrgPerson selects the supported person fields and inherits person, organizationalPerson and top. cn and sn are required. In this exercise, also include the uid used in the name.

concepts.title: One attribute can have several values
concepts.text: Repeat an attribute line to supply another value. Attribute and record order do not define the solution. Names and values are data; they are never executed as commands. The simulator supports printable ASCII values and a bounded LDIF subset.

concepts.title: Apply, inspect, then check
concepts.text: Apply LDIF runs the data against the selected original sample. Read the record results and the actual directory. Check work repeats the same draft against all samples and verifies both new people and preserved data. A supplied operator already has delegated permission to create these entries; this is not a login or an ACL lesson.

goal: Repair optional contact data and retire one leaf without disturbing the directory.
context: Prerequisites: LDAP queries and person-entry imports. Learn ordered attribute edits and per-request failure boundaries before repairing the complete directory.

concepts.title: Add an entry versus modify its fields
concepts.text: The earlier import created new distinguished names. Here the people already exist. A record with changetype: modify changes one existing entry; add: mail inside it appends a mail value. That is different from changetype: add, which creates an entry.

concepts.title: Choose the intended value set
concepts.text: replace: mail followed by mail: value sets the whole list, whether the old field had zero, one or several values. add: mail preserves old values and fails if the new one already exists. delete: mail needs an existing field or listed value. An empty replace: mail removes the field if present and succeeds if absent.

concepts.title: Order and failure boundaries matter
concepts.text: Finish each edit with a line containing only -. Edits in one Modify run in order and commit together. If one fails, none of that Modify is applied. Blank lines separate requests: earlier successful requests remain when a later one fails, and later records are not attempted.

concepts.title: Retire a leaf, preserve the rest
concepts.text: A separate record with dn and changetype: delete removes that entry. It cannot recursively remove children. The supplied operator can edit mail/description and delete person entries in this branch. These delegated rights are scenario facts; the activity does not perform real authentication or teach server ACL configuration.

concepts.title: A utility applies your LDIF input

goal: Repair a protected self-service password change and prove that only the requested credential changed.
context: Prerequisites: full directory names, supplied credential profiles and the preceding LDAP utility lessons. Connection protection, client trust and the three password prompts are taught here before independent work.

concepts.title: Protect the connection before logging in
concepts.text: A password should not travel over an unprotected connection. -ZZ asks ldap clients to start TLS and requires that step to succeed before the command proceeds. A trusted issuer, a server name matching the directory host and a valid certificate all matter. This lab models those checks with supplied facts; it does not establish real TLS or contact a server.

concepts.title: Select the supplied CA input
concepts.text: TLS_CACERT identifies the CA certificates a real client trusts. Here its /work/ path selects a supplied virtual input containing symbolic CA facts. Match the displayed sample certificate issuer to that input. TLS_REQCERT demand, its hard synonym or its omitted demand default keeps peer checking enabled. The simulator reads no host configuration, environment or system trust files.

concepts.title: Keep the three password roles separate
concepts.text: A script or command does not create these passwords: the lab supplies fictional profiles. -W asks for the bind password used to log in. -A asks for the current password of the target whose password is changing. -S asks for its replacement. In this self-service exercise the bind and old-target values usually match, but they are separate inputs with separate failure messages. Select profiles rather than entering any personal password.

concepts.title: Verify the resulting credential state
concepts.text: ldappasswd uses a dedicated password-modify operation; it is not an ordinary attribute edit. After the command, try fresh authentication: the requested replacement must be accepted, the previous credential rejected and unrelated identities unchanged. A successful command that simply sets the old value again does not meet that rotation task. Every run here starts from the selected original sample.

concepts.title: Choose the entry and fields first
concepts.text: Each access to rule selects the target entries and attributes. A DN subtree includes the named branch and its descendants; attrs selects fields such as mail or description. Here you edit one combined static ACL fragment for established callers, not a whole server configuration.

concepts.title: Then match the caller
concepts.text: Within that rule, the first matching by clause chooses the caller’s access. self means the established caller and target have the same complete directory name, not merely the same uid. users means every authenticated caller. An exact helper name must not accidentally grant that role to everybody.

concepts.title: Order matters at both levels
concepts.text: The first matching target rule and then the first matching caller clause decide the result. Later restrictions do not undo an earlier broad grant. Put specific field rules before a catch-all denial; a by * rule must follow more specific caller clauses.

concepts.title: Permission is checked before committing changes
concepts.text: write permits updates and includes lower access levels such as read. read does not permit writing. A nonempty policy denies unmatched requests; an empty list defaults to read, not write. For a multi-field Modify request, every field needs permission. If one field is denied, the whole request leaves the entry unchanged. These tasks test write outcomes, not complete search or fresh Bind behavior.

worked.label: Workshop target

    by self write
    by * none
access to dn.subtree="ou=People,dc=delegation-workshop,dc=test" attrs=mail
    by self write
    by * none
access to * by * none
worked.explanation: description lets the named desk identity or self write; mail lets only self write. The final rule denies unmatched writes.

goal: Delegate contact changes while protecting unrelated people and branches.
context: Builds on full directory names, the preceding LDAP utility tasks and protected established identities. This lesson teaches ordered write controls; it does not configure a full server. A caller here is a person whose identity has already been established before the edited write policy is tested.

goal: Deploy a directory policy to the intended backend and verify that its neighbour stays unchanged.
context: Builds on full directory names, LDAP change records and the preceding static access-policy task. Configuration-editing rights are provided by the lab; contact requests use the established person shown in the workspace. Apply and verify changes here, rather than editing server backing files.

concepts.title: Settings and contacts have different names
concepts.text: People entries hold contact data. The separate cn=config directory holds settings. A database entry’s olcSuffix tells you which data branch it serves. Find that branch in the inventory, then use its complete olcDatabase name. The numeric index belongs to this supplied name; do not assume that every data backend is number 1.

concepts.title: Send a change record to the configuration entry
concepts.text: An LDIF Modify says which entry and attribute to change. Start with version: 1, put the configuration entry after dn, then write changetype: modify and replace: olcAccess. This replaces that entry’s entire access list. Real directory configuration is changed through LDAP operations; directly editing slapd.d backing files is not the workflow taught here.

concepts.title: Values start with to, and order still matters
concepts.text: Each olcAccess value contains a to selection followed by by caller clauses. Omit the static access keyword used in the previous lesson. Repeat olcAccess for each rule. Readback adds {0}, {1} and later order tags automatically; an explicit complete indexed list is also supported. Specific rules must still precede a catch-all. In the worked LDIF below, each continued by line starts with two spaces. LDIF removes the first space and joins the rest to the previous value, keeping a space between its words.

concepts.title: Verify the change and its effect
concepts.text: Apply and try request shows which configuration entry changed, then the selected contact request’s actual result. An allowed own update can still work under an old overbroad policy, so it cannot prove success by itself. Check the other database remains unchanged, try protected writes, and use the complete check across all samples. Each trial starts from its original sample settings and directory.

  by dn.exact="uid=desk,ou=Service,dc=deployment-workshop,dc=test" write
  by self write
  by * none
olcAccess: to dn.subtree="ou=People,dc=deployment-workshop,dc=test" attrs=mail
  by self write
  by * none
olcAccess: to *
  by * none
-
worked.explanation: The dn names the configuration entry. Each olcAccess line is one complete ordered rule; replace sets the whole list, not just the last line. These workshop names differ from the assignment. The two-space continuations keep the same values while making each caller clause readable; they are real LDIF syntax, not visual soft wrapping.

goal: Extend a directory schema and prove which entry data it permits.
context: Builds on LDAP entry names, fields and directory configuration. The editor applies simulated schema Add records; you do not prepare or alter a real server.

concepts.title: A schema describes fields and entry types
concepts.text: An attribute is a named field, such as cn. An attribute type defines which values that field accepts. An object class lists the fields an entry requires or allows. Each definition has a numeric OID and can have a short NAME used in entries. These workshop OIDs use a reserved documentation branch, not a production namespace.

concepts.title: Format, comparison and number of values are separate rules
concepts.text: SYNTAX defines the value format. Directory String is text; this model accepts printable ASCII. Integer uses whole-number text such as 7 or -3, without a plus sign, leading zeros or negative zero. EQUALITY defines comparison: caseExactMatch preserves letter case while ignoring repeated/outer spaces; integerMatch compares valid integers. SINGLE-VALUE limits a field to one value. Without it, several distinct values are allowed.

concepts.title: Required fields belong to the object class
concepts.text: SUP person inherits required cn and sn fields. MUST workshopBadge adds a required badge; MAY allows optional uid and workshopPoints fields. MUST does not itself limit a field to one value, so the badge attribute also needs SINGLE-VALUE. The class is STRUCTURAL: each entry must follow one structural inheritance chain. A valid entry can list both person and the custom class because they belong to that same chain.

concepts.title: Add the schema, then test real entry data
concepts.text: A schema Add creates cn=workshop below cn=schema,cn=config with objectClass: olcSchemaConfig. olcAttributeTypes carries the field definitions; olcObjectClasses carries the class definition. Define dependencies before their users. Schema applies across the modeled directory, unlike a backend access list. The lab supplies editing rights. Use the editor rather than changing slapd.d files.

worked.label: Choose the value format
worked.explanation: These registered syntax OIDs go after SYNTAX. The numeric identifier selects a value format; EQUALITY separately names its comparison rule. New field and class OIDs use the supplied documentation branch.

goal: Repair the schema and filter so a consumer selects the right people.
context: Builds on custom schema definitions and parenthesized filters. Work in the native schema editor and filter field; no real directory or server is prepared.

concepts.title: Value format and comparison answer different questions
concepts.text: SYNTAX determines whether a value has the right format. EQUALITY determines which valid values count as the same. Two text fields can use different equality rules: a team label may ignore letter case while a state code preserves it. Keep field names, OIDs and the person inheritance intact.

concepts.title: Case-exact text still ignores insignificant spaces
concepts.text: caseIgnoreMatch treats Kelp and KELP as equal. caseExactMatch distinguishes active from Active. Both supported text rules ignore outer spaces and collapse repeated spaces inside a value; case-exact does not mean byte-for-byte comparison. This activity supports printable ASCII, not complete Unicode preparation.

concepts.title: A filter tests the actual stored values
concepts.text: Write a parenthesized filter in the Filter field. & means every child condition must be True; | means at least one must be True. Equality on a multi-valued team field succeeds if any team value matches. A known but missing field does not match.

concepts.title: Undefined is different from False
concepts.text: An unknown field, a missing equality rule or an invalid assertion can make a comparison Undefined. Only True selects an entry. NOT reverses True and False but keeps Undefined; it cannot turn a typo into a correct exclusion. Run a sample to inspect actual results, then check every roster and required rule.

worked.label: Choose the comparison behavior
worked.value:
Field           Requirement                  EQUALITY
workshopTeam    Kelp equals KELP             caseIgnoreMatch
workshopState   active differs from Active   caseExactMatch
worked.explanation: The fields share Directory String syntax but compare letters differently. These workshop names and values are separate from the assignment.

goal: Restore a removable recovery path that works without the internal disk while preserving normal startup.
requirements: Repair the x64 default loader on the supplied removable EFI partition /dev/vdb1.
With /dev/vda unavailable, reach the Recovery system UUID 7240d4ce-f757-4103-be48-d903f6e7e9c9 with the supplied 7.0 kernel, initially read-only root and rescue.target.
Keep ordinary Linux startup through Boot0010. Preserve the original firmware entries, BootOrder and all files outside the removable default loader.
Choose Test recovery paths after your final change.
context: Build on the LPIC-1 named EFI loader lesson. The supplied rescue environment has already mounted both devices. The recovery test temporarily treats the internal disk as unavailable, then reads the removable device's default x64 path.

concepts.title: Select the default application
concepts.text: Selecting the removable device uses the x64 default application path inside its EFI partition. An ordinary named entry in BootOrder still controls normal startup. The supplied grub-install --removable form writes the default path without changing the normal order.

concepts.title: Follow the dependency beyond the loader
concepts.text: The EFI file starts GRUB. GRUB then needs its configured boot directory, menu, kernel and initial RAM filesystem. The menu's root UUID must identify a filesystem that is still available. Copying a menu can preserve an old internal root UUID.

concepts.title: Verify normal and recovery startup
concepts.text: Test recovery paths checks the current normal boot and a second startup with the internal disk unavailable. Repair the removable path, then read both results. Preserve the original entries and unrelated files.

worked.label: Inspect both possible boot directories
worked.explanation: The copied and recovery directories both live on removable storage. Their menus ask for different root UUIDs. Only the recovery menu points to the root on the removable device.

worked.label: Observe the copied-menu failure
worked.explanation: Run as one command, then test. The default application and menu are present, but the copied menu asks for the internal root.

worked.label: Install using the independent recovery directory
worked.explanation: Run as one command, then choose Test recovery paths. Recovery reaches its own root and ordinary startup stays available through Boot0024.

practice.title: Test the current recovery path
practice.action: Choose Test recovery paths. Run lsblk -o NAME,TYPE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINTS and inspect the supplied directories.
practice.observe: Read the normal startup result and the first blocked recovery stage, if there is one.

practice.title: Try the copied menu
practice.action: Open Worked practice and insert the command using /workshop/copied-boot. Run it and choose Test recovery paths.
practice.observe: The boot directory and images are available. The selected root UUID still needs the missing disk.

practice.title: Repair the dependency
practice.action: Read the supplied recovery grub/grub.cfg. Insert or type the installation using /workshop/recovery-boot, run it, and test both paths.
practice.observe: The separate recovery root and rescue target now work. Normal Boot0024 and its original order stay available.

practice.title: Verify the handover
practice.action: Check the normal and recovery outcomes and inspect BootOrder. If you rerun a different installation, test again.
practice.observe: The current results must show both paths and preserved firmware records.

review.introduction: Native Introduction shows the default EFI path, the root dependency, and the complete wrapped worked commands.
review.example: Native practice distinguishes unavailable boot directory and unavailable root before both paths pass. The assignment stays separate.
review.assignment: Native Assignment presents both checks without a starter answer. Retry clears stale success, and the narrow Light view at 200% shows both outcomes beside the console controls.

goal: Start an inspection system with a temporary GRUB edit while preserving normal startup.
requirements: Choose the supplied inspection entry for the 6.14 kernel.
Edit its temporary linux line to use the Inspection root and start it read-only.
Request rescue.target for this boot.
Choose Boot once. Confirm the edited handoff and the later ordinary startup from the saved menu.
context: Build on GRUB menu and removable recovery practice. Both kernel and root inventories are supplied. GRUB has already reached its saved menu.

concepts.title: Choose an entry that has the right images
concepts.text: A GRUB menu entry names the kernel and the initial RAM filesystem that helps it find the system disk. Select the entry for the kernel you need. The first menu item can still be the ordinary default.

concepts.title: Edit the arguments for one boot
concepts.text: The linux line names the kernel followed by its arguments. root=UUID= identifies the system filesystem and ro requests an initially read-only mount. In GRUB, e opens a menu entry for editing and Ctrl-X boots the edited entry. In this exercise, choose an entry and use Boot once.

concepts.title: Compare the two boot attempts
concepts.text: Use systemd.unit=rescue.target to ask Linux to start in rescue mode on the edited boot. This simulation stops at the init handoff and reports the request. The later ordinary boot starts from the saved menu, so it keeps its default and original arguments.

worked.label: Choose the inspection entry and observe its failure
worked.explanation: Boot once with the saved line. The kernel and its matching initramfs are available, but the old root UUID belongs to no supplied filesystem.

worked.label: Replace the outdated root request and keep it read-only
worked.explanation: Replace the old root=UUID= argument. With the correct UUID, the kernel can mount the Inspection root.

worked.label: Request rescue for this boot
worked.explanation: Add this argument to the same linux line and boot again. The edited boot requests rescue; the later ordinary boot still uses the saved default.

practice.title: Select the inspection entry
practice.action: Choose maple inspection from the supplied menu.
practice.observe: Compare its kernel path and the saved default. The selected entry is only for this boot.

practice.title: Test the root and repair it
practice.action: Choose Boot once. Compare the old root UUID with the supplied roots, replace it with the Inspection root UUID, then boot once again.
practice.observe: The original line cannot find its root. After replacing the UUID, Linux can reach init.

practice.title: Request rescue
practice.action: Keep ro and add systemd.unit=rescue.target to the linux line. Choose Boot once.
practice.observe: The edited boot requests rescue. The later ordinary boot still requests multi-user startup.

practice.title: Compare both outcomes
practice.action: Read Edited boot and Later ordinary boot. Open See boot stages to inspect the two selections.
practice.observe: The changed arguments apply only to the edited boot.

review.introduction: Native Introduction teaches selection and kernel arguments before the worked example. The revised two-column values wrap and show the complete practice UUID.
review.example: Native practice distinguishes missing root, successful handoff with the wrong target, and both correct outcomes. The revised editor wraps one command and shows the first blocked stage without repeated pending checks.
review.assignment: Native Assignment uses different kernel and root values, accepts an alternate argument order, clears stale success, and displays both handoffs and the full edited command at narrow 200% Light.

goal: Repair the startup check in a temporary rescue session and verify ordinary startup.
requirements: Use a simulated rescue session while repairing the supplied startup configuration.
Repair the saved startup check in /etc/ridge/startup.conf so it publishes ready-east.
Verify an ordinary startup starts ridge-app.service on the supplied port 9143.
Leave the current recovery tools available and preserve the saved default, unit files and other configuration.
context: Review required service jobs and one-time GRUB target selection. This exercise begins with the Linux handoff complete.

concepts.title: A target groups startup jobs
concepts.text: A target is a named group of units. A required job can stop its target from being reached. Here, the ordinary target needs a startup check before its application.

concepts.title: Use a recovery target for one boot
concepts.text: The temporary recovery choice uses the supplied rescue target and its own required jobs. It does not change the saved ordinary default. Compare both startup reports to see which units actually ran.

concepts.title: Repair the saved cause and verify ordinary startup
concepts.text: The configuration editor changes a saved sample file. A later startup uses that text. Check work tests the saved ordinary path separately while leaving the current recovery session available.

worked.label: Observe the blocked ordinary path
worked.explanation: The required startup check fails. Its dependent application and ordinary target do not reach a working state.

worked.label: Start the supplied recovery jobs
worked.explanation: The rescue target has its own required jobs. The saved default stays multi-user.target.

worked.label: Repair and test the saved path
worked.explanation: Save this practice configuration and check it. The ordinary path can start while the current rescue session remains active.

practice.title: Observe the failed startup
practice.action: Choose Start ordinary session and read the first failed job.
practice.observe: The ordinary target depends on a check that reads the saved startup configuration.

practice.title: Start recovery and save the repair
practice.action: Choose Start recovery session. Inspect the startup configuration, fix its key and save the editor.
practice.observe: Recovery jobs are available while the saved default remains ordinary.

practice.title: Compare the repaired outcomes
practice.action: Check the example. Try Start ordinary session and then return to rescue with Start recovery session.
practice.observe: The repaired ordinary path can start. Returning to rescue still does not change the default.

review.introduction: Native Introduction teaches which required jobs start in each target and demonstrates a working repair. Editor and terminal reference details are optional.
review.example: Native guided practice shows a single current action and actual failed and successful startup jobs. Worked assistance stays optional and the independent draft remains separate.
review.assignment: Native Assignment uses different fixtures, accepts an equivalent configuration, identifies the actual wrong value and blocked application, and verifies both outcomes at 150% Light and 200% Dark.

goal: Compare actual CPU windows and runnable work before publishing a measured report.
context: Review Linux command input and processes.

concepts.title: A report describes a time window
concepts.text: A busy moment can be hidden inside a quiet average. vmstat without an interval reports CPU and activity averages since boot. In vmstat 1 3, 1 is the interval in seconds and 3 is the total number of rows: the first since-boot row plus two one-second interval rows.

concepts.title: Read running work separately from waiting
concepts.text: us is application CPU time, including nice-priority work. sy is kernel and interrupt work. gu is guest execution; it is zero in these recordings. Add us + sy + gu for executing work. id is idle, wa is I/O-wait accounting and st is stolen time; keep those separate. These percentages are normalized across the supplied CPUs.

concepts.title: Processes and memory are snapshots
concepts.text: r counts runnable processes: those running or waiting for CPU time. b counts processes blocked for I/O. Unlike CPU percentages, these columns describe the instant at the end of each row. A large r or wa alone does not prove a bottleneck.

concepts.title: Replay first, then attach the row
concepts.text: Choose an Observation, type the command in Command and select Run command. The simulator replays supplied samples immediately; it does not wait or inspect your computer. Choose the appropriate Result row before using Attach row beside a report value.

concepts.title: Compare the same-sized intervals
concepts.text: Inspect each one-second interval in the requested range. Choose the rows with the highest and lowest displayed executing-work totals; ties are equally valid. Type the measured number, not a cumulative tick counter. Check report explains wrong rows, blank values and incorrect calculations.

requirements: Use the boot-a recording to compare every one-second interval wholly inside 3000–5000 ms. Report the highest and lowest executing-work percentages and the largest runnable-process reading from those interval rows.
Executing work is the displayed us + sy + gu total. Attach an actual interval row to each claim; do not use the first since-boot row. Enter whole numbers with the units already shown.
Run commands against the supplied recording, then choose Check report. Equivalent supported commands and tied eligible intervals are valid.

practice.title: Replay the worked interval
practice.action: At trial-a · 6.000 s, type vmstat 1 3 in Command and choose Run command.
practice.observe: Row 1 is since boot. Rows 2/3 describe 6000–7000 and 7000–8000 ms; their executing-work totals are 45% and 10%.

practice.title: Build a report from specific rows
practice.action: Choose Row 2, attach it beside Highest executing work and Largest runnable-process reading, then enter 45 and 5. Choose Row 3 for Lowest executing work and enter 10. Select Check example report.
practice.observe: Each report row names its evidence. Attaching Row 1 instead explains why a boot average cannot establish an interval result.

practice.title: Try an honest alternate command
practice.action: Choose trial-a · 7.000 s and run vmstat -S K 1 2. Attach its interval row to the quiet claim. Then change the claim to 45 and check again.
practice.observe: The alternate command reports the same quiet 10%. A wrong entered value clears the previous check and leaves the other correct rows intact.

worked.label: Compare the worked windows
worked.explanation: The first row is a since-boot average; compare rows 2 and 3.

worked.label: A tempting ineligible value
worked.explanation: This average covers the whole boot, not the two requested worked intervals. Their highest executing-work total is 45%.

worked.label: Busiest worked interval
worked.explanation: Use us + sy + gu from the interval row.

worked.label: Quiet worked interval
worked.explanation: Use the same one-second duration.

worked.label: Runnable work
worked.explanation: r is instantaneous; it is not a CPU percentage.

review.introduction: CPU first/interval definitions, executing-work sum and snapshot r/b are taught before the different worked45/10% example; actual obs-0-introduction/worked inspected at100dark.
review.example: Actual separate trial-a native terminal run, Row2/3 attachments and45/10/5 report pass; deliberate wrong value yields local feedback, leaves assignment blank. Actual populated100dark and200Light controls inspected.
