goal: Use activity rates and available memory to avoid diagnosing pressure from a footprint alone.
context: Builds on the preceding recorded-host investigation; all new measurement concepts are introduced below.

concepts.title: A footprint is different from activity
concepts.text: swpd is how much swap space is allocated now, in KiB for this subset. si and so measure swap transferred in and out per second. Previously swapped pages may remain allocated when current transfer rates are zero. High swpd alone does not establish current memory pressure.

concepts.title: Use interval rates for current activity
concepts.text: vmstat 1 4 produces one since-boot row and three one-second interval rows. Compare si/so in those interval rows. bi/bo are whole KiB per second of block input/output; they are not swap-only counters or proof that a device is saturated.

concepts.title: Available memory is not simply free memory
concepts.text: cat /proc/meminfo reads this recording’s virtual memory snapshot. MemFree is unused memory. MemAvailable estimates memory available to applications without swapping. Cached and SReclaimable are separate fields; vmstat cache combines them. Do not replace MemAvailable with total minus free.

concepts.title: Calculate the allocated amount
concepts.text: In the virtual meminfo, subtract SwapFree from SwapTotal to calculate allocated swap. All kB values here mean 1024-byte KiB. The snapshot at the selected Observation is instantaneous; it does not measure a transfer rate.

concepts.title: Compare the burst with the recovery
concepts.text: Measure every eligible interval, then inspect the final snapshot. A report can show allocated swap still present alongside zero current swap-out and available memory. That supports a narrower statement than claiming the host is out of memory; real diagnosis needs additional evidence.

requirements: Inspect paging-a over 60000–63000 ms. Find the highest and lowest one-second swap-out rates, using actual interval rows as evidence.
At 63000 ms, report allocated swap and MemAvailable. Use the final snapshot; allocated swap is SwapTotal minus SwapFree, while MemAvailable is supplied directly.

Enter whole KiB/s or KiB as labeled, attach the corresponding evidence and choose Check report. Any tied minimum-rate interval is valid. The task asks for measured facts, not an unsupported diagnosis.

practice.title: Measure the worked paging burst
practice.action: At paging-practice · 120.000 s, run vmstat 1 4. Compare the three interval so readings.
practice.observe: The first interval has 256 KiB/s of swap-out; the next two have 0. The since-boot average describes a different period.

practice.title: Attach activity and snapshot evidence
practice.action: Attach interval rows for peak/minimum so and enter 256/0. Choose 123.000 s, run cat /proc/meminfo, attach the snapshot to the remaining two claims and enter 524288/786432. Check example report.
practice.observe: The report distinguishes rate units from allocated/available KiB. Both zero-rate intervals are legitimate evidence.

practice.title: Test the common misconception
practice.action: Change the lowest current swap-out claim to 524288, then check again. Restore 0. Try a different tied zero-rate interval.
practice.observe: Feedback explains that allocated swap is not a transfer rate. Switching to another valid zero-rate interval is accepted after checking.

worked.label: Replay three worked intervals
worked.explanation: Start the paging-practice recording at 120.000 s.

worked.label: Worked swap-out activity
worked.explanation: The last two intervals tie for the minimum.

worked.label: Inspect the final snapshot
worked.explanation: Choose 123.000 s before running this command.

worked.label: Worked allocated swap
worked.value:
SwapTotal: 2097152 KiB
SwapFree: 1572864 KiB
difference: 524288 KiB
worked.explanation: Allocated space remains even when so is zero.

worked.label: Worked available memory
worked.explanation: Do not substitute MemFree or infer pressure from swpd alone.

review.introduction: Allocated swap versus si/so activity and free versus available memory are explicitly taught; worked table separates256/0KiB/s from524288/786432KiB. Actual obs-1-introduction/worked inspected.
review.example: Actual paging-practice command replay, final virtual meminfo and independent evidence attachments pass. Guided instructions name real controls and experiments; no assignment credit. Actual practice and checked report inspected.
review.assignment: Actual blank paging-a task/report and wrong rate feedback inspected. Native assignment passes, edits invalidate current success, tied minimum evidence is covered by content tests, final snapshot and protected other attempts survive selected reset/save.

goal: Recover useful observations without joining incompatible boots or reporting the wrong period.
context: Builds on the preceding recorded-host investigation; all new measurement concepts are introduced below.

concepts.title: Recognize that the clock restarted
concepts.text: This recording contains an old boot followed by a new boot. Uptime returns to a smaller number after restart. The Observation picker shows both the boot label and time: a matching number alone is not a matching source.

concepts.title: Do not average across the restart
concepts.text: A counter difference needs one continuous source and an increasing time. Replaying a request across different boots fails instead of inventing a rate. A real monitoring process does not continue through its machine’s reboot; this simulator is replaying recorded observations.

concepts.title: Start a new measurement on the new boot
concepts.text: Select the first observation from the requested new boot, then use a finite vmstat request covering its samples. The first row is still a since-boot average, even when it belongs to the correct boot. Use interval rows for the requested peaks.

concepts.title: Interpret block throughput narrowly
concepts.text: bo is the rate of block output in KiB/s over that row’s interval. A higher rate establishes more output, not by itself an overloaded disk or high latency. Attach the actual peak bo row independently of the CPU peak; they need not coincide in other recordings.

concepts.title: Keep the final snapshot separate
concepts.text: Use cat /proc/meminfo at the requested final new-boot Observation for MemAvailable. The final snapshot and earlier activity intervals describe different kinds of evidence. Publish only claims supported by the correct boot, interval and units.

requirements: Report only handover-new, using all eligible one-second intervals inside 1000–5000 ms. Find the highest executing-work percentage and the highest block-output rate.
Report MemAvailable at the final 5000 ms post-restart snapshot. Attach actual measurements for all three claims; do not mix handover-old averages or rows into the report.
Use the supported terminal and report controls, then Check report. You may avoid an incompatible request or recover after its diagnostic. A failed command is never usable evidence.

practice.title: Observe a safe refusal
practice.action: At trial-old · 3.000 s, run vmstat 1 3. Read the command diagnostic, then select trial-new · 1.000 s.
practice.observe: The old/new boot boundary prevents one continuous measurement. A failed command cannot be attached as evidence; no host command was attempted.

practice.title: Recover a coherent worked report
practice.action: Run vmstat 1 5 from trial-new · 1.000 s. Attach its first interval row to the two peak claims and enter 60/512. At 5.000 s run cat /proc/meminfo, attach the snapshot and enter 786432. Check example report.
practice.observe: Every claim names a new-boot source. The report passes without using an old-boot or since-boot activity row.

practice.title: Challenge the evidence rather than the number
practice.action: Run vmstat on trial-old · 3.000 s and try attaching that row to a peak claim. Check, then restore the valid new-boot interval evidence.
practice.observe: A plausible-looking value does not make another boot or a boot-average row valid evidence. The unaffected correct report rows stay intact.

worked.label: An incompatible request
worked.value: Old boot 3000 ms → new boot 5000 ms
worked.explanation: A request bridging the restart is refused; it does not yield partial fake readings.

worked.label: Replay the new boot
worked.explanation: Five rows cover the initial average and four valid intervals.

worked.label: Worked post-restart peaks
worked.explanation: Choose the appropriate interval row for each metric.

worked.label: Worked final snapshot
worked.explanation: Use the new-boot virtual meminfo, not an earlier snapshot.

goal: Choose a current growth window and an affordable upgrade that keeps space available throughout the planning horizon.
context: Builds on recorded-host measurements and filesystem capacity. This activity plans a supplied volume; it does not resize your disks.

concepts.title: Occupied space is a stock, not a transfer counter
concepts.text: Each observation states how much space is occupied on that day. A later reading minus an earlier reading gives net growth over the days between them. Day numbers belong to this recording, not your computer’s calendar. Planning begins at the latest observation.

concepts.title: Choose a window that matches the current operating period
concepts.text: A long average may hide a recent increase. In the worked volume, day 0 to day 5 grows from 20 to 25 GiB:1 GiB/day. From day 5 to day 12 it grows from 25 to 39 GiB:14 GiB over 7 days, or 2 GiB/day. Choose both dates deliberately; the graph shows the selected projection.

concepts.title: Keep capacity, occupancy and reserve separate
concepts.text: Capacity is the total volume size. Occupancy is what the data already uses. Reserve is space that must stay unused. In the worked volume,80 GiB capacity minus 8 GiB reserve gives a 72 GiB safe occupancy limit. Reaching that limit still retains the reserve; exceeding it fails.

concepts.title: Allow time for an upgrade to arrive
concepts.text: A quote lists its final capacity, lead time and fictional cost. Order day plus lead days gives arrival day. Capacity becomes available at the beginning of that simulated day, before its workload is added. The model is deliberately exact; real procurement and demand have uncertainty.

concepts.title: A projection and a workload test answer different questions
concepts.text: The dashed projection assumes your chosen growth rate continues. Test plan instead replays every published workload and extra arrival, checking each day. It does not use the projection as a substitute for those cases. An affordable, eventually large volume can still run short before arrival.

concepts.title: Use the units shown beside each control
concepts.text: The planner stores KiB:1 GiB equals 1048576 KiB. For the worked 8 GiB reserve, enter 8388608. Observation and quote tables also show GiB for readability. Dates are whole recording-day numbers; costs are fictional credits, not actual purchasing advice.

worked.label: Worked growth window
worked.explanation: Both dates describe the newer operating period. Day 10 to day 12 gives the same rate and is also a valid two-day window.

worked.label: Worked safe limit
worked.explanation: The 8 GiB reserve is 8388608 KiB, independent of the quote’s cost.

worked.label: One workable quote
worked.explanation: An order on day 12 arrives on day 16; this is a worked example, not the assignment’s quote decision.

worked.label: Test the whole horizon
worked.explanation: The busier case includes a 6 GiB addition on day 16. Every case must retain reserve before and after arrival.

worked.label: A larger quote can still fail
worked.explanation: Its capacity cases can pass while the overall plan fails its budget. Read the policy results as well as individual cases.

practice.title: Choose and inspect the worked window
practice.action: Set Growth window start to day 5 and Growth window end to day 12. Read the observed points and dashed projection. Try day 10 to day 12 as an alternative.
practice.observe: Both recent windows give 2 GiB/day. Choosing day 0 instead includes the earlier, slower period and fails the requested-window policy when tested.

practice.title: Test a complete worked plan
practice.action: Choose the standard quote, enter Order day 12 and Reserve 8388608 KiB, then select Test example plan. Read both the policy results and every workload result.
practice.observe: This plan stays within 90 credits and retains the 8 GiB reserve throughout all three worked workloads. The projected line is an assumption; the tested curves use each supplied workload.

practice.title: Separate case success from overall success
practice.action: Choose costly and test again. Inspect the budget result even if every workload passes. Return to standard, then try ordering later and observe when a workload first loses reserve.
practice.observe: Editing removes the previous test result. Restoring valid values needs a fresh test; eventual capacity does not erase an earlier failure.

requirements: Use the report-volume observations from day 7 onward, including the latest day 14. Compare at least 3 days of that operating period when choosing a growth window.
Leave at least 10485760 KiB (10 GiB) free on every simulated day through day 34. Order from day 14 onward and stay within 120 fictional credits.

Choose a supplied quote and test the complete plan against every listed workload, including its extra arrivals. Preserve the existing data; neither a later upgrade nor a passing individual case excuses an earlier reserve failure.

goal: Repair an inherited capacity forecast and deliver a plan that survives known imports before and after the upgrade arrives.
context: Uses the preceding trend-planning lesson. The existing plan deliberately includes an old window and a slow quote for you to diagnose.

concepts.title: A cleanup changes occupancy once
concepts.text: The worked volume falls from 54 GiB on day 24 to 36 GiB on day 25 after cleanup. That is a real drop in stored data, not proof that usage will keep falling. Capacity snapshots can decrease; they are not cumulative CPU or I/O counters.

concepts.title: Measure the period after the change
concepts.text: After cleanup the worked observations are 36 GiB on day 25,37 GiB on day 26 and 39 GiB on day 28. Recent growth is 1 GiB/day. A window starting before cleanup mixes two different operating conditions and gives misleading net growth.

concepts.title: Include events that an average cannot predict
concepts.text: A scheduled import adds its stated amount once, on its supplied day. Each workload also adds its daily amount. The worked busy-import case adds 12 GiB on day 31 on top of 1.5 GiB/day. A quiet-looking linear projection cannot cancel that known arrival.

concepts.title: Check the days before delivery
concepts.text: In the worked plan, bulk-expansion arrives on day 34 when ordered on day 28. The busy import already needs more than the original 60 GiB capacity minus 6 GiB reserve on day 31. Its larger eventual volume cannot repair that earlier failure. The faster 80 GiB quote arrives on day 30.

concepts.title: Repair the plan and test all constraints again
concepts.text: Use recent observations, a possible order date, enough final capacity and an affordable quote. Test example plan reports each workload and the overall policy result separately. Changing any planning field clears the previous result; changing only the displayed workload does not change the plan.

concepts.title: Keep the forecast honest
concepts.text: A straight line is an assumption based on the selected window. The simulator tests only its published finite cases, not every possible future. It performs no real order, file cleanup, monitoring or disk change. Quote timing and daily loads are simplified day-boundary events.

worked.label: Identify the one-off change
worked.explanation: Do not extend this cleanup drop as ongoing negative growth.

worked.label: Use a recent window
worked.explanation: Day 26 to day 28 is also valid. Both include the latest observation.

worked.label: A tempting but late plan
worked.explanation: The busy-import case first fails reserve on day 31, before that delivery.

worked.label: One workable repair
worked.explanation: 90 credits fits the 100-credit budget. Enter 6291456 KiB to retain 6 GiB of free space.

worked.label: Why every case matters
worked.explanation: It can retain reserve for some workloads while failing the busy import. Overall success requires every case and the policy checks to pass.

practice.title: Diagnose the inherited worked plan
practice.action: Select Test example plan before editing. Read the old-window feedback and locate the first failing day in busy-import. Compare the quote’s arrival day with the import day.
practice.observe: The existing plan has two independent problems: it mixes the cleanup into its growth window and brings capacity online too late.

practice.title: Repair evidence and delivery
practice.action: Set Growth window start to day 25 and end to day 28. Choose rapid-expansion, keep Order day 28 and Reserve 6291456 KiB, then test again.
practice.observe: The newer window gives 1 GiB/day. Capacity arrives on day 30 and every supplied case retains reserve. The assignment uses different dates, volumes and quotes.

practice.title: Explore a valid alternative and a partial failure
practice.action: Try urgent-expansion or the recent day 26–28 window. Then choose small-expansion and test all cases. Restore your preferred valid plan and test again.
practice.observe: Equivalent affordable repairs pass. A passing selected workload is still only one part of the overall result; the failing workload names the day and space shortfall.

requirements: Repair the inherited archive-volume plan using post-cleanup observations from day 27 onward. Include the latest day 30 and at least 2 days of that period; a one-off cleanup is not continuing negative growth.
Retain at least 12582912 KiB (12 GiB) free on every simulated day through day 44. Orders start on day 30 or later; the total quote must fit 160 fictional credits.

Account for every published import case and the quote’s arrival date. Keep current data. Use Test plan after repairs; a valid plan may use any supplied affordable quote and date that satisfies all cases.

goal: Notify current sessions and future logins about the archive maintenance window while preserving the existing pre-login notice.
context: Builds on editing virtual files and understanding local users. No previous wall or shutdown knowledge is assumed.

concepts.title: A person can have several working terminals
concepts.text: A session is one active login, often a terminal window. who lists the supplied usernames, terminals and recorded login times. Casey has two terminals here; notifying one user name does not prove every working terminal received the message.

concepts.title: Choose the channel by when the message is needed
concepts.text: The login process traditionally shows /etc/issue before its prompt and /etc/motd after a successful login. Edit motd for future successful logins. Existing sessions do not reread that file automatically. This exercise supplies local terminal behaviour; it does not configure an SSH banner.

concepts.title: Make the handover details checkable
concepts.text: The team uses four labelled lines: Service, Starts, Ends and Contact. Starts and Ends use the recording’s same-day HH:MM clock, such as 18:00. This is the exercise’s bulletin format, not a Linux requirement. Reordered labels and supported case/spacing work; the check does not interpret arbitrary prose.

concepts.title: Send a live message with wall
concepts.text: Standard input means the text a command receives. Select Live message · wall input and type the bulletin in the composer, then type wall in Simulated terminal and choose Run command. Successful wall prints no normal output. The separate simulator receipts show which supplied terminals received the text.

concepts.title: Save, send and check are different actions
concepts.text: Save file applies the selected login file. Run command applies a supported virtual command; it does not grade the assignment. Check notices compares saved messages, latest live receipts and any requested plan. Unsent composer edits or unsaved files need attention before a check can pass.

concepts.title: Read the recording clock
concepts.text: date +%H:%M prints the supplied host’s simulated hour and minute. These lessons use recording UTC, not your desktop clock or time zone. The optional clock activity can make an upcoming notice expire; it changes only this exercise.

practice.observe: The saved post-login preview changes, but saving alone does not notify active terminals.

practice.observe: who lists the supplied sessions. wall has no standard output; inspect Live delivery observations for actual receipts.

Save the approved post-login notice in /etc/motd and deliver its full current details to every supplied terminal. Preserve the original /etc/issue bytes.
Do not schedule a restart: this is a notice-only request. Save changed files and send edited live input before Check notices, while the window is still upcoming.

goal: Repair a conflicting restart announcement and schedule, then leave a consistent handover for current sessions and future logins.
context: Uses live/login notices from the preceding lesson and a deliberately conflicting inherited schedule.

concepts.title: Check a pending schedule as well as the notice text
concepts.text: A convincing bulletin does not prove the system’s pending time agrees. Read Current simulated state and use date +%H:%M for the recording clock. This inherited plan announces an earlier window and schedules the restart too early.

concepts.title: Cancel before replacing this simulated request
concepts.text: shutdown -c cancels a pending restart. It does not rewrite motd, and its cancellation message is not a complete replacement bulletin. This finite subset requires cancellation before rescheduling; it does not claim that every host version has identical replacement rules.

concepts.title: Calculate a relative delay from the current clock
concepts.text: shutdown -r +30 schedules a restart 30 simulated minutes from now. In the worked recording it is 16:00 and the approved start is 16:30. If you advance five minutes first, +25 reaches the same deadline. The task also requires at least 20 minutes remaining when you check.

concepts.title: Correct both audiences after a plan changes
concepts.text: Future logins need the corrected motd bulletin; active sessions need the latest full live announcement. A shutdown cancellation or default schedule broadcast does not include every required Service, Starts, Ends and Contact line. Send the corrected composer with wall after rescheduling. The four labelled lines are this exercise’s bulletin format, not a Linux requirement.

concepts.title: Notice the ordinary-login gate before the deadline
concepts.text: Five minutes before a pending restart, this model blocks ordinary successful logins. Cancelling removes that pending gate. Root/PAM exceptions and repeated countdown broadcasts are outside scope. Advancing to the deadline ends only this recorded activity, so inspect timing before advancing.

concepts.title: Verify a coherent current handover
concepts.text: Check notices reports the saved file, each terminal and the pending plan separately. A correct file cannot hide a missing live announcement or wrong deadline. The original issue notice must stay unchanged. Saving and sending different approved values, or leaving unsent edits, requires another repair/check.

goal: Turn a supplied source package into a correctly configured, tested virtual program while preserving the existing packaged copy.
context: Builds on archive navigation and package ownership. Source, configure, prefix and build targets are introduced here.

concepts.title: Start with the source ingredients
concepts.text: A source archive holds a project’s ingredients and instructions. Unpacking it creates a source directory. Building produces a program from the supplied project; installing later copies its declared outputs to their destinations. This lesson stops at a tested build.

concepts.title: Inspect before unpacking
concepts.text: tar -tf ARCHIVE lists members: -t means list and -f names the archive. tar -xf ARCHIVE -C DIRECTORY extracts: -x means unpack and -C chooses an existing directory. This activity supplies an uncompressed structured archive. /usr/src is a common source location, not a required home for every project.

concepts.title: Configure the package settings
concepts.text: Change into the unpacked directory with cd and read INSTALL. ./configure chooses this package’s settings and generates its Makefile/config.status. Here --prefix selects the intended installed location; --with-greeting selects the greeting. These greeting/uppercase options belong to this supplied package, not to every configure script. Quote a value containing spaces.

concepts.title: Build targets describe work and dependencies
concepts.text: A target is a named job in a Makefile. For this supplied project, make or make all builds the program. make check depends on that build, so it builds first if needed and runs two package self-checks. You do not need to type every possible target as a ritual. Exit status 0 means that command reported success; the task requirements are checked separately.

concepts.title: Run the copy you actually built
concepts.text: ./demo-hello Mira runs the example program in the current directory. Give one name; quote a name containing spaces. --version reports its package identity and --prefix reports its compiled-in prefix. A passing package self-check does not prove that you chose the settings requested by an assignment.

concepts.title: Know this activity’s boundary
concepts.text: All paths and programs here are virtual. The simulator models a supplied project and fixed build targets; it does not execute C, configure scripts or arbitrary Makefile recipes. It supplies accessible build paths. Real installations also depend on permissions and package ownership; those are separate skills.

worked.label: List the example archive
worked.explanation: Expected: demo-hello-1.0/ and its supplied instructions. Actual command output appears only after Run command.

worked.label: Unpack into an existing virtual directory
worked.explanation: Creates the example source tree. Non-verbose tar normally prints no output on success.

worked.label: Enter the source directory
worked.explanation: pwd and Current directory now identify this project. Read its INSTALL file before choosing settings.

worked.label: Configure different worked values
worked.explanation: The greeting and prefix differ from the assignment. This generates configuration; it does not install anything.

worked.label: Build and self-check
worked.explanation: The supplied check target builds its dependency and runs two package checks.

worked.label: Test a name
worked.explanation: Expected standard output: Greetings, Mira followed by a newline. Try a different name and observe it in the actual output.

worked.label: Inspect the compiled prefix
worked.explanation: Expected: /opt/demo. The program reports the settings of this particular build.

practice.title: Inspect and prepare the example
practice.action: Use the worked-command dropdown and Insert command, then Run command, for tar listing, extraction and cd. Run cat INSTALL in the source directory.
practice.observe: Source tree and Current directory identify the unpacked example. Non-verbose extraction can succeed with no standard output.

practice.title: Configure, build and test actual behavior
practice.action: Insert the example configure command and run it, then run make check. Run ./demo-hello Mira and ./demo-hello --prefix separately.
practice.observe: The build reports Greetings, Mira and /opt/demo. A different name produces a different greeting result.

practice.title: Check, then diagnose a changed setting
practice.action: Choose Check example build. Change the greeting to Howdy, with another configure command and run make check; check again. Restore the worked settings and retry.
practice.observe: Package self-checks can pass while the example’s requested greeting fails. Reconfigure and rebuild the requested values to repair it.

requirements: Use the supplied site-greet 2.3 source archive. Configure the package for prefix /opt/site-tools, greeting “Welcome,” and uppercase disabled. You may choose another virtual source directory; /usr/src is already available.

Produce a current build and run its current package self-check. The program must greet Alex and Sam Lee with the requested greeting and preserve name case; its version and compiled prefix must match the request.
Preserve the supplied existing packaged file and its mode. Choose Check build after inspecting the actual program results.

goal: Stage a complete supplied package without changing its compiled-in prefix or replacing the existing live program.
context: Uses the preceding build/check workflow. Staging roots and installation manifests are new in this lesson.

concepts.title: Keep the build and installed copies separate
concepts.text: The program in the source directory is the build copy. make install copies the supplied project’s declared program and README to installation paths. This project’s install target depends on the build; other projects may define different targets, so read INSTALL. Live means the existing installed copy that users would normally run.

concepts.title: Distinguish prefix from a staging root
concepts.text: For this package, prefix selects the final layout and is compiled into the program. DESTDIR is an extra temporary root used only while copying installation files. It does not change the prefix reported by the program. This lets you inspect a release before replacing a live installation.

concepts.title: Combine the two paths
concepts.text: In the worked example, prefix /opt/demo and staging root /practice/package put the program under /practice/package/opt/demo/bin/demo-stage. The README goes under the same combined root in share/doc/demo-stage. To locate staged files, prepend the staging root to the absolute installation path.

concepts.title: Protect the existing package
concepts.text: Omitting DESTDIR installs to the virtual live prefix and can replace the supplied existing program. The simulator makes those paths writable so the consequence is visible. It does not promise that real make is safe, atomic or integrated with a package manager.

concepts.title: Verify the staged program and documentation
concepts.text: Run the staged copy by its full path, rather than accidentally testing the build or live copy. Check different names, --version and --prefix. For this supplied project, install sets the executable to 0755 and README to 0644. Inspect virtual files to compare actual paths, bytes and modes.

concepts.title: Separate package checks from task completion
concepts.text: make check tests the current build. Check example installation or Check installation evaluates the requested configuration, staged behavior, documentation and preserved live file. One correct program case cannot hide a wrong destination or overwritten live copy.

worked.label: Worked layout
worked.explanation: The final prefix and temporary staging root have different jobs.

worked.label: Unpack the example
worked.explanation: Then enter /usr/src/demo-stage-1.2 and read INSTALL; these are example-specific values.

worked.label: Enter the example source directory
worked.explanation: Run configure from this directory, or use make -C for supported targets later.

worked.label: Configure the supplied project
worked.explanation: The intended installed prefix is /opt/demo; it is not the temporary staging path.

worked.label: Build and self-check
worked.explanation: This tests the current build. It does not copy anything into the staging tree.

worked.label: Stage the complete package
worked.explanation: Expected destinations include /practice/package/opt/demo/bin/demo-stage and its share/doc/demo-stage/README. Read the actual install output.

worked.label: Run the staged program
worked.explanation: Expected: Hi, Mira followed by a newline. This explicitly tests the staged copy.

worked.label: Check the prefix remains unchanged
worked.explanation: Expected: /opt/demo, without the temporary staging root.

practice.title: Prepare the worked build
practice.action: Use the worked-command dropdown and Insert command, then Run command, for the example tar, cd and configure commands separately. Finish with make check; read INSTALL if a target is unfamiliar.
practice.observe: The build uses /opt/demo and Hi,. No staged program exists merely because the build passes.

practice.title: Stage and inspect the actual copy
practice.action: Run make DESTDIR=/practice/package install. Read its actual destination list; run the staged program with Mira and --prefix. Open Inspect virtual files to read its README and modes.
practice.observe: Staged paths include the temporary root, while --prefix still reports /opt/demo. The existing live file remains unchanged.

practice.title: Check and explore another input
practice.action: Choose Check example installation. Run the staged program with a quoted two-word name, then inspect the build and staged paths again.

goal: Find and repair the mismatch between current project settings, an old build and an old staged release.
context: Uses both preceding lessons. The inherited project has updated settings but an old build and staged copy; this is intentional.

concepts.title: Compare three current facts
concepts.text: Configuration, build and staged copy are separate. This inherited project’s settings were updated after the earlier build and installation. Read Current simulated project, inspect config.status, and run the build and staged programs. A matching version number can coexist with wrong compiled settings. In these supplied programs, the uppercase option capitalizes the complete greeting line, including the name; disabling it preserves name case.

concepts.title: A changed configuration makes the old check stale
concepts.text: For this supplied project, changing configured settings makes an earlier build/check out of date. make check rebuilds its dependency if necessary, then checks that current build. This finite model tracks configuration identity; it is not a complete simulation of every real Makefile timestamp rule.

concepts.title: Rebuilding does not refresh an installed copy
concepts.text: After rebuilding, the source-directory program can be correct while a previously staged copy still says Earlier,. Installed copies keep their own compiled settings. Reinstall to the requested staging root before expecting that copy to change.

concepts.title: Keep the live installation outside the repair
concepts.text: Use the release’s staging root again when copying the repaired package. A correct staged greeting does not excuse replacing the unrelated live program. The activity’s independent checks compare the preserved file and each resulting program behavior.

concepts.title: Use a mistake to locate the broken link
concepts.text: If current settings pass but name cases fail, inspect the tested copy instead of repeatedly reconfiguring. If the build’s self-check passes but staged cases fail, rebuilding alone may be insufficient. Expected versus actual output is available beside failing cases; it does not execute another command for you.

concepts.title: Finish with independent verification
concepts.text: The requested settings, current package self-check, staged program cases, README and existing file must all agree. Unsupported shell syntax or commands fail explicitly. This activity remains a bounded supplied-project model, not general compiler, patching or source-editing coverage.

concepts.title: Separate three kinds of answer
concepts.text: An authoritative answer comes from this server’s own published zone. A recursive lookup fetches a name outside that zone; here it uses supplied offline data. A cached answer reuses external data already held by the simulator. Public access to your own names does not require offering all three services to everyone.

concepts.title: Read an address list
concepts.text: allow-query controls who may ask. allow-recursion controls new recursive work; allow-query-cache controls access to cached data. In this activity, a /24 list such as 192.0.2.0/24 matches all 192.0.2.x address values. A host without /prefix matches that one address. any means every simulated IPv4 client; none means no clients.

concepts.title: Write and apply an explicit configuration
concepts.text: Each list uses braces and semicolons: allow-query { any; };. Keep the supplied zone declaration and file name. This parser requires all five options explicitly; it does not guess BIND defaults. Save configuration changes the virtual file. Reload configuration applies the saved access rules; saving alone does not apply them.

concepts.title: Test both a new and an existing answer
concepts.text: A warm-cache test already has the external answer. Turning recursion off or restricting only allow-recursion can still expose it. Test a public name, a new external name and a cached external name from permitted and outside clients. Each grading case starts with its own stated empty or supplied cache; your assignment draft is not changed by the tests.

concepts.title: A lookup is smaller than a whole-zone copy
concepts.text: An ordinary query asks for one name/type. A zone transfer supplies a complete published zone to another client. Keeping ordinary queries public does not mean every client should receive a whole-zone copy. These are separate permissions.

concepts.title: Find the effective transfer rule
concepts.text: The options allow-transfer list supplies a global default. A zone’s own allow-transfer replaces that default for that zone. A broad zone override can reopen access even after the global default is narrowed. A single IPv4 host, or its equivalent /32, permits that one source address.

A different allowed client receives its own simulated data; it does not magically update the supplied secondary. Serial and record rows show whether the secondary changed. Saving/reloading policy alone does not copy a zone.

concepts.title: Keep the restriction honest

goal: Close a staff-only proxy leak while keeping the intended web requests working.
context: Builds on IPv4 prefixes, destination ports and the static-web unit. The supplied proxy is ready; no machine setup or network access is needed.

concepts.title: A proxy decides whether a request may pass
concepts.text: A client asks a proxy to contact a destination. This unit supplies the client address, HTTP method and destination port. The proxy is already running in the simulator; your task is its access policy, not installation. GET asks to retrieve something. A policy decision does not establish a real connection.

concepts.title: Name each test before using it
concepts.text: An ACL is a named yes/no test. acl staff src 172.20.4.0/24 tests the client address against that whole subnet. acl web port 8080 tests the destination port, not the client port. acl reads method GET tests the exact request method. Defining a test alone grants no access.

concepts.title: Combine tests, then stop at the first matching rule
concepts.text: http_access allow staff web reads permits a request only when all three named tests match. Multiple values inside one ACL are alternatives. Rules run from top to bottom; the first matching rule decides. Finish with http_access deny all to refuse every request you have not permitted.

concepts.title: Save, apply and verify are different actions
concepts.text: Editing changes your draft. Save configuration updates the virtual file. Check syntax checks whether the parser can read that saved file; it does not prove the access rules are right. Apply saved policy changes the current decisions. Check policy verifies both the applied and saved rules against the whole task.

worked.label: Workshop staff
worked.explanation: This address test matches the whole supplied staff prefix; neighbouring 172.20.3.x and 172.20.5.x clients do not match.

worked.label: Source test
worked.explanation: Name the staff address test.

worked.label: Destination test
worked.explanation: Only this workshop destination port is permitted.

worked.label: Method test
worked.explanation: Method names are case-sensitive.

worked.label: Permit rule
worked.explanation: All three tests must match together; an individual staff ACL does not grant access.

worked.label: Final rule
worked.explanation: A neighbouring client, a POST or a different destination port reaches this refusal.

practice.title: Narrow the workshop client test
practice.action: Read the starter squid.conf. Change the staff source from 172.20.0.0/16 to 172.20.4.0/24, keeping its GET and destination-port tests. Fill worked configuration can populate this example editor.
practice.observe: The editor changes immediately; the current proxy decisions do not change just because you typed.

practice.observe: The repaired policy refuses neighbours but permits every workshop staff GET to 8080. Unsaved edits and saved-but-unapplied repairs are not finished work.

practice.title: Inspect the applied result
practice.action: Choose Before staff in Request and open Inspect applied decision. Read which source line decides and which ACL tests match.
practice.observe: The repaired policy refuses this neighbour while allowing staff GET requests to 8080. If you only edit again without applying, the current decision stays the same.

goal: Keep intended web requests working while closing a rule-order bypass.
context: Builds on IPv4 prefixes, destination ports and the static-web unit. The supplied proxy is ready; no machine setup or network access is needed.

concepts.title: CONNECT requests a tunnel
concepts.text: Ordinary HTTP methods such as GET and POST identify web operations. CONNECT asks a proxy for a tunnel to a destination port. This assignment permits the supplied secure destination port, not arbitrary tunnel ports. A port number does not prove TLS or let this simulator inspect tunnel contents.

concepts.title: A reversed test means not this match
concepts.text: In an access rule, !web matches a destination outside the named web ports. A rule with tunnels !secure matches only a CONNECT request whose destination is outside the secure-port test. Both tests on that rule must match.

concepts.title: A later refusal cannot undo an early permit
concepts.text: If http_access allow staff web matches first, a staff CONNECT to a plain web port is already permitted. A later tunnel refusal will never see it. Put the port and tunnel guards before the broader staff permit, while keeping ordinary web requests and the allowed secure tunnel working.

concepts.title: Test what must keep working as well as what must stop
concepts.text: Blocking all clients or all CONNECT requests closes a leak but breaks required service. Inspect both allowed and refused requests. Save and apply the repaired policy, then check its full range of addresses, methods and ports; the sample table is not the whole population.

worked.label: Workshop staff
worked.explanation: Only these clients may use the workshop proxy.

worked.label: Web destinations
worked.explanation: Both are allowed for non-CONNECT requests in this workshop.

worked.label: Secure tunnel destination
worked.explanation: CONNECT to 8080 or 25 must be refused even for staff.

worked.label: First guard
worked.explanation: Refuse destinations outside the allowed web ports.

worked.label: Tunnel guard
worked.explanation: Refuse a tunnel unless its destination matches the secure-port test.

worked.label: Staff permit
worked.explanation: Reached only after the request passes both earlier guards.

worked.label: Final refusal
worked.explanation: Non-staff requests do not match the staff permit.

practice.title: Repair the workshop rule order

practice.observe: A later refusal cannot undo the early permit. Restoring both guards ahead of the permit repairs the leak without blocking ordinary staff requests.

practice.title: Compare the two tunnel decisions
practice.action: Choose CONNECT plain, then CONNECT secure in Request. Open Inspect applied decision and read the first matching rule; Read applied configuration distinguishes it from your draft.
practice.observe: After applying the repair, CONNECT plain is refused and CONNECT secure stays allowed. The first matching rule explains both outcomes.

Save and apply a policy that satisfies these requirements; preserve independent practice work.

goal: Make shared caching useful without keeping somebody else’s personal response.
context: Builds on HTTP GET and the static-web unit. A shared cache can reuse one response for several people. The origin and requests are supplied; no service setup is needed.

concepts.title: A cache keeps a response for later
concepts.text: The website’s server (the origin) supplies the response body. A full download is shown as a 200 response here. A shared cache can keep a copy under its path and reuse it for another GET. Here you edit the Cache-Control value sent with each origin response; type the value beside the supplied path.

concepts.title: Storage and freshness are separate
concepts.text: max-age=45 allows this workshop response to stay fresh until its age reaches 45 seconds. A fresh stored copy can be reused without contacting the origin. At exact expiry it needs an origin check. This model uses explicit freshness, not a guessed lifetime.

concepts.title: Personal responses need a different storage rule
concepts.text: private prevents shared storage. no-store also prevents storage and applies to any cache. no-cache has a different meaning: a response may be stored, but reuse requires a successful check with the server (validation). It does not mean “never store this personal page.”

concepts.title: Run the same policy against different requests
concepts.text: A trace is a short sequence of requests. Choose one after running the example. Compare Required with Actual, including whether a body was stored. Each trace starts with its own sample inputs and an empty simulated cache; requests within that trace share the resulting cache. The personal bodies are supplied facts, not real logins.

goal: Replace an overlong shared lifetime while preserving useful cache hits and origin checks.
context: Builds on storage, freshness and private/no-store from the preceding lesson. A response can already be several seconds old when it arrives. The times and origin revisions below are fixed sample inputs.

concepts.title: Shared freshness can override the general value
concepts.text: max-age=900 is the workshop’s general freshness value. s-maxage=20 supplies a different lifetime for shared caches and takes precedence here. Keep the stated max-age value while changing the shared policy. These traces model a shared cache; they do not run a browser.

concepts.title: Count the response’s age, not just your waiting time
concepts.text: The workshop’s first response arrives with Age 5. At 7 s, it is age 12: still below a 20-second shared lifetime. At 20 s, it is age 25 and needs an origin check. The response’s Date, supplied transit and residence also contribute to age. At exact expiry it is no longer fresh.

concepts.title: Validation can renew a stored body
concepts.text: An ETag is a label the server assigns to one response version. When a stale response’s ETag still matches, the supplied origin returns 304. The cache reuses the body with updated freshness metadata. A changed tag produces a 200 response with a new body. A fresh cache hit does not ask whether the origin has changed.

concepts.title: A request can insist on checking the origin
concepts.text: A request carrying no-cache requires an origin check even when the stored copy is fresh. This differs from banning response storage. If a required origin check cannot succeed, this model returns no usable body rather than serving stale content.

worked.label: Workshop response value
worked.explanation: The general value remains supplied; shared traces use the shorter 20-second lifetime.

worked.label: Repeat at 7 s
worked.explanation: 12 is below 20, so reuse the stored Revision 1 without contacting the origin.

worked.label: Origin unavailable at 20 s
worked.explanation: The copy is too old and cannot be validated; return no usable body.

worked.label: Matching tag at 30 s
worked.explanation: Reuse the body with renewed metadata. At 37 s it is fresh for reuse; a newer supplied origin revision is not contacted on that hit.

worked.label: Request no-cache at 2 s
worked.value: Origin check despite a fresh copy
worked.explanation: The supplied changed tag produces a new full response. Its body can be reused at 5 s.

practice.title: Repair the workshop’s shared lifetime
practice.action: In /workshop-bulletin, keep max-age=900 and replace s-maxage=3600 with s-maxage=20. Fill worked headers can populate this separate example.
practice.observe: The source Age and request times stay fixed. Editing clears the old check; it does not rerun requests.

practice.title: Run and compare a longer lifetime
practice.action: Choose Run example traces. Then try s-maxage=60 while keeping max-age=900 and run again.
practice.observe: The 20-second request can now reuse an overold copy. The overall result names the failing trace while correct request rows stay correct. Restore a policy that meets the stated timing.

practice.title: Follow the validation and forced-check traces
practice.action: Choose Validate once, then reuse renewed metadata, followed by A request asks for an origin check. Inspect body and cache decision for a 304 and a changed-tag 200.
practice.observe: Successful validation renews freshness without downloading the body. A request no-cache forces an origin check even inside the shared lifetime.

requirements: For /release-notes, keep the supplied max-age=600 while repairing the policy for shared caches.

In the validation trace, validate Revision 1 at 60 s, reuse that renewed copy at 75 s, then download Revision 2 at 120 s. Fresh reuse can keep the earlier revision even when the supplied origin has changed.
Honor the supplied request no-cache directive by contacting the origin at 5 s. Meet every trace by editing only the response Cache-Control value.

concepts.title: One request has two addresses to understand
concepts.text: A reverse proxy accepts a client request and chooses where to send it. The public port belongs to the proxy; the backend address and port identify the application behind it. Here you calculate those virtual routing decisions; no server or network starts.

concepts.title: Read the small server fragment
concepts.text: server { ... } groups this site’s settings in an HTTP configuration. The listen 8090; directive selects its public port. Each location chooses an action for a path. Directives end with a semicolon; braces group a block. Edit only this fragment in the workspace.

concepts.title: Match the path, then construct the backend path
concepts.text: A prefix location /charts/ matches /charts/daily.csv and deeper paths. The optional path portion after the endpoint is called the URI here. With proxy_pass http://198.51.100.60:9100/v1/, replace /charts/ with /v1/. Without that path portion, keep the entire client path. The final slash is literal.

concepts.title: Saving and applying do different jobs
concepts.text: Save configuration keeps your virtual document. Check syntax diagnoses supported syntax without changing routing. Apply saved configuration activates that document only if it parses. Check routing then compares the saved and applied behavior with the requirements. An exact location uses = before its path.

concepts.text: An exact location such as = /staff/health wins for that one path. Otherwise, the longest matching prefix wins. A later broad location does not override a longer prefix; moving configuration lines is not a reliable repair.

concepts.title: A prefix is a string, not a directory boundary
concepts.text: The prefix /staff also matches /staff-directory/start. To protect the staff subtree, use /staff/ for descendants and an exact /staff for the bare path. A narrow health exception can still return a deliberate local response.

goal: Diagnose a wrong public identity, ownership and writable key paths using supplied virtual files.
requirements: Allow morgan’s supplied admin-key and remove retired-key from /home/morgan/.ssh/authorized_keys.
Repair the owner and ordinary permissions of that file and .ssh so StrictModes and directory traversal allow the intended access.
Keep StrictModes, other account files and the supplied user/group inventory unchanged.
context: Builds on the earlier SSH identity lesson and ordinary Linux file-permission practice.

concepts.title: A public key authorizes an account
concepts.text: A server account’s authorized_keys file lists public user keys that may be accepted. It does not contain the client’s private key. Use the supplied client record and preserve its complete type and base64 field; a friendly comment cannot turn the wrong key into the right one.

concepts.title: A file is reached through folders
concepts.text: The target account needs search permission on its home and .ssh directories, then read permission on authorized_keys. Ordinary permissions use 4 for read, 2 for write and 1 for search/execute. The three octal digits describe the owner, group and everyone else. For example, 750 gives the owner all three actions, the group read/search and others none.

concepts.title: Read access is different from safe ownership
concepts.text: StrictModes adds a safety check: the home, .ssh directory and key file must belong to the target user or root and must not be writable by group or others. 600 and 700 are common choices, but public records need not be secret: 640 or 644 can also be valid when the intended user can read them. Check the access requirement instead of memorizing one mode.

concepts.title: Repair as the simulated administrator
concepts.text: The Owner, Group and Permissions controls represent administrator actions on the supplied virtual paths. On Linux, changing another owner’s file normally needs administrator authority. Save the key file and the directory attributes separately. Then test that the administrator identity works, the retired key is absent and unrelated notes remain unchanged.

worked.label: Practice account key
worked.explanation: Expected: the intended supplied client identity is present, while the temporary record is removed.

worked.label: Practice directory
worked.explanation: Read/search for the group is allowed; group write is absent.

worked.label: Practice key file
worked.explanation: The intended user can read the public record and other users cannot rewrite it.

practice.title: Inspect the failing key file
practice.action: With the authorized_keys document selected, compare its public data and owner with the supplied administrator identity. Choose Check example to see which stage fails, then Fill worked edits.
practice.observe: After Fill worked edits, expect the practice drafts to contain the intended key and file attributes. Nothing is applied or checked automatically.

practice.title: Save both required paths
practice.action: Save file. Select the practice .ssh directory under Virtual document, inspect its owner/group/octal permissions and choose Save permissions. Then Check example.
practice.observe: Expected: the directory can be searched safely and the public key can be read safely. Fixing only the file while leaving a writable parent is insufficient.

practice.title: Explore a valid alternate mode
practice.action: On the key file, try a read-only group/other access choice that still leaves the target user able to read it. Save and check again; then try group write and compare the feedback.
practice.observe: Readable public records can be valid. Group/other write is a different risk and StrictModes rejects it.

goal: Combine trusted server identity, key retirement and active access policy while protecting recovery access.
requirements: Restore trusted key-based administration for morgan and rescue on control.lab.test using the supplied server identity.

Apply a saved policy that offers only public-key authentication with StrictModes enabled, permits both required administrators and refuses guest and root at the policy stage.
Verify the supplied accepted and refused requests; saved-only edits do not change the active server policy.
context: Builds on the earlier SSH identity lesson and ordinary Linux file-permission practice.

concepts.title: Saved configuration is not active policy
concepts.text: Save file stores sshd_config in the virtual server. Apply saved policy validates the supported configuration and changes the active copy. If validation fails, the prior active copy remains. This handover starts with a proposed saved policy and an older active policy; check the actual access results rather than assuming the editor is already in force.

concepts.title: Keep a recovery path while restricting methods
concepts.text: AllowUsers names the supplied accounts allowed by policy. Keep both the main and rescue administrators. PasswordAuthentication and keyboard-interactive authentication are separate methods; disabling one alone does not disable the other. AuthenticationMethods publickey is another supported way to require the public-key method. The words yes and no turn these options on and off. PubkeyAuthentication yes offers user-key authentication; PermitRootLogin no refuses root. Edit the existing directive rather than adding a contradictory duplicate: for ordinary directives the first value wins.

concepts.title: Retire one identity instead of blocking everyone
concepts.text: Remove the temporary public key from the requested account, keep its intended administrator key and retain the rescue account’s protected key file. StrictModes must stay enabled. Emptying every key file or breaking trust may refuse the temporary identity, but it also loses required administration.

concepts.title: Verify accepted and refused requests
concepts.text: Check access evaluates the supplied identities against host trust, active policy and key paths. Both required administrators must pass. The guest and root must stop at policy, while the retired identity must fail key authorization. A malformed or unsupported operation is not counted as a successful refusal.

practice.observe: Expected: dana and support pass; the retired identity fails key authorization; guest and root are refused by policy. The archive trust record and protected files remain.

goal: Restore the supplied SMB accounts and the folder access needed by two team members.
context: Prerequisites: local-account lifecycle and Linux access-policy skills. Reopen those Introductions if Unix users, groups or directory search are unfamiliar. This standalone sharing unit supplies the server, local identities, files and fixed test credentials.

concepts.title: A Unix user and an SMB login are different records
concepts.text: An SMB share is a named folder other computers can open over a network. Samba provides these shares on Linux. The Unix identity supplies file ownership and group membership; an enabled SMB account is also needed for a named login. This lab supplies fixed valid/invalid test credentials. Its account controls model server administration without taking real passwords.

concepts.title: Reach the folder before opening its file
concepts.text: Folder x means search: the user can reach a known file name. Folder r permits listing names. A file needs its own r or w bit for reading or updating. Updating an existing file needs folder search and file write permission; creating files is outside this unit.

concepts.title: Find the failed layer, then retry
concepts.text: An account can authenticate and still fail directory or file permissions. A share can also impose read-only policy even when Unix permits a write. Run a client trial, read the named failure layer, repair that layer, then retry. id -Gn USER and ls -ld PATH inspect the supplied Unix facts.

requirements: Enable the supplied test SMB accounts for mira and noor; their Unix identities and groups already exist.
Let both team members list /srv/team-reports and reach its existing files. The writer must read and replace draft.txt; the reviewer must read checklist.txt and be denied writes by share policy.

Keep casey and anonymous clients out of the team share. Preserve every supplied regular-file mode, the configuration/payroll ownership, and the payroll and public-notice text. Keep the public share read-only and available.

practice.title: Inspect the separate test identities
practice.action: Run a Read file trial as riley against notes/draft.txt. Use the filesystem terminal to run id -Gn riley and ls -ld /practice/notes.
practice.observe: The first trial reports a disabled SMB account. The Unix identity still exists; file modes alone cannot enable its login.

practice.title: Repair accounts and folder search
practice.action: Enable riley and add/enable the supplied sam SMB account. In the terminal run chmod g+rx /practice/notes. Run the writer’s Read file trial again.
practice.observe: The same client now reaches the draft. The account table and folder mode solve different parts of the access path.

practice.title: Verify writing and rejection
practice.action: Choose Replace file, enter a short trial text, and select Run trial as riley. Switch back to Read file as sam, then try a reviewer Replace file. Select Check answers.
practice.observe: The writer changes the simulated file; the reviewer reads it but is denied a write by share policy. Checking uses its own sample contents and does not overwrite these trial files.

worked.explanation: project authors identifies the supplied groups. It does not establish an SMB account.

worked.explanation: In the separate guide folder, adding group read/search permits listing and reaching existing files. Its regular-file modes stay unchanged.

riley: SMB Enabled

goal: Apply a share policy that permits team writing and review while preserving a read-only public share.
context: Prerequisites: local-account lifecycle and Linux access-policy skills. Reopen those Introductions if Unix users, groups or directory search are unfamiliar. This standalone sharing unit supplies the server, local identities, files and fixed test credentials.

concepts.title: A share maps a name to a directory
concepts.text: A share section names the resource a client opens; path selects its supplied directory. valid users admits named users or @Unix-groups, and invalid users can exclude a match. In this standalone model the Unix identities and enabled SMB accounts are already supplied.

concepts.title: Default policy and exceptions have different jobs
concepts.text: read only = yes sets the default. write list grants named users or @groups a write exception; read list makes its matches read-only. A write-list match wins when an identity appears in both lists. These share settings never grant missing Unix file rights.

concepts.title: Keep public reading separate from team editing
concepts.text: guest ok permits an anonymous client only where that share admits it. A public notice can be readable without being writable. Checking syntax is not an access test: save the file, apply the settings, then run separate named and anonymous client trials.

requirements: Publish team for mira to read/update the supplied draft and for noor to read while share policy rejects reviewer writes.
Reject casey and anonymous connections to the team at authentication/share policy, rather than relying on an inaccessible file. A failed named login must not become guest access.

Keep bulletin available for public reads, with a default read-only policy and no write-list exceptions. Preserve supplied regular-file modes, configuration/payroll ownership, and the private and notice contents.
Save a supported configuration and apply its policy. The supplied Unix identities, SMB accounts and file inventory remain in place.

concepts.title: The saved file is not the applied configuration
concepts.text: The editor and cat show the same saved virtual file. Applying supported settings changes the policy used for new simulated connections. A successful syntax check alone does not prove that clients reach the intended directory.

concepts.title: Verify the file you reached, not just success

concepts.title: A mail address identifies a recipient and domain
concepts.text: In mila@team.dispatch.test, mila is the recipient and team.dispatch.test is the destination domain. A mail transfer agent (MTA), such as Postfix, decides whether to deliver locally or forward the message. It is different from a mail-reading program.

concepts.title: Local means this server owns the destination

concepts.title: Queued means accepted, not delivered
concepts.text: A queue holds mail waiting for delivery. postqueue -p lists pending samples and their last failure. An empty queue alone cannot prove delivery: a permanently failed sample is also absent. Inspect the retained sample states and intended mailbox results.

concepts.title: Follow each next hop and its immediate peer
concepts.text: A relay evaluates the address of the server currently connecting to it, not the original distant sender. A next hop pointing back toward an earlier relay can cycle. This simulator reports the finite repeated path; it does not fabricate real SMTP hop headers, bounce timing or retry schedules.

concepts.title: Repair, reload, then retry
concepts.text: Saving a correct file does not update the running route. postfix reload applies this server’s supported saved settings. postqueue -f requests a retry of its queued mail; the simulator advances one bounded attempt immediately. A successful command exit is not evidence that recipients received mail. Recheck delivery and relay boundaries together.

goal: Write a mail filter that files one named list and safely keeps other messages.
context: Start after the local-mail and SMTP introductions. A mailbox is a named destination for delivered mail, not a host folder you must create. You do not need shell scripting knowledge. All messages, mailboxes and filter execution here are simulated.

concepts.title: A header is a named field in a message
concepts.text: A message has fields such as Subject. This exercise also supplies X-List, a custom field identifying a list. The filter reads that field and chooses a mailbox. These supplied fields are practice inputs, not proof that a sender is trustworthy.

concepts.title: Read a small Sieve rule
concepts.text: Sieve is a mail-filter language. require "fileinto"; enables filing. if introduces a condition; braces group the action to take when it matches. End each simple action with a semicolon. Double quotes contain literal text; nothing runs in a shell.

concepts.title: Exact matching and the default mailbox
concepts.text: header :is compares the entire field value, ignoring ASCII letter case by default. An absent field does not match. fileinto chooses a mailbox and cancels the default INBOX copy. When no filing action matches, Sieve keeps the message in INBOX. An unconditional keep after filing would add another copy.

requirements: File messages with an X-List value exactly equal to staff-updates in News only. Ignore ASCII letter case in field names and values; one matching duplicate field is sufficient.
Keep all other messages in INBOX only, including a missing or empty X-List, a different list, and the same words appearing only in Subject.
Run the filter against every sample. A correct filter must preserve legitimate unmatched mail and avoid extra mailbox copies. Equivalent supported rules are accepted.

practice.title: Run the separate club filter
practice.action: Select Woodland club in Sample message. Select Fill worked example, then Run filter. Read Actual results for every sample.
practice.observe: Woodland and mixed-case club mail go to Club; other mail remains in INBOX. The selected sample changes what you inspect, not which cases run.

practice.title: Change the matching value
practice.action: In Filter, change woodland to not-woodland in the quoted test value, then select Run filter.
practice.observe: The other club now matches, and the original Woodland club remains in INBOX. A whole-value test is different from a substring test.

practice.title: Observe an unwanted extra copy
practice.action: Fill the worked example again. Add keep; after the closing brace and run it. Remove that final keep; and retry.
practice.observe: Filing does not prevent a later explicit keep. The additional INBOX copy fails the Club-only requirement; retrying the repaired script clears that failure.

worked.explanation: This declaration comes before all rules.

worked.label: Test the whole value
worked.explanation: This separate example uses a different field and value from the assignment.

worked.label: Matching action
worked.explanation: Put the action inside the matching if block. Unmatched messages use the default INBOX keep.

goal: Combine project membership, review status and message size without moving unrelated mail.
context: Build on exact-header filing. You already know require, if, fileinto and the default INBOX copy. This lesson adds combined tests and strict size comparisons; it does not require Bash knowledge.

concepts.title: All conditions versus any condition
concepts.text: allof (test, test) means every enclosed test must be true. anyof (test, test) means at least one must be true. Separate tests with commas. Parentheses preserve the intended grouping: team membership AND (review needed OR large message).

concepts.title: Measure the entire represented message
concepts.text: size :over compares complete message bytes, including headers and the separating blank line. K means 1024 bytes, so size :over 1K means strictly larger than 1024. At exactly the threshold, neither :over nor :under matches.

concepts.title: Keep the outer restriction
concepts.text: A large message from another team must not pass a team-specific rule. Keep the team test outside the anyof group; otherwise size alone could admit unrelated mail. Missing headers do not match, but another true condition inside anyof can still make that group true.

requirements: File in Review only when X-Project exactly matches atlas and either X-Review exactly matches pending or the complete represented message is larger than 1024 bytes. Ignore ASCII letter case for these exact comparisons.
Size includes headers, the blank separator and body, not just body length. Exactly 1024 bytes is not over 1024; pending project mail still qualifies at that boundary.
Keep every nonqualifying sample in INBOX only. Run all samples and avoid extra mailbox copies. Equivalent supported conditions are accepted.

practice.title: Inspect two different reasons to review
practice.action: Fill worked example and select Run filter. Select Small orchard todo, then Large orchard ready. Read their headers, represented size and Actual results.
practice.observe: Either todo status or a size over 512 bytes can satisfy the inner group, while X-Team must still be orchard.

practice.title: Test the exact boundary
practice.action: Select Ready orchard mail at 512 bytes. Change :over 512 to :over 511 in Filter and run again; restore 512 afterward.
practice.observe: The whole-message size is displayed. Moving the threshold changes this boundary case; :over is a strict comparison.

practice.title: Compare anyof and allof
practice.action: Replace the inner anyof with allof, then run. Compare the small todo and large ready cases. Restore the worked example and rerun.
practice.observe: Each has only one of the two inner conditions, so requiring both leaves them in INBOX. Actual results explain the mismatches.

worked.label: Outer restriction
worked.explanation: Every reviewed sample in this worked problem must belong to this team.

worked.label: Inner alternatives
worked.explanation: Either alternative is sufficient inside this group.

worked.label: Combine the tests
worked.explanation: The runnable filter above places the team condition outside the anyof alternatives.

goal: Repair a filter whose overlapping rules create extra copies and override priority.
context: Apply the earlier exact-header and combined-condition lessons. The starter contains intentional logic errors. Investigate Actual results before editing; a syntactically valid rule can still file the wrong copies.

concepts.title: A filing action does not end the script
concepts.text: Separate if rules are independent. When both match, both bodies run; fileinto does not stop processing. A later keep also adds INBOX, even after another mailbox was chosen.

concepts.title: Choose one branch or stop deliberately
concepts.text: An if / elsif / else chain runs only the first matching branch. Alternatively, stop; ends the entire filter at that point. Use these tools to implement priority, rather than relying on the position of a filing action alone. The Stop button cancels the sample run; stop; inside a rule ends processing of that one message.

concepts.title: Preserve the default delivery
concepts.text: stop without an earlier delivery action still permits implicit keep. discard cancels implicit keep and does not undo other actions, so it is not a repair for an unwanted extra copy. Leave unmatched mail with a deliberate keep or the default INBOX behavior.

requirements: Urgent mail, identified by X-Priority exactly equal to urgent, must go to Review only, even when it also belongs to the staff list.
Otherwise, mail with X-List exactly equal to staff-updates must go to News only. Keep all remaining mail in INBOX only. Ignore ASCII letter case and accept one matching duplicate field.
Repair the supplied filter and run every sample. Preserve unmatched mail, respect priority and avoid duplicate destinations. Equivalent supported control flow is accepted.

practice.title: Diagnose the overlapping starter

goal: Classify mail by its parsed sender domain without moving look-alike addresses.
context: Start after Mail filters: filing and rule recovery. You already know if, require "fileinto", filing and the default INBOX copy. This lesson distinguishes an address from the surrounding header text; no shell commands are needed.

concepts.title: Read the mailbox, not its display name
concepts.text: In Gardener <plants@orchard.guide.test>, Gardener is a display name and plants@orchard.guide.test is the mailbox address. The part before @ is the local part; the part after it is the domain. Names and parenthesized comments describe an address but are not the address.

concepts.title: Choose the address part before comparing
concepts.text: address :domain reads the domain from each actual mailbox in a named field. :is compares the entire selected domain. In contrast, header :contains searches the raw field text, including names and longer domains. The default comparison ignores ASCII letter case. Multiple mailboxes or duplicate fields match when any actual mailbox qualifies.

concepts.title: An exact domain is not a substring or authentication
concepts.text: orchard.guide.test differs from orchard.guide.test.elsewhere.test and team.orchard.guide.test. An exact test excludes both. Missing or malformed address fields do not match; spaces and comments around @ do not change the mailbox. Filing by a visible From field classifies mail; it does not authenticate its sender.

requirements: File in Partners only when an actual mailbox in From has the domain exactly partners.dispatch.test. Ignore ASCII letter case. Accept a matching mailbox in a list or any one matching duplicate From field.

Keep every other sample in INBOX only. Display names, comments and Subject mentions do not supply a sender address. Longer or child domains do not equal the required domain; malformed or missing From does not match.
Repair the supplied substring filter and run all samples. Avoid extra copies and preserve unmatched mail. Equivalent supported rules are accepted; this is classification, not sender authentication.

practice.observe: The rule now reads a recipient instead of a sender. Changing a field changes the task; matching text elsewhere in a message is not a substitute for the required field.

goal: Recover recipient routing without treating sender names or message mentions as recipients.
context: Build on parsed sender-domain filtering. This task needs a complete mailbox address in To or Cc. The starter contains an intentional broad-search error; use each failing sample to identify what the rule actually read.

concepts.title: Sender, recipient and mention are different
concepts.text: From describes a sender; To and Cc describe visible recipients. A Subject line may mention an address without sending the message to it. A display name can contain an address-like phrase while its actual mailbox points elsewhere. These visible fields are not the SMTP delivery envelope.

concepts.title: Match one complete mailbox in either recipient field
concepts.text: address :is ["To", "Cc"] "visits@clinic.guide.test" checks actual mailboxes in either field. With no part option, :all is the default: local part and domain stay together as one address. An address split between two different mailboxes is not a match. The default comparison ignores ASCII letter case.

concepts.title: Repair the condition and keep unmatched mail
concepts.text: A word search for visits or a test of only the local part can match another mailbox or domain. Use the full required mailbox when that is the policy. The matching fileinto cancels the default INBOX copy; leaving other messages alone keeps them in INBOX. Run every sample, not only the selected one.

requirements: File in Support only when an actual mailbox in To or Cc is exactly helpdesk@service.dispatch.test. Ignore ASCII letter case in the full address. One matching mailbox in a list or duplicate recipient field is sufficient.

Keep every other sample in INBOX only. A mention in From, Subject or a display name is not a recipient. A longer local part, another domain, or matching local/domain parts found in separate mailboxes must not pass.

Repair the supplied broad text search, run all samples, and avoid extra mailbox copies. Preserve malformed or missing recipient samples in INBOX. Equivalent supported full-address conditions are accepted.
