goal: Repair filing when a visible recipient differs from the actual delivery recipient.
context: Build on structured mailbox tests and rule-based filing. A mail server has delivery information outside the message. This lesson supplies it explicitly; you do not configure or contact a server.

concepts.title: A message label and its delivery envelope are different
concepts.text: To and Cc are visible message fields. A group or hidden-copy delivery can reach another mailbox. The simulated delivery envelope states the actual recipient for this user: RCPT TO. MAIL FROM supplies a return address and can be empty; it is not the visible From field. Neither field authenticates the sender.

concepts.title: Choose the recipient from the envelope
concepts.text: Declare require ["envelope", "fileinto"]; before using an envelope test. In the studio example, envelope :is "to" "orders@studio.guide.test" compares the actual recipient. The existing default comparison ignores ASCII letter case; :all, :localpart and :domain select parts just as for address tests.

concepts.title: File only the matching delivery

Other recipients retain the default INBOX copy even when their To header mentions orders. Envelope :is "from" "" would test a null sender; it would not identify a recipient.

requirements: File only actual envelope deliveries to tickets@dispatch.test in Tickets, ignoring ASCII letter case in the full address. The visible From/To/Subject fields must not decide whether the recipient matches.

goal: Forward an alias to its virtual archive while preserving unrelated local deliveries.
context: Build on actual envelope recipient tests. Forwarding changes the delivery action, not the message headers. All destinations here are named simulated mailboxes; no real mail is sent.

concepts.title: Forwarding and local filing are separate effects
concepts.text: redirect records a virtual forward to a named destination. It is a base Sieve action: require "envelope" enables the recipient test, not redirect. The source message and return address are unchanged, including a null sender.

concepts.title: Forwarding does not stop the script
concepts.text: A redirect cancels the default INBOX copy. It does not end processing: an unconditional keep later in the script adds INBOX back. Use a suitable branch or stop when that is the intended policy. Other unmatched deliveries still need their default local copy.

concepts.title: Check where forwarding points
concepts.text: The studio example forwards photos@studio.guide.test to album@studio.guide.test. An album delivery itself stays local. This site rejects direct forwarding to the current recipient and unknown destinations, and permits at most four forwarding actions per sample. An error cancels all proposed effects and keeps the original in INBOX with a diagnostic.

requirements: Forward actual envelope deliveries to alerts@dispatch.test to the supplied virtual target archive@dispatch.test, ignoring ASCII letter case in the full alias comparison. Do not retain a local mailbox copy for these matches.

goal: Give a retired delivery recipient a clear refusal while preserving normal update filing.
context: Build on envelope routing and the difference between actions and stop. A silent discard is not a refusal. This task models a refusal decision; it does not generate SMTP replies or bounces.

concepts.title: Tell refusal apart from discard
concepts.text: discard silently removes the default local copy. require "reject" enables reject "reason"; which instead records a refusal with your explanation. Choose a useful nonblank reason; the exact wording is not graded. No real reply is sent.

concepts.title: Give the retired recipient priority
concepts.text: In the studio example, the old-desk recipient must be refused even if Subject says Studio notice. A current desk notice goes to Notices; ordinary current mail remains in INBOX. An if/elsif chain chooses only the first matching branch. Equivalent explicit stop logic is also valid.

concepts.title: Avoid contradictory actions
concepts.text: Reject cancels implicit keep but does not automatically stop later rules. This simulated site rejects a second refusal or a mixture of refusal and delivery for one sample. Separate branches or end processing at the correct point. A null return address does not remove the supplied delivery recipient; this exercise records the refusal decision without generating a bounce.

requirements: Refuse actual envelope deliveries to retired@dispatch.test with a nonblank reason of your choice, ignoring ASCII letter case. Leave no local copy or virtual forward for those recipients, even when their Subject matches the update rule.
For every other recipient, file Subject exactly Dispatch update in Updates, ignoring ASCII letter case. Keep other messages in INBOX only; similar longer subjects must not match.

goal: Prepare useful personal absence replies without replying to every arrival or losing the incoming mail.
context: Build on Sieve declarations and actual delivery envelopes. A vacation responder adds a reply; it does not file or remove the incoming message. All mail, reply content and time here are simulated.

concepts.title: Keep delivery and replies separate
concepts.text: An absence reply tells a person who can help while you are away. The original message still needs delivery. Enable the vacation extension with require "vacation"; then use vacation with a quoted reply message. Unlike fileinto or redirect, vacation does not cancel the default INBOX copy.

concepts.title: Choose a useful interval and message
concepts.text: In the studio example, vacation :days 2 "I am away; contact cover@studio.guide.test."; supplies the replacement contact and allows another reply after two days. :days is an interval for the same sender and response, not a daily schedule. Without :days the default is seven days; this site clamps requested intervals to 1–365 days.

concepts.title: Follow the shared timeline
concepts.text: Read Arrival in Shared reply timeline. One day is 86400 seconds: two days is 172800. The first personal message gets a reply, a repeat at 172799 does not, and an otherwise identical arrival at 172800 can get one. A suppressed repeat does not restart the timer. Run filter starts the timeline again; Stop retains the draft and partial observations.

concepts.title: Avoid automatic reply loops
concepts.text: Replies go to the actual MAIL FROM return address, not the visible From label. The simulated responder itself suppresses null returns, list metadata, automatic messages, unattended-address patterns and self-replies. A supported To/Cc/Bcc or Resent recipient must identify the user, a configured alias or final delivery recipient. A message merely mentioning the user is not enough. These safeguards do not prevent normal INBOX delivery.

requirements: For learner@absence.test, prepare a personal vacation reply identifying cover@absence.test as the cover contact. Use your own wording. Keep incoming messages in INBOX only.
Allow another reply to the same sender and response after three full days (259200 seconds), not before. Each different sender has independent reply history. Follow all arrivals in their listed order.
Do not reply to the supplied automatic, list, null-return, self or non-personal messages. Run filter must pass every arrival.

practice.observe: The actual reply goes to writer@outside.test, contains the studio contact and declares Auto-Submitted: auto-replied. The original remains in INBOX.

practice.observe: The same message receives no repeat at 172799 seconds and becomes eligible at 172800. The last reply time changes only when a reply is prepared.

worked.explanation: Two full days is 172800 seconds in this separate worked timeline.

goal: Restore both absence replies and selective delivery without reply storms or extra local copies.
context: Use vacation eligibility and shared sender history, actual envelope tests, fileinto and stop. Diagnose the supplied early-stop error and verify both delivery and reply outcomes.

concepts.title: One filter can have two responsibilities
concepts.text: The studio example files actual desk@studio.routing.test deliveries in Desk and leaves other mail in INBOX. Independently, eligible personal messages need an absence reply containing the studio contact. A reply and a delivery destination are separate outcomes.

concepts.title: An early stop can skip a necessary action
concepts.text: In the starter, desk mail is filed and stop ends processing before vacation is reached. Those incoming messages arrive in the right folder but never get a reply. Move shared reply processing to a reachable place, or use equivalent branches that execute at most one vacation action for each arrival.

concepts.title: History belongs to the responder, not a folder
concepts.text: A sender who writes to the desk and then to the general recipient still shares the same responder history. Reusing the same reply content and raw options keeps the same response identity. If different reply bodies are intentional, an explicit :handle can give them a shared identity. :days is not part of that identity.

concepts.title: Keep the two outcomes independent
concepts.text: Automatic or non-personal desk mail still belongs in Desk even when no reply is allowed. A visible Cc mentioning the desk does not replace RCPT TO. fileinto cancels implicit INBOX; an extra keep creates an unwanted second copy. A later conflict cancels proposed replies and delivery effects for that arrival, with a diagnostic and INBOX recovery.

requirements: Repair the supplied rule order. Actual envelope deliveries to desk@dispatch.away.test belong in Desk only; every other recipient stays in INBOX only. A visible desk mention must not choose the destination.

Keep one shared response identity across desk and general mail: no repeat to a sender until one full day (86400 seconds) has elapsed. Different senders have independent history.

goal: Preserve copying, final delivery and default delivery while migrating a legacy mail filter.
context: Build on Sieve header tests, fileinto, keep and stop. Read the supplied traditional recipe; write and run Sieve against simulated messages. No procmail or real mail is executed.

concepts.title: Read a recipe before translating it
concepts.text: Procmail is a traditional mail-delivery/filtering tool. A recipe begins with :0 and flags, followed by * condition lines and a destination. In this lesson, conditions search message headers, not the body. The leading ^ and trailing $ anchor a whole header line; [space or tab]* allows whitespace around the value. Matching ignores letter case unless the D flag is used. These simple recipes are supplied as read-only source policy, not a language this simulator runs.

concepts.title: A copy lets the original continue
concepts.text: In the worked recipe, :0 c: makes a copy for Sketches when X-Group is design. The c means copy and continue; it does not stop later recipes. A normal successful delivery, such as the Review recipe, finishes processing. If nothing finishes delivery, the site default is INBOX. The final colon requests a local lock in real procmail; this exercise uses virtual destinations and no lockfiles.

concepts.title: Translate behavior, not punctuation
concepts.text: Sieve uses require "fileinto"; before fileinto actions. header :is compares a complete header value, ignoring case with the default comparator; leading/trailing whitespace is removed. A fileinto cancels Sieve’s implicit INBOX copy, and does not itself stop later rules. To preserve the legacy copy behavior, explicitly keep the original when it reaches default delivery. To preserve the normal delivery rule, stop after filing to Review.

concepts.title: Test overlapping and unmatched messages
concepts.text: The worked design-and-review message needs both Sketches and Review, with no INBOX copy. A design-only message needs Sketches plus INBOX. Review-only needs Review alone; unmatched mail needs INBOX. Read Expected and Actual for each sample after Run filter. The assignment uses different header names, values and destinations. Programs, pipes, variable expansion and arbitrary regular expressions are outside this migration exercise.

requirements: Translate the supplied read-only procmail policy into a Sieve filter. Match whole X-Team values equal to operations and whole X-Priority values equal to urgent, ignoring letter case and surrounding whitespace; body mentions and substring lookalikes must not match.

The team rule makes an Archive copy and continues. The priority rule delivers to Urgent and finishes. Messages matching both need Archive and Urgent only; team-only messages need Archive and INBOX; priority-only messages need Urgent alone; unmatched messages need INBOX alone.

concepts.title: A mailbox server is not a mail sender
concepts.text: SMTP delivers mail to a destination. Dovecot lets a client read stored mail using IMAP or POP3. These lessons use one virtual endpoint with two sample accounts; nothing connects to a real server. The editor uses Dovecot 2.4 syntax. Its first two version lines and supplied authentication/storage facts are already provided.

concepts.title: Choose a protocol and a protected connection
concepts.text: protocols = imap pop3 enables both services. IMAP commonly uses 143 with STARTTLS or 993 with TLS from the start; POP uses 110 with STLS or 995 with TLS from the start. A port number alone does not make a connection secure. The selected client profile states its mode. Each TLS client must trust the issuing CA and request a name present on the certificate.

concepts.title: Keep passwords protected and mail separate
concepts.text: ssl = required rejects remote password login before TLS. The worked accounts have separate /srv/practice/ACCOUNT/Maildir directories; the assignment supplies different locations. mail_path = /srv/practice/%{user}/Maildir substitutes the signed-in username; ~/Maildir is another supported per-user form. A fixed path to one account cannot locate the other account’s supplied mail.

concepts.title: Save, apply, then verify
concepts.text: Save configuration changes the simulated file. Restart service applies it and ends older connections; a failed restart leaves the service stopped but does not erase mail. Enable at boot is a separate setting. In the client, Connect opens the chosen profile; Send transmits one protocol command. Check work tests fresh clients for both accounts and rejects an inaccessible port as proof of a secure policy.

goal: Mark the support request as read, permanently remove only the expired probe, and preserve the unread report and the other account’s mail.
requirements: Use the supplied IMAP server; its configuration is read-only in this activity.

concepts.title: Sign in before inspecting a mailbox
concepts.text: Connect with imap-tls for the supplied endpoint. An IMAP command starts with a short tag, such as a1, which the server repeats in its final OK, NO or BAD reply. LOGIN takes the supplied username and sample password. LIST "" "*" lists this account’s flat mailboxes; no command accesses another account or a host file.

concepts.title: Choose inspection or editing
concepts.text: EXAMINE INBOX selects the mailbox read-only. SELECT INBOX selects it for reading and writing. The reply reports EXISTS (message count), UIDVALIDITY (the mailbox’s UID identity) and UIDNEXT (the next unused UID). Sequence numbers count the current positions; UIDs identify existing messages even after positions change. A failed SELECT deselects the old mailbox.

concepts.title: Reading can change the read flag
concepts.text: FETCH 1:* (UID FLAGS BODY.PEEK[]) inspects every supplied message without setting its Seen flag. BODY[] normally marks the message read in a read/write selection. UID STORE 201 +FLAGS (\Seen) can also mark a supplied UID read. EXAMINE stays read-only, even when BODY[] is requested. A minus sign removes a flag; FLAGS without a sign replaces the supported flag set.

concepts.title: A deletion flag is not removal
concepts.text: UID STORE 209 +FLAGS (\Deleted) marks a message; EXPUNGE permanently removes all messages currently marked Deleted in the selected read/write mailbox. CLOSE also expunges in read/write mode, without individual EXPUNGE replies. EXAMINE followed by CLOSE does not expunge. LOGOUT, reconnecting and selecting another mailbox do not commit IMAP deletion flags automatically.

concepts.title: A POP session has stages
concepts.text: After Connect, USER names a sample account and PASS supplies its sample password. With the required remote policy, establish TLS before USER/PASS. A successful login begins a transaction with stable message numbers. STAT reports count and wire octets; LIST gives sizes; UIDL gives opaque stable message IDs; RETR reads a message. These are protocol commands, not Linux shell utilities.

concepts.title: Inspect before removing
concepts.text: Use LIST and RETR to identify the expired probe before DELE. The number in DELE is the message’s current POP transaction position, not an IMAP UID. Numbering does not close up after DELE during this transaction. RETR adds Seen by default in this Dovecot profile; pop3_no_flag_updates = yes can suppress that side effect. It does not delete the message.

concepts.title: Cancel a mark or commit it deliberately
concepts.text: DELE only marks. RSET clears all pending deletion marks; a disconnect or lost server session also leaves the stored messages intact. QUIT after successful login commits the pending deletions. QUIT before login commits nothing. After reconnecting, LIST and UIDL reflect the remaining messages and new positions. The remaining messages’ opaque IDs stay stable.

concepts.title: Combine configuration and recovery
concepts.text: The service can run while POP is unavailable because only IMAP is enabled. Preserve TLS/password protection, the other protocol and both per-user stores when correcting the configuration. Save and restart before reconnecting. Check work compares fresh secure access, rejection of unprotected login, the precise committed removal and every message that must remain.

context: Prerequisites: service save/restart/enable, host networking and local/SMTP mail concepts. This unit introduces the client protocols; commands here are not Linux shell commands.

goal: Audit a pending mail-path change, then preview and remove only read expired notices without touching protected mail.
requirements: Keep saved and running per-account mail locations consistent for both rowan and tess; keep the service running and enabled at boot.
Keep both accounts' protected IMAP/POP access working and reject unprotected remote passwords.
In rowan's INBOX and Archive, permanently remove every read message whose Subject contains [EXPIRED].
Keep unread [EXPIRED] notices unread and unmarked, preserve all other rowan messages, and preserve every tess message.

concepts.title: Inspect the saved file before applying it
concepts.text: A running server can be healthy while its saved file would break the next restart. doveconf mail_path prints the saved setting; -h hides the setting name. It does not read unsaved editor text or apply changes. Here only named-setting queries are supported, not full/default dumps.

concepts.title: Administration is different from a client login
concepts.text: doveadm works on a server-side mail store. This workspace supplies that administrator role; it does not ask you to run sudo or contact a real server. mailbox list names a supplied user’s folders; search identifies matching messages by mailbox identity and UID. UIDs are not POP positions.

concepts.title: Preview a precise selection before removing it
concepts.text: Search terms combine with AND. For example, mailbox INBOX seen subject '[DRILL]' selects read notices containing that marker in one mailbox. Quote 'uid flags hdr.subject' so fetch receives one field-list argument. Fetch inspects without marking mail read here. Expunge immediately removes matches; it does not wait for a Deleted flag or QUIT.

concepts.title: Know which server the tools belong to
concepts.text: Dovecot and Courier can both provide access to Maildir mail. Courier has its own configuration and uses Authlib to map accounts to their mail locations and identities. These files and commands model Dovecot; they are not Courier administration. Courier is supporting awareness only in this lesson.

context: Prerequisites: protected mailbox configuration and IMAP/POP recovery. This capstone introduces server-side inspection and compound selection; no external service or host shell is used.

practice.title: Inspect, repair and save the pending setting
practice.action: Run doveconf -h mail_path before editing. Fill worked configuration, then Save configuration and run the query again. Restart service only after the saved value is correct; Enable at boot.
practice.observe: The first query names only elin. Unsaved edits do not change its output; Save updates the file that doveconf reads. Restart applies saved settings. A per-account path keeps both supplied users reachable.

practice.title: Preview and apply the same precise query
practice.action: Insert and Run command for mailbox list, then search and fetch for elin/INBOX with seen subject '[DRILL]'. Inspect the UID and Subject before running expunge with that same query. Repeat for Archive.
practice.observe: Only the read notice in each folder matches; the unread [DRILL] notices and gabe’s mail are outside this selection. Expunge changes the stored mail immediately; another search shows no remaining matches.

practice.title: Check and try a useful counterexample

practice.observe: The broader query selects a remaining protected unread notice; the precise query has no remaining matches. Previewing changes no mail. If you remove protected mail, read the failed outcome and the Reset confirmation before restoring this lesson’s supplied work.

goal: Separate traffic addressed to the router from traffic passing through it, then allow only the supplied administration, web and DNS uses.
context: A Linux router can be both a computer and a path between computers. Build on IPv4 routes and SSH administration: the destination decides which filter chain to inspect. The supplied diagram and traffic table are read-only policy analysis, not real packet capture.

concepts.title: Choose the chain before the rule
concepts.text: INPUT handles traffic whose destination is this router. FORWARD handles traffic routed through it. OUTPUT handles traffic created by the router. An INPUT web rule cannot allow a LAN workstation to reach a remote web server.

concepts.title: Read a rule as a set of requirements
concepts.text: Every option on one rule must match: -i names the incoming interface, -o the outgoing interface, -s the source subnet, -d the destination, -p the protocol and --dport the destination port. Use numeric addresses and ports here; /32 means one IPv4 address. A TCP web rule does not allow UDP DNS.

concepts.title: Order matters
concepts.text: iptables -S shows each chain policy and its rules in order. The first matching ACCEPT or DROP ends the decision; the chain policy applies when no rule matches. A broad early ACCEPT can admit traffic you meant to block. -F empties rules but retains the policy; it does not mean block everything.

concepts.title: Allow only the assignment uses
concepts.text: Use the supplied LAN subnet and exact router or remote destination. Keep unsolicited WAN administration and other transit blocked. These one-way header checks do not model connection tracking, reply traffic, NAT or a complete deployable firewall.

worked.label: Inspect the example
worked.explanation: Read the broad SSH and DNS rules before changing them. INPUT and FORWARD serve different destinations.

worked.label: Clear obsolete permits
worked.explanation: Remove the example’s obsolete rules. The DROP policies remain; OUTPUT continues to permit router-originated traffic.

worked.label: Permit example administration
worked.explanation: Only LAN SSH addressed to this router matches. A WAN SSH header and a TCP/443 header addressed to the router do not.

worked.label: Permit example web transit
worked.value: iptables -A FORWARD -i lan0 -o wan0 -s 172.20.4.0/24 -d 198.51.100.9 -p tcp --dport 443 -j ACCEPT
worked.explanation: The LAN source, output interface, remote destination and web port are all constrained.

worked.label: Permit example DNS transit
worked.value: iptables -A FORWARD -i lan0 -o wan0 -s 172.20.4.0/24 -d 198.51.100.53 -p udp --dport 53 -j ACCEPT
worked.explanation: DNS uses its own supplied destination and UDP port in this exercise. Check the example after adding both transit rules.

practice.title: Inspect and predict
practice.action: Run iptables -S, then select LAN web transit in Traffic cases and choose Trace policy. Compare its destination with the router’s own addresses.
practice.observe: The router-local web permit does not admit this transit header. Trace policy explains a modeled decision and does not change rules.

practice.title: Repair the example

practice.observe: Re-run a permitted case and a blocked case. A rule that is too broad may pass the chosen case while failing the full policy check.

practice.observe: The broad early allow breaks the policy. Feedback identifies the responsible rule or fallback policy; checking also considers addresses and ports beyond the displayed cases.

goal: Diagnose a failed LAN-to-server path without opening an already-correct filter.
context: The filter now expresses the intended policy, but a permit alone cannot make a route work. Build on the previous lesson: investigate the forwarding setting and the route chosen for the destination before editing rules.

concepts.title: Permission and reachability differ
concepts.text: The filter can allow a header while the router still cannot forward it. Read the forwarding setting, interface state and route before broadening a firewall rule. Keep the stated SSH, web and DNS policy intact.

concepts.title: Forwarding is a separate switch
concepts.text: sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward reads the simulated switch. A value of 0 disables transit; 1 enables it. sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 changes the running setting only. It does not repair a route or save a startup file.

concepts.title: The most specific route wins
concepts.text: A matching /24 route is preferred over a /0 default, even when the default uses an available gateway. Route metrics decide between otherwise equally specific candidates. A syntactically valid gateway can still be unavailable in the supplied topology.

concepts.title: Trace the layered repair
concepts.text: Trace policy first reports a blocking path condition, then the selected chain or filter decision once reachable. Repair one cause, trace again and verify the allowed and blocked uses. The supplied peer availability is fixed scenario evidence, not real ARP or a network probe.

worked.label: Inspect the switch
worked.explanation: The example starts at 0. Traffic addressed to the router can still use INPUT while transit is disabled.

worked.label: Read routes
worked.explanation: The example’s 198.51.100.0/24 route selects unavailable gateway 192.0.2.253; the available default gateway is 192.0.2.254.

worked.label: Enable transit
worked.explanation: This exposes the next problem rather than hiding it. Trace the LAN web case again.

worked.label: Repair the selected path
worked.value: ip -4 route replace 198.51.100.0/24 via 192.0.2.254 dev wan0 metric 5
worked.explanation: Replacing the specific route with the supplied available next hop restores the path. Removing the bad specific route so the valid default is used is also supported.

worked.label: Verify policy and path
worked.value:
iptables -S
sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward
ip -4 route show
worked.explanation: Recheck that the narrow rules remain in place and all required allowed and blocked traffic outcomes pass.

practice.observe: The initial transit failure is forwarding off; the route table also contains a more-specific path to inspect.

practice.title: Repair one cause at a time
practice.action: Enable IPv4 forwarding and trace the same case again. Use the supplied gateway evidence to repair the route; do not replace the filter with ACCEPT.
practice.observe: The feedback changes from disabled forwarding to the unavailable selected gateway, then to the permitted path after both repairs.

practice.action: Choose Check example and inspect the blocked cases as well as the successful web and DNS cases. Try disabling wan0, trace, then bring it back up and retry.
practice.observe: Link state is a separate failure condition. Correct filtering does not compensate for a down interface.

goal: Preserve a working router policy in valid simulated configuration files, then verify that reloading those files preserves its behavior.
context: The current router passes its live checks, but its saved files would reopen transit and turn forwarding off if reapplied. Build on the two previous repairs. Here the editor and terminal deliberately control different things.

concepts.title: Working now is not saved for later
concepts.text: iptables -S and sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward describe running state. cat /etc/lab-filter.rules and cat /etc/sysctl.d/lab-forwarding.conf describe saved simulated files. A correct live state does not prove the saved setup is correct.

concepts.title: Export and edit deliberately
concepts.text: iptables-save -t filter prints a snapshot; adding -f /etc/lab-filter.rules writes that snapshot to the simulated file. The file editor has an independent draft. Save file writes that draft; it does not apply the file to running state. Unsaved edits survive command queries and exports.

concepts.title: Validate before applying
concepts.text: iptables-restore --test /etc/lab-filter.rules parses the saved snapshot without replacing live rules. A valid snapshot can still express an unsafe policy. sysctl -p /etc/sysctl.d/lab-forwarding.conf and iptables-restore /etc/lab-filter.rules explicitly apply the selected saved settings.

concepts.title: Verify both versions of the policy
concepts.text: Check work tests your running settings and checks the result of loading the saved files again. Save both drafts before checking. This does not reboot a real computer or set up a distribution’s boot service.

worked.label: Compare active and saved
worked.explanation: The example’s live rules are narrow, but the saved file has ACCEPT policies and the saved switch is 0.

worked.label: Save the active filter
worked.explanation: Export the already-correct active policy. If you have an unsaved editor draft it stays intact; Reload editor explicitly replaces only the selected draft.

worked.label: Edit the saved forwarding file
worked.explanation: Choose the forwarding file, enter the setting and Save file. Editing or saving does not change the live switch.

worked.label: Validate and apply
worked.explanation: The first command validates only. The next two apply. Re-run inspection and policy traces before checking the whole task.

practice.title: Compare two sources of truth
practice.action: Inspect running rules and forwarding, then read both saved files. Choose a file in the editor and compare its text with cat output.
practice.observe: A correct live policy can coexist with an unsafe saved file. A saved editor draft and the running setting are separate.

practice.title: Save and reapply the example
practice.action: Export the example’s active filter, set the saved forwarding value to 1 with the editor and Save file. Validate the saved filter, then explicitly apply both files.
practice.observe: The terminal reports parsing or unsupported-syntax errors without pretending to run a shell. Saving alone does not run an apply command.

practice.title: Check the reloaded outcome
practice.action: Choose Check example. Change the forwarding draft to 0, save it and check again; then restore 1, save, apply and retry.
practice.observe: The live switch can still be on while Reloaded setup checks fail. Unsaved edits clear the old success before you check again.

requirements: Preserve the currently correct live forwarding, routes, interface addresses and narrow INPUT, FORWARD and OUTPUT policies.
Save a valid filter snapshot to /etc/lab-filter.rules and the required forwarding setting to /etc/sysctl.d/lab-forwarding.conf.
Save both current editor drafts. The saved setup must reproduce every required policy and supplied traffic outcome when reapplied.
Use the supplied virtual files only. No boot service, host firewall, real packet counter or actual reboot is part of this simulator task.

goal: Share one public address while returning tracked replies and blocking new inbound traffic.
context: Builds on the Linux routers unit: numeric prefixes, FORWARD rule order, protocol/port matches and route inspection. This lesson introduces tracked conversations and address translation; no real router or root access is required.

concepts.title: Recognize one conversation
concepts.text: A connection is identified by its protocol and both address/port pairs. 172.20.4.55:41000 means address 172.20.4.55 using port 41000. Two clients can choose the same source port because their private addresses differ. TCP and UDP remain different conversations.

concepts.title: Give replies a path back
concepts.text: NEW means this tracked conversation has not been seen in both directions. The first observed reply is ESTABLISHED; this does not prove a complete TCP handshake or working application. An ESTABLISHED permit lets tracked traffic return without permitting an unrelated NEW arrival.

concepts.title: Share the public source address
concepts.text: Source NAT (SNAT) replaces the outgoing source address after the FORWARD filter. The router retains a mapping so replies return to the right client. If two clients would produce the same public tuple, they need different translated source ports. NAT alone does not allow traffic through the filter.

concepts.title: Inspect, change and test
concepts.text: iptables -S lists filter rules; iptables -t nat -S lists the supported translation rules. The first matching rule wins. Run traffic test uses separate sample flows and an empty simulated connection table each time; your rules and command draft stay in place. These native tests send no real packets.

worked.label: Permit tracked traffic
worked.explanation: Permit tracked traffic that has been observed in both directions; this is not an unsolicited NEW permit.

worked.label: Source translation
worked.value: iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -o wan0 -s 172.20.4.0/24 -p tcp -j SNAT --to-source 192.0.2.1
worked.explanation: Use the example public source address. With no explicit port range, preserve a free port or allocate another in its modeled class.

worked.label: Read the address changes
worked.explanation: The first client can keep port 41000 when free; the second needs another public port. This is a worked illustration, not a run result.

practice.title: Inspect both rule sets
practice.action: Choose iptables -S and iptables -t nat -S from Example command; Insert command only fills the field, then Run command applies it.
practice.observe: The example admits new outgoing web traffic, but its incoming state rule is wrong and the source translation has only one available public port.

practice.title: Repair and observe two clients
practice.action: Use the complete worked commands if needed. Select Two clients share one address and Run traffic test. Use Inspect event to compare the second request and both replies.
practice.observe: Correct rules allow two distinct public source ports and return each reply to its original private client. Expected results and actual tuples are labeled separately.

practice.title: Check, then diagnose a new mistake
practice.action: Choose Check example. Try the one-port rule from the command picker, run the traffic test and check again; remove that inserted first POSTROUTING rule and retry.
practice.observe: A correct first request does not prove that both clients or their replies work. Each test starts new sample flows, so a previous mapping cannot hide the new error.

requirements: Allow NEW traffic from LAN 10.20.30.0/24 on lan0, leaving wan0, only to 203.0.113.9 using TCP destination port 443.
Keep ESTABLISHED traffic passing in the supplied topology. Refuse other NEW traffic, including new inbound requests and UDP impostors.

Translate the required outbound source to public address 198.51.100.1. Clients 10.20.30.55 and 10.20.30.56 both use source port 40000; they need distinct usable public mappings and replies to the correct private client.
Keep PREROUTING, INPUT, OUTPUT and the supplied route/interface facts unchanged. Equivalent supported FORWARD and source-translation rules are accepted.

goal: Publish one public TCP endpoint without opening direct private-address access or breaking existing outbound traffic.
context: Builds on the Linux routers unit: numeric prefixes, FORWARD rule order, protocol/port matches and route inspection. This lesson introduces tracked conversations and address translation; no real router or root access is required.

concepts.title: Follow the public request to the private server
concepts.text: Destination NAT (DNAT) changes the destination before route selection and FORWARD filtering. In this worked network, public 192.0.2.1:9443 becomes private server 172.20.4.42:443. The filter must match the rewritten private address and port, rather than the public tuple.

concepts.title: Keep requests and replies consistent
concepts.text: The retained connection mapping reverses the destination change for replies. The external client therefore sees replies from 192.0.2.1:9443, not from the server’s private address. Source translation for unrelated outbound clients is a separate POSTROUTING rule set.

concepts.title: Require actual destination translation
concepts.text: The conntrack DNAT flag says this connection’s destination was rewritten. It is independent of NEW/ESTABLISHED. A comma list means either condition: NEW,DNAT would also match a NEW request sent directly to the private server. Require DNAT for this inbound service permit and keep the separate ESTABLISHED permit.

concepts.title: Verify the scope as well as one success
concepts.text: A working public request is only part of this task. Other public ports, UDP and direct private requests must remain unpublished or filtered. Read incoming, at-filter and outgoing tuples in a traffic result. The full check also compares the stated address/port domains beyond the displayed clients.

worked.label: Destination translation
worked.value: iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -i wan0 -d 192.0.2.1 -p tcp --dport 9443 -j DNAT --to-destination 172.20.4.42:443
worked.explanation: Rewrite only the example public TCP/9443 endpoint to private 172.20.4.42:443, before routing and filtering.

worked.label: Filter the rewritten endpoint
worked.value: iptables -A FORWARD -i wan0 -o lan0 -d 172.20.4.42 -p tcp --dport 443 -m conntrack --ctstate DNAT -j ACCEPT
worked.explanation: Permit the rewritten example server endpoint only when destination translation actually happened.

worked.label: Read the address changes
worked.value:
Incoming destination: 192.0.2.1:9443
At-filter destination: 172.20.4.42:443
Reply source: 192.0.2.1:9443
worked.explanation: The public client and the FORWARD filter see different destination stages. This is a worked illustration, not a run result.

practice.title: Find the address stage that is wrong
practice.action: Inspect filter and NAT rules, then select Reach the published service and Run traffic test. Inspect the first external request.
practice.observe: Incoming uses public 192.0.2.1:9443. At filter shows the destination after DNAT; the intentional wrong server address is visible there.

practice.title: Repair the target and the permit
practice.action: Use the separate worked commands to correct PREROUTING and the FORWARD permit. Run the published-service, direct-private and outbound two-client tests.
practice.observe: The filter must use the private server/443 plus the DNAT flag. Replies use the public endpoint; the separate outbound source rules still work.

practice.title: Check the boundary, not only the server
practice.action: Choose Check example. Try the NEW,DNAT rule from the picker, then run Direct private address stays protected. Delete that inserted first FORWARD rule and retry.
practice.observe: Comma means either state. A direct private request has NEW without DNAT and must still be refused. Full checks also catch unwanted redirects beyond the displayed cases.

requirements: Publish only 198.51.100.1 TCP/8443 arriving on wan0, forwarding it to private server 10.20.30.42 TCP/443 on lan0.
Permit that rewritten endpoint only when destination translation actually occurred. Refuse NEW requests sent directly to the private address; keep ESTABLISHED traffic passing.
Leave other incoming destinations unchanged: no other public port, address or UDP endpoint is published by these rules.
Preserve NEW LAN TCP/443 access to 203.0.113.9 and its public source translation to 198.51.100.1, including clients 10.20.30.55 and 10.20.30.56 using source port 40000 and their replies.
Keep router-local INPUT/OUTPUT, routes and interfaces as supplied. Equivalent supported policy/translation rules are accepted.

goal: Match IPv6 control headers by direction, LAN prefix, type and code.
context: Builds on Linux host IPv6, fixed router paths and direction tracking. Read colon-separated addresses as whole values and /64 as a prefix range. No real router, root privileges or outside setup is needed.

concepts.title: Use the IPv6 rule table
concepts.text: A packet header contains addresses and protocol information. ip6tables handles the supplied IPv6 headers; an IPv4 iptables permit does not apply to them. Read the rules from top to bottom: the first match decides, then the chain policy applies if none matched.

concepts.title: Match the path, not just a number
concepts.text: FORWARD handles traffic crossing the router. lan0 to wan0 leaves the LAN; wan0 to lan0 enters it. INPUT is for this router itself and stays supplied here. In the worked example, fd42:11:22::/64 is the LAN range. A /128 is one address, not the whole LAN.

concepts.title: Read an ICMPv6 type and code
concepts.text: ICMPv6 uses a type and a code instead of TCP/UDP ports. Type 2/code 0 is Packet Too Big, type 128/code 0 an echo request, and type 129/code 0 an echo reply. --icmpv6-type 2/0 checks both numbers; --icmpv6-type 2 alone accepts every numeric code for that type.

concepts.title: Separate a header permit from working networking
concepts.text: These exercises compare selected headers, not a production firewall policy. An echo-reply permit here is stateless: it does not prove a request existed. A real IPv6 network also needs appropriate neighbor discovery and other control behavior. Link-local addresses stay on their link; documentation prefixes here are not Internet targets.

worked.label: Incoming size-control header
worked.value: ip6tables -A FORWARD -i wan0 -o lan0 -d fd42:11:22::/64 -p ipv6-icmp --icmpv6-type 2/0 -j ACCEPT
worked.explanation: Permit exactly the example LAN’s incoming Packet Too Big type 2, code 0 headers. This is a header predicate, not validation of an actual error message or working PMTU discovery.

worked.label: Outgoing echo-request header
worked.value: ip6tables -A FORWARD -i lan0 -o wan0 -s fd42:11:22::/64 -p ipv6-icmp --icmpv6-type 128/0 -j ACCEPT
worked.explanation: Permit the example LAN’s outgoing echo-request headers; type 128 and code 0 are separate numbers.

worked.label: Incoming echo-reply header
worked.value: ip6tables -A FORWARD -i wan0 -o lan0 -d fd42:11:22::/64 -p ipv6-icmp --icmpv6-type 129/0 -j ACCEPT
worked.explanation: Permit echo-reply headers toward the example LAN. This stateless match does not establish whether a request was sent.

practice.title: Inspect the actual IPv6 rules
practice.action: Choose ip6tables -S in Example command, Insert command, then Run command. Run Selected control headers and inspect its two events.
practice.observe: A broad type permit can admit the wrong code, even when the required type 2/code 0 sample passes.

practice.title: Repair the separate example
practice.action: Use the worked commands if needed. Run Selected control headers, Echo header directions and Other protocols stay blocked.
practice.observe: Only the specified directions, LAN prefix and type/code combinations pass. TCP/UDP remain outside this control-only assignment.

practice.title: Test a missing code
practice.action: Choose Check example. Insert and run the type-2-only experiment; rerun Selected control headers. Delete the inserted first rule and retry.
practice.observe: Type 2 without /0 matches the wrong-code header. A passing example requires the entire stated policy, not just one green event.

requirements: Permit incoming ICMPv6 type 2, code 0 through wan0 to lan0, destination LAN fd20:30:40::/64.
Permit outgoing echo requests (type 128, code 0) from that LAN through lan0 to wan0.
Permit incoming echo replies (type 129, code 0) toward that LAN through wan0 to lan0. These are stateless header matches.
Drop other ICMPv6 headers, including wrong codes/directions, and all TCP/UDP for this control-only task.
Keep supplied INPUT/OUTPUT, forwarding, interfaces and routes unchanged. A filter cannot route link-local addresses to another link.

goal: Restore precise outgoing web requests, tracked replies and the selected control header.
context: Builds on Linux host IPv6, fixed router paths and direction tracking. Read colon-separated addresses as whole values and /64 as a prefix range. No real router, root privileges or outside setup is needed.

concepts.title: Keep the complete IPv6 address
concepts.text: IPv6 prefixes still describe ranges. In the worked example, fd42:11:22::/64 identifies the LAN and 2001:db8:90::/64 the remote service range. A /128 rule for the displayed client would omit other required clients. ULA fd00::/8 is locally assigned private addressing; the documentation addresses here stand in for a remote role, not real Internet targets.

concepts.title: Follow a request and its actual reverse
concepts.text: A TCP conversation uses both addresses and both ports. The original request goes to destination port 443. Its reverse has source port 443. NEW means the simulator has not observed both directions; the first observed reverse is ESTABLISHED. Both directions stay ESTABLISHED afterward. This is not a completed TCP handshake.

concepts.title: Keep direction and state together
concepts.text: The worked outbound rule allows NEW,ESTABLISHED but still restricts interfaces, both prefixes and destination port. The inbound rule allows only ESTABLISHED with the reverse prefixes and source port. Putting NEW in that inbound list would admit an unrelated arrival.

concepts.title: Handle control headers separately
concepts.text: ICMPv6 has types/codes, not TCP ports. This profile does not track ICMPv6 or RELATED errors, so type 2/code 0 is an explicit stateless requirement. Passing it does not prove neighbor discovery, PMTU discovery or a working application.

worked.label: Outgoing request and follow-up
worked.value: ip6tables -A FORWARD -i lan0 -o wan0 -s fd42:11:22::/64 -d 2001:db8:90::/64 -p tcp --dport 443 -m conntrack --ctstate NEW,ESTABLISHED -j ACCEPT
worked.explanation: Keep the example’s TCP web request permitted both before and after its reply is observed. Both address prefixes, direction and destination port still restrict the permit.

worked.label: Tracked reverse direction
worked.value: ip6tables -A FORWARD -i wan0 -o lan0 -s 2001:db8:90::/64 -d fd42:11:22::/64 -p tcp --sport 443 -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED -j ACCEPT
worked.explanation: Permit the reverse example TCP tuple only after a reply direction is observed. Its source port is 443; an unrelated NEW inbound header must still be dropped.

worked.label: Incoming size-control header
worked.value: ip6tables -A FORWARD -i wan0 -o lan0 -d fd42:11:22::/64 -p ipv6-icmp --icmpv6-type 2/0 -j ACCEPT
worked.explanation: Permit exactly the example LAN’s incoming Packet Too Big type 2, code 0 headers. This is a header predicate, not validation of an actual error message or working PMTU discovery.

practice.title: Read the broken direction rules
practice.action: Choose ip6tables -S, Insert command, then Run command. Run Request, reply and follow-up and inspect each event.
practice.observe: The original can pass while the actual reverse and later original fail. Read NEW/ESTABLISHED and the running rule number beside each actual result.

practice.title: Repair the separate example
practice.action: Use the worked example commands if needed. Run Request, reply and follow-up, Another client and server in the ranges, and Keep the selected ICMPv6 header.
practice.observe: The reply uses reversed addresses/ports. A second client must also work; ICMPv6 remains stateless.

practice.title: Try an overbroad reply permit
practice.action: Choose Check example. Insert and run the NEW,ESTABLISHED experiment for the inbound permit; run Unsolicited traffic stays blocked. Delete its inserted first rule and retry.
practice.observe: An apparently valid source port does not make an unrelated arrival a tracked reply. The independent policy comparison also checks unlisted addresses.

requirements: Permit only TCP from LAN fd20:30:40::/64 on lan0 toward 2001:db8:60::/64 through wan0, destination port 443, in NEW and ESTABLISHED contexts.
Permit reverse TCP from that remote /64 to the LAN through wan0 to lan0, source port 443, only in ESTABLISHED context.
Retain incoming ICMPv6 type 2, code 0 from wan0 to the LAN through lan0. Other ICMPv6 headers are outside this task’s permit.
Drop other TCP/UDP, including unsolicited inbound headers, UDP impostors, wrong prefixes and wrong service ports.
Keep the supplied INPUT/OUTPUT, forwarding, interfaces and routes unchanged. No source or destination translation is needed.

goal: Repair saved service names and replace obsolete numeric permits without widening access.
context: Builds on protocol-specific service-file repair and IPv6 tracked filtering. TCP/UDP listener numbers are supplied; focus on the link between a saved mapping and an installed rule. No real router or outside setup is needed.

concepts.title: A name selects a port within one transport
concepts.text: A local services entry links a name and aliases to one port/protocol pair. These supplied names are lab mappings, not universal port assignments. In the worked example, preview/tcp must select 9443 and preview/udp must select 9553. One shared alias can have a different number under each transport.

concepts.title: Read the saved file before changing it
concepts.text: cat /etc/services shows the simulated saved file. getent services previews/tcp asks for the TCP meaning of that alias; /udp asks separately. A successful lookup proves a mapping exists, not that a server is running or traffic can pass. The supplied listener ports are the task facts.

concepts.title: Saving a name does not reload a rule
concepts.text: When a named ip6tables port is used, the simulator resolves it when creating the rule and stores the number. After saving a repaired file, ip6tables -S can still show the obsolete number. Replace the affected permit; new rule creation then uses the saved mapping. A numeric port is also a valid solution when the required file meanings are correct.

concepts.title: Verify the policy as well as the sample
concepts.text: Run both TCP and UDP request/reply tests, then test old and crossed ports and unsolicited traffic. A reverse permit needs ESTABLISHED, the reversed prefixes and the service source port. Preserve the selected control header. Check example compares the entire stated address and port ranges as well as the samples; it does not prove a real application or TCP handshake.

worked.label: Example local mappings
worked.value:
preview 9443/tcp previews
preview 9553/udp previews
clock 123/udp time
worked.explanation: Two protocol-specific entries share one alias. Keep the unrelated clock mapping; Save virtual file changes future lookups.

worked.label: Observe the saved TCP name
worked.explanation: The correct example lookup selects 9443/tcp. Actual output appears only after Run command; this row is the worked expectation.

worked.label: Create a new outgoing permit
worked.value: ip6tables -A FORWARD -i lan0 -o wan0 -s fd55:60:70::/64 -d 2001:db8:160::/64 -p tcp --dport previews -m conntrack --ctstate NEW,ESTABLISHED -j ACCEPT
worked.explanation: Use the saved example alias when recreating the permit; -S will show the number actually stored. The complete example sequence also restores UDP, reverse rules and the selected control header.

practice.title: Repair the example mapping
practice.action: The example listeners use preview/tcp 9443 and preview/udp 9553, both with alias previews. In the editor, repair those two entries, keep clock and time at 123/udp, then choose Save virtual file.
practice.observe: Saved changes future lookups. It does not change the numbers in already installed rules.

practice.title: Compare the lookup with installed rules
practice.action: Choose getent services previews/tcp, Insert command, then Run command; repeat with /udp. Run ip6tables -S and compare the stored port numbers. Replace the obsolete permits using the separate worked sequence if needed.
practice.observe: An apparently correct saved name can coexist with an obsolete numeric rule. New named rules print the numbers actually resolved.

practice.title: Test the repair and its boundaries
practice.action: Run TCP request, reply and follow-up, then the UDP test. Test old/crossed ports, unsolicited arrivals and the selected control header. Choose Check example after the repair.
practice.observe: Both transports and actual reverse directions must pass while unwanted traffic stays blocked. The assignment keeps its own file, commands and rules.

requirements: Save only these lookup meanings: report/tcp and reports/tcp select port 7443; report/udp and reports/udp select port 8853; clock/udp and time/udp select port 123. Comments, spacing, row order and canonical/alias choice may differ.

Permit outgoing TCP/7443 and UDP/8853 from LAN fd66:70:80::/64 on lan0 toward 2001:db8:180::/64 through wan0 in NEW and ESTABLISHED contexts. Permit their reverse traffic only in ESTABLISHED context with the matching service source port.

Replace the obsolete numeric permits: saving a mapping alone does not update installed rules. Block other TCP/UDP, including old ports, crossed protocol numbers, unsolicited arrivals and wrong ranges/directions. All addresses in the stated ranges must work, not only displayed samples.
Keep incoming ICMPv6 type 2, code 0 from wan0 to that LAN through lan0; block other modeled ICMPv6 headers. Keep supplied INPUT/OUTPUT, forwarding, routes and interfaces unchanged.

goal: Choose a valid LAN address and the correct scoped next hop without widening the route.
context: Builds on Linux IPv6 address/route investigation and router path practice.

concepts.title: An address belongs to an interface and a network
concepts.text: A /64 identifies the network in these supplied links. fd35:40:50::10/64 belongs to fd35:40:50::/64, a unique-local network used here for the client LAN. 2001:db8::/32 addresses are documentation examples. Neither prefix sends traffic to the real Internet. IPv6 has no broadcast address; this task excludes the all-zero interface ID and known peer addresses.

concepts.title: A link-local next hop needs its interface
concepts.text: fe80::1 is a link-local next hop: it identifies a neighbor on one link. fe80::1 can name different routers on different links. The worked upstream router is fe80::1 on uplink0; the same number on edge0 is a different neighbor with a different onward path. Always read both via and dev. A route alone does not establish neighbor availability or the remote host.

concepts.title: Repair the complete route plan
concepts.text: The worked router needs only 2001:db8:45::/64 through uplink0, plus its directly connected networks. An obsolete default sends unrelated destinations to the wrong link. Delete that route before removing its interface address, add an unused address in the supplied LAN, then add the required remote prefix. Forwarding is already enabled in this lesson.

concepts.title: Verify more than one displayed client
concepts.text: Check example compares every destination region, supplied reachable hosts and separate transit headers. Equivalent split prefixes and different unused LAN addresses can work. A /128 for one displayed server is insufficient when the assignment requires its whole /64.

worked.label: Remove the broad default
worked.value: ip -6 route del ::/0 via fe80::1 dev edge0 metric 10
worked.explanation: Delete the route through the client link before removing its primary address. Unrelated destinations must not keep using that next hop.

worked.label: Remove the wrong primary address
worked.explanation: Remove the address from the wrong network after deleting dependent gateway routes. This model gives each interface one primary address.

worked.label: Choose an address in the supplied LAN
worked.value: ip -6 address add fd35:40:50::10/64 dev edge0
worked.explanation: Install an unused address in fd35:40:50::/64 on edge0. Another unused interface ID in that same /64 is also valid.

worked.label: Route the whole remote network
worked.value: ip -6 route add 2001:db8:45::/64 via fe80::1 dev uplink0 metric 10
worked.explanation: Reach all of 2001:db8:45::/64 through fe80::1 on uplink0. A host route for only one displayed server does not meet the network requirement.

practice.title: Inspect the wrong scope
practice.action: Run ip -6 address show, ip -6 route show and sysctl net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding. Compare edge0 with its supplied fd35:40:50::/64 LAN.
practice.observe: The primary address is outside the supplied LAN, and the broad default points at the same-named router on the wrong interface.

practice.title: Repair in dependency order
practice.action: Delete the obsolete default before deleting edge0’s bad address. Add an unused /64 address in its supplied LAN, then add the remote /64 through uplink0. Use the command picker for separate examples.
practice.observe: The route table should cover both connected networks and the required remote network, without an extra default.

practice.title: Verify and try a misleading shortcut
practice.action: Run the supplied transit cases, then Check example. Try replacing the remote /64 with a /128 for just one server and check again.
practice.observe: A displayed server can work while the complete route-plan requirement fails; restore full coverage before the assignment.

requirements: Choose an unused primary address in fd62:70:80::/64 on lan0; avoid supplied peers and the all-zero interface ID. Keep wan0 and all IPv4 settings unchanged.
Route the entire 2001:db8:99::/64 through fe80::1 on wan0. Outside connected networks and that remote prefix, retain no IPv6 route. Preserve enabled forwarding.
Verify both supplied remote hosts, client transit and the link-local scope boundary; Check work must pass the complete route plan.

goal: Enable transit and learn a default only from the upstream link.
context: Builds on the previous lesson’s scoped routes and supplied path tests.

concepts.title: Choosing a route and forwarding are different
concepts.text: A host can know a route without being allowed to carry another computer’s traffic. net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding=1 sets the supplied interfaces to router mode. In the worked example, traffic enters edge0 and leaves uplink0; both the route and forwarding must work. The dotted sysctl key net.ipv6.conf.uplink0.accept_ra corresponds to /proc/sys/net/ipv6/conf/uplink0/accept_ra; cat reads that same virtual value.

concepts.title: A router normally stops accepting advertisements
concepts.text: A router advertisement is a message received from a local router. accept_ra=1 accepts it only while that interface is a host; accept_ra=2 explicitly permits it in router mode. Set uplink0 to 2 and the client-facing edge0 to 0 so only the upstream message can supply a default.

concepts.title: A setting does not create a message
concepts.text: Choose the supplied upstream advertisement and Observe supplied message after configuring the flags. This native simulator action represents an already-received message, not a Linux command or a packet sent to a real network. ip -6 route show then displays the actual learned default via fe80::1 on uplink0 at metric 1024.

concepts.title: Verify rejection and withdrawal too
concepts.text: Observe the client-link message: it must be ignored. An accepted zero-lifetime upstream message withdraws the default; observe the positive upstream message again to recover. Check example independently tests all three cases using their own sample messages, and requires an actual active upstream default. No clocks, expiry, SLAAC or full neighbor discovery are modeled.

worked.label: Enable IPv6 transit
worked.explanation: Set the supplied interfaces to router mode. With accept_ra=1, a forwarding write can remove an earlier learned default; configure upstream acceptance and observe a new message afterward.

worked.label: Allow upstream advertisements in router mode
worked.explanation: Value 2 explicitly keeps advertisement acceptance enabled while uplink0 acts as a router. This changes policy; it does not create a received message.

worked.label: Ignore client-link advertisements
worked.explanation: Value 0 prevents the client-facing link from supplying a default. The same fe80::1 on that link is a different scoped neighbor.

practice.title: Compare role and advertisement policy
practice.action: Read global forwarding and each example interface’s accept_ra setting using the command picker. Observe the upstream message before changing the role.
practice.observe: A host can learn a default, but transit still fails while forwarding is off. Enabling forwarding with accept_ra=1 can remove the learned default.

practice.title: Configure, then observe
practice.action: Enable global forwarding; set uplink0.accept_ra to 2 and edge0.accept_ra to 0. Choose the positive upstream message and Observe supplied message.
practice.observe: Read the actual ip -6 route show output: the learned default appears only after the supplied observation.

practice.title: Exercise rejection and recovery
practice.action: Observe the client-link message and the zero-lifetime upstream withdrawal. Run a transit test, then observe the positive upstream message again and Check example.
practice.observe: The client message is ignored. Withdrawal removes the route; a new accepted upstream observation restores it.

requirements: Preserve both supplied IPv6 addresses and all IPv4 configuration; enable global IPv6 forwarding.
Accept upstream advertisements on wan0 while it is a router; ignore advertisements on lan0. Observe the supplied upstream message to create the active learned default.
Keep the default selected through fe80::1 on wan0. Verify the supplied paths and message acceptance, rejection and withdrawal cases.

goal: Keep live and saved router settings correct, then test them separately.
context: Builds on the previous lesson’s scoped routes and supplied path tests.

concepts.title: Live changes and future startup are separate
concepts.text: sysctl -w changes current virtual settings. The editor holds a draft of one simulated settings file. Save virtual file validates and stores that draft; it does not load the settings into the current router. cat reads the saved file, not unsaved text.

concepts.title: Load the saved file deliberately
concepts.text: For the worked example, put forwarding=1, uplink0.accept_ra=2 and edge0.accept_ra=0 under their full net.ipv6.conf keys. sysctl -p /etc/sysctl.d/70-learning-lab-ipv6.conf loads this saved file. Then observe the supplied upstream message: loading flags alone does not produce a new learned route.

concepts.title: Test what survives fresh settings
concepts.text: Run saved-settings test resets only modeled IPv6 flags and learned routes, loads the saved file and supplies the new upstream message. The addresses and network configuration are already persistent in this exercise. This is a simulated settings restart test, not a complete Linux reboot, interface activation or firewall boot test.

concepts.title: Keep the file understandable
concepts.text: Use one supported decimal assignment per line. Whole-line # or ; comments and surrounding whitespace are supported. Duplicate keys apply in order, so the last value wins. The grade checks resulting behavior, not exact text. Unsupported keys, includes, wildcards and shell syntax are diagnosed rather than executed.

worked.label: Separate example saved file
worked.value:
# Forward transit and accept upstream messages only
net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding = 1
net.ipv6.conf.uplink0.accept_ra = 2
net.ipv6.conf.edge0.accept_ra = 0
worked.explanation: Save the example draft, load this file with sysctl -p, then observe the supplied upstream message. These are worked values, not actual run output.

practice.title: Edit and save deliberately
practice.action: Use the example editor to set the three required keys. Choose Save virtual file, then read the file with cat from the command picker.
practice.observe: Saved means stored in the virtual file. It does not mean the current router has loaded the new flags.

practice.title: Load and observe
practice.action: Run sysctl -p for the supplied file, then Observe supplied message for the upstream advertisement. Inspect settings and ip -6 route show.
practice.observe: Current flags and an actually learned default must both be present.

practice.title: Test restart and a forgotten save
practice.action: Choose Run saved-settings test. Change only the editor’s forwarding value to 0 without saving, then Check example; read the unsaved-draft feedback. Restore, save, reload and check.
practice.observe: The saved-settings test shows actual results separately from the current router; unsaved edits do not count as the required saved configuration.

requirements: Preserve the supplied addresses and IPv4 configuration. Save the virtual IPv6 settings file with global forwarding enabled, upstream router advertisements accepted on wan0 and client-link advertisements ignored on lan0.
Load the saved file into the current router and observe the supplied upstream message. An unsaved draft, live-only changes or flags without a learned default are insufficient.
Run the saved-settings test and Check work. Both the current router and fresh settings loaded from the saved file must satisfy the path, scope and advertisement requirements.

goal: Keep the required IPv6 filter policy working now and after startup.
context: Capstone: first complete scoped Linux IPv6 configuration and tracked IPv6 router policy. Those lessons teach prefixes, next-hop scope, filter chains and direction-state matches.

concepts.title: One policy, three places
concepts.text: The running table filters traffic now. The saved rules file is only text until restored. The provided startup loader reads that file at the next simulated startup only when enabled. A correct current table cannot repair an outdated saved file by itself.

concepts.title: Inspect before replacing
concepts.text: Use ip6tables -S to inspect all chains and cat /etc/lab-ipv6-filter.rules to inspect the saved file. This capstone preserves INPUT and OUTPUT exactly. Repair FORWARD using your earlier IPv6 direction-state skills; opening every port is not a working firewall solution.

concepts.title: Save and validate the intended table
concepts.text: ip6tables-save -f /etc/lab-ipv6-filter.rules copies the running table into the simulated file. You can also edit that file and choose Save virtual file. ip6tables-restore --test followed by the exact file path checks its supported syntax without applying it. A successful syntax check says nothing about whether its policy is safe.

concepts.title: Load now, enable separately, test startup
concepts.text: The supplied lab-ipv6-filter.service is a custom oneshot loader, not a universal Linux firewall service. systemctl enable records future startup; systemctl restart reads the file now. active (exited) means that one load succeeded, not that its rules meet your assignment. Run startup test begins with fresh ACCEPT rules, then applies the enabled loader and tests the resulting policy.

concepts.title: Keep conversation and control traffic distinct
concepts.text: A passed TCP request creates the supported simulated direction-state entry; its reversed reply must actually pass to establish both directions. ICMPv6 type 2/code 0 is a selected Packet Too Big header permit, not RELATED tracking or proof of path-MTU discovery. Each traffic case starts with empty simulated connections. The full-range comparison also checks addresses and ports beyond these samples.

worked.label: Example policy
worked.explanation: Allow requests and established replies; keep the selected control header and the supplied local chains.

worked.label: Save current example rules
worked.explanation: The saved table is separate from current rules until restored.

worked.label: Validate without loading
worked.explanation: Successful parsing is not a policy grade.

worked.label: Enable and reload the provided loader
worked.value:
systemctl enable lab-ipv6-filter.service
systemctl restart lab-ipv6-filter.service
worked.explanation: Enable selects startup; restart loads now. Run startup test for actual fresh-startup results.

practice.title: Compare current and saved
practice.action: Run ip6tables -S, cat /etc/lab-ipv6-filter.rules and systemctl status lab-ipv6-filter.service. Select Request, reply and follow-up, then Run traffic test.
practice.observe: The current request uses an obsolete port; the saved FORWARD default is broader, and the provided loader is disabled. Actual results appear only after a command or test.

practice.title: Repair the example policy
practice.action: Use the example command picker to repair FORWARD for fd68:11:22::/64 → 2001:db8:78::/64 TCP 8443. Retain INPUT/OUTPUT. Run the request/reply and unsolicited-traffic cases.
practice.observe: The reply must be accepted as established traffic. Check example compares all addresses/ports in the stated policy, not only the sample servers.

practice.title: Save, load and prove the restart path
practice.action: Run ip6tables-save -f /etc/lab-ipv6-filter.rules, then the example --test command. Enable and restart the provided service. Choose Run startup test and Check example.
practice.observe: Saving, syntax validation, loading and enabling are separate operations. The startup result is separate from your current running table.

practice.title: Find a persistence regression
practice.action: Change the editor’s :FORWARD DROP line to :FORWARD ACCEPT; Save virtual file and Run startup test. Read the failing startup policy cases. Restore the intended file or save the correct running table again, then repeat the startup test.
practice.observe: Saving a bad file does not immediately alter current traffic. The fresh startup must expose it. CLI save preserves an unsaved editor draft; Reload saved file intentionally discards that draft.

requirements: On lan0, permit TCP requests from fd69:12:23::/64 to 2001:db8:79::/64 on destination port 9443, plus their established follow-up traffic. Permit the actual established reversed replies through wan0; unsolicited inbound TCP and all UDP must remain blocked.
Permit forwarded ICMPv6 type 2/code 0 from wan0 to fd69:12:23::/64 through lan0. Block other forwarded ICMPv6 headers. Keep link-local destinations on their own link.
Preserve the complete supplied INPUT and OUTPUT policies and rules. Keep the supplied persistent addresses, routes and forwarding settings unchanged.

Make both the running filter and saved /etc/lab-ipv6-filter.rules implement the complete policy. Save your intended editor draft; an unsaved draft or rules limited to the displayed clients is insufficient.
Enable the provided lab-ipv6-filter.service and verify that a fresh startup loads the saved file successfully and satisfies the same traffic and full-range requirements.

goal: Allow Mira to list and download the files supplied in her own FTP root, while refusing other login identities and preventing access outside that root.
context: Builds on Unix file access and saved-versus-running services.

concepts.title: Login and file access are different decisions
concepts.text: An FTP client asks a server to list, download or upload files. Login first selects an identity; Unix permissions then decide which files that identity can use. Use the lab’s supplied valid or invalid login examples. Type server commands in Server terminal and file-transfer commands in FTP client.

concepts.title: Choose who may log in
concepts.text: local_enable=YES permits supplied local accounts. anonymous_enable=NO refuses public anonymous login. With userlist_enable=YES and userlist_deny=NO, only exact names in /etc/vsftpd.user_list may log in. This login list does not grant file read/write permission.

concepts.title: A confined home becomes the client’s root
concepts.text: With chroot_local_user=YES, the example user Ravi sees /srv/practice/ravi as /. His /brief.txt is the server’s /srv/practice/ravi/brief.txt. Absolute client paths start inside that root, and .. stops there. Local login must first be able to search the home and its parent directories.

concepts.title: Save, restart and reconnect
concepts.text: Save virtual file keeps your edit. systemctl restart vsftpd in Server terminal applies saved configuration and ends this simulation’s existing client connection. Choose a client identity and Connect again. get brief.txt creates a simulated client download; it never reads your computer’s files.

worked.label: Example identity
worked.explanation: The assignment uses Mira; this separate practice uses Ravi.

worked.label: Login policy
worked.explanation: Permit named local accounts and refuse anonymous login.

worked.label: Login allowlist
worked.explanation: Only Ravi is allowed through the example login list.

worked.label: Root mapping
worked.explanation: The example FTP client uses /brief.txt, not the server’s full path.

worked.label: Apply and observe
worked.value: Save virtual file; systemctl restart vsftpd; Connect
worked.explanation: pwd shows /; get brief.txt downloads the real simulated text.

requirements: Allow the supplied valid Mira identity to log in; refuse Noah, anonymous, unknown and invalid-credential logins.
Mira’s home /srv/mira must appear as / to her FTP client. Listing and downloading /brief.txt must work for changing sample contents.
Absolute paths and repeated .. must not expose /srv/records/notice.txt outside Mira’s root. /private.txt must remain unreadable.
Save the required configuration/account-list edits and apply them to the running simulated service. Preserve all supplied identities and outside files.

practice.title: Configure Ravi’s identity and root
practice.action: In the editor, set local_enable=YES, anonymous_enable=NO, chroot_local_user=YES, userlist_enable=YES and userlist_deny=NO. Save virtual file. Select /etc/vsftpd.user_list, replace sara with ravi and save.
practice.observe: Saving does not apply the new service settings yet. The login list and Unix file permissions are separate.

practice.title: Apply the saved policy
practice.action: In Server terminal run cat /etc/vsftpd.conf, then systemctl restart vsftpd.
practice.observe: The service now uses the saved policy. Restart ends this simulation’s earlier client connection.

practice.title: Explore through the FTP client
practice.action: Choose Ravi’s valid identity and Connect. Run pwd, ls and get brief.txt. Then run cd ../../ and get /srv/records/notice.txt. Try connecting as Sara.
practice.observe: Ravi starts at / and downloads real sample text. Parent traversal stays at /. The outside file and Sara login are refused. Client files shows the download.
