goal: Restore Mira’s useful uploads into her inbox while keeping the jail root non-writable, private files unreadable and newly uploaded files private.
context: Builds on the preceding FTP identity lesson; keep server administration separate from the FTP client.

concepts.title: A writable root can prevent login
concepts.text: A confined FTP root must not be writable by the transfer identity in this subset. Use a non-writable home root and a separate writable child, rather than chmod 777 everywhere. In the example, admin owns Ravi’s root; mode 755 lets Ravi read/search it without writing.

concepts.title: Uploads need two independent permissions
concepts.text: write_enable=YES opens the service’s local-upload gate. Creating a file also needs write and search (w+x) on the target directory. The example inbox belongs to group uploads and Ravi is in that group; mode 770 grants its group r+w+x and grants others nothing. chmod is run as the supplied directory owner, admin.

concepts.title: The FTP mask controls newly created files
concepts.text: local_umask is a setting in vsftpd.conf, not the administrative terminal’s shell mask. A new ordinary file starts with permission bits 666; local_umask=077 removes group/other permissions, leaving 600. A leading 0 means octal. Changing the mask does not repair existing files.

concepts.title: Prove a useful transfer and its limits
concepts.text: put sample.txt inbox/report.txt sends the supplied simulated client text into the server inbox. get inbox/report.txt received.txt reads it back into Client files. A failed login is not a safe upload solution: the intended transfer must work, while root uploads and private-file reads fail.

worked.label: Example root
worked.explanation: Ravi can search this admin-owned root without writing to it.

worked.label: Example inbox
worked.explanation: The uploads group can create entries; other identities cannot.

worked.label: Upload policy
worked.explanation: New ordinary files become private mode 600.

worked.label: Actual client commands
worked.value:
put sample.txt inbox/report.txt
get inbox/report.txt received.txt
worked.explanation: The supplied text can be inspected in Client files; neither operation touches the host.

requirements: Allow the supplied valid Mira identity; refuse Noah, anonymous, unknown and invalid credentials. Mira remains confined to /srv/mira.
Make the jail root non-writable by Mira. Permit useful uploads into /inbox through both the service write policy and the directory’s Unix permissions.
New uploaded files must be owned by Mira with mode 600, and their actual contents must download correctly across distinct test inputs.
Uploading directly into the root, reading /private.txt or reaching outside the jail must fail. Save and apply configuration; preserve outside files.

practice.title: Open the upload gate and choose a mask
practice.action: Select /etc/vsftpd.conf. Keep the correct identity/root settings; change write_enable to YES and local_umask to 077. Save virtual file.
practice.observe: This only saves the upload policy; directory permissions and the running service still need repair.

practice.title: Repair only the example directories
practice.action: In Server terminal inspect ls -ld /srv/practice/ravi and ls -ld /srv/practice/ravi/inbox. Run chmod 755 /srv/practice/ravi and chmod 770 /srv/practice/ravi/inbox, then systemctl restart vsftpd.
practice.observe: The root is non-writable to Ravi; its uploads-group child has write/search permission. No chmod 777 is needed.

practice.title: Transfer, inspect and retry
practice.action: Connect as Ravi. Run put sample.txt inbox/report.txt, then get inbox/report.txt received.txt. In Server terminal run ls -l /srv/practice/ravi/inbox/report.txt. Try put sample.txt /bad.txt.
practice.observe: The inbox file contains the supplied text with mode 600. Client files shows the download. Uploading into / fails with a directory-permission explanation.

goal: Keep Mira confined for private uploads, let Noah inspect the supplied maintenance record outside his home, and preserve Unix file privacy for both identities.
context: Builds on the preceding FTP identity lesson; keep server administration separate from the FTP client.

concepts.title: The chroot list changes meaning with the default
concepts.text: chroot_local_user=YES confines local users by default. When chroot_list_enable=YES, names in /etc/vsftpd.chroot_list are exceptions: those users are NOT confined. With chroot_local_user=NO, the enabled list instead identifies users who ARE confined. Read both settings before editing the list.

concepts.title: Login policy and root policy use separate lists
concepts.text: userlist_enable/userlist_deny decide who may log in. chroot_local_user/chroot_list_enable decide the namespace after login. In this example Ravi needs a confined upload root, while Sara has a supplied maintenance role that requires the global simulated namespace. Unix permissions still apply to Sara.

concepts.title: Verify each role with useful and refused operations
concepts.text: Ravi must read and upload within his root and fail to reach the maintenance record. Sara must read /srv/records/notice.txt but fail to read Ravi’s administrator-only private file. A configuration that refuses both users, or opens everything, fails the handover.

concepts.title: Apply the complete handover
concepts.text: Save each edited list/configuration file, repair only the required directory permissions, restart the service and reconnect each identity. Check configuration runs fresh behavior cases with distinct inputs. It does not require one exact configuration spelling; equivalent supported policies may pass.

worked.label: Example login allowlist
worked.explanation: Both legitimate roles must log in; anonymous/invalid identities must not.

worked.label: Default confinement
worked.explanation: Start by confining everyone; the enabled list is the exception list.

worked.label: Example exception list
worked.explanation: Sara keeps the global namespace. Ravi remains confined.

worked.label: Useful tests
worked.value:
Ravi: put sample.txt inbox/report.txt
Sara: get /srv/records/notice.txt
worked.explanation: Private-file reads must still fail for both users.

requirements: Allow both supplied valid identities; refuse anonymous, unknown and invalid credentials.
Mira’s /srv/mira must be her FTP root. She must upload/download private mode-600 files in /inbox; the root itself remains non-writable.
Noah must retain the global simulated namespace and download /srv/records/notice.txt from his starting directory /srv/noah.
Neither identity may read the administrator-only private file. Mira must not reach the maintenance record outside her root.
Reconcile the login list, root policy, child permissions and saved/running configuration. Preserve outside files and supplied account identities.

practice.title: Read both lists before changing them

goal: Compare local listeners with two client views, then repair access without losing useful services.
context: Builds on local socket ownership and ordered numeric host-filter rules. This lesson adds client-view evidence; it does not require a real scanner or network.

concepts.title: A local listener is only one part of a connection
concepts.text: A listener is a socket waiting for connections. ss -lntp shows the supplied TCP listeners and their owning processes on this server. A listening SSH socket can still be unreachable from a client because a host rule blocks it.

concepts.title: Read open, closed and filtered as evidence
concepts.text: Open means this modeled connection reaches a retained listener. Closed means the request and response are permitted but no listener accepts that port. Filtered means a dropped request or reply prevents a conclusion about the listener. None of these labels identifies a vulnerability or proves application health.

concepts.title: Choose whose view you are testing
concepts.text: The Observe from selector supplies the client source address. In this worked example, Admin is 10.50.0.30 and Public is 10.60.0.40, both testing 192.0.2.10. The same server can be filtered from one client and open from another. -n keeps numbers, -Pn skips discovery, -sT chooses TCP connect, and -p selects individual ports.

concepts.title: Repair the range while preserving useful access
concepts.text: The initial SSH drop names the Admin range by mistake. Inspect rule order, then repair the current INPUT decisions for the full client networks. OUTPUT must also permit replies. Keep required connections working; dropping everything or naming only a displayed client is not a complete repair.

worked.label: Supplied example server
worked.explanation: Practice uses different addresses and ranges from the independent assignment.

worked.label: Local SSH evidence
worked.value: ss -lntp → a TCP 22 listener is retained
worked.explanation: A local listener does not prove that a client request reaches it.

worked.label: Before repair · Admin
worked.explanation: The wrong range drop blocks SSH; the permitted diagnostic port has no listener.

worked.label: Before repair · Public
worked.explanation: The useful socket evidence and two observer views point to a range-policy error.

worked.label: Example policy repair
worked.value:
iptables -D INPUT 1
iptables -A INPUT -s 10.60.0.0/24 -p tcp --dport 22 -j DROP
iptables -A INPUT -s 10.60.0.0/24 -p tcp --dport 9000 -j DROP
worked.explanation: Only this example starts with the wrong first rule. Read the current list before changing another workspace.

worked.label: After repair · both views
worked.value:
Admin:22/443/9000 open
Public:443 open;22/9000 filtered
Both:80 closed
worked.explanation: The policy protects the whole two client ranges while preserving the stated diagnostic and useful connections.

practice.title: Read the server evidence
practice.action: In Server terminal, run ss -lntp, then iptables -S INPUT. Find TCP 22 and read the source range on its drop rule.
practice.observe: SSH is listening locally, but the current drop names Admin 10.50.0.0/24.

practice.title: Compare the client views
practice.action: In Observer terminal, type nmap -n -Pn -sT -p 22,80,443,9000 192.0.2.10 and Run command. Change Observe from to Public, then run the same scan again.
practice.observe: Admin SSH is filtered while Public SSH is open. Port 80 is closed because no listener exists there.

practice.title: Repair, repeat and check
practice.action: In Server terminal, remove the wrong first rule with iptables -D INPUT 1. Add Public-range drops for TCP 22 and 9000 as shown in the worked example. Repeat the scan from both positions, then Check example.
practice.observe: The new reports are actual results. After a policy change the earlier scan is cleared; an entire /24 is graded, not only the displayed sample clients.

requirements: On virtual server 198.51.100.20, keep TCP ports 22, 443 and 9000 reachable for the whole Admin range 10.20.0.0/24.
For the whole Public range 10.30.0.0/24, keep 443 reachable but filter 22 and 9000. A single displayed client address is not the whole range.
Keep diagnostic TCP 80 reachable enough to report closed from both observer positions; no service should be started there.
Preserve all supplied processes and listener owners. Repair the current host filter, then Check configuration.

goal: Retire one exposed service using process and listener evidence. Preserve the other instances and useful client access.
context: Builds on the preceding client-policy lesson and careful runtime retirement. The full assignment combines local owner evidence with two observer views.

concepts.title: A process name can have more than one instance
concepts.text: Two supplied processes are both called previewd. One owns the wildcard 9000 listener, which can be observed remotely; the other owns only loopback 9001. Match the bind address, port and owning process in ss -lntp before choosing an instance.

concepts.title: Pausing and retiring are different actions
concepts.text: STOP pauses a process but retains its socket in this subset. A pending TERM on a paused owner also does not remove that socket until its lifecycle ends. A completed TERM, INT or KILL retires the selected owner. This assignment must preserve the approved instances and services.

concepts.title: A quiet scan does not prove that the owner ended
concepts.text: A firewall drop can make an existing listener look filtered. Verify both the process state and the observer results. After the unused owner ends, closed or filtered is acceptable for its port; the approved SSH and HTTPS connections must still work.

concepts.title: Use the second view as a preservation check
concepts.text: Admin and Public have different SSH access, while HTTPS is required for both. Scan from both supplied positions after the repair. Do not end all processes with the same name or stop a useful service merely to make one negative test pass.

worked.label: Separate example
worked.explanation: The independent assignment has different server/client addresses and owner IDs.

worked.label: Example socket ownership
worked.explanation: pgrep lists both names; the socket row identifies which one is exposed.

worked.label: Before repair
worked.explanation: The wildcard listener remains while its owner is active or paused.

worked.label: Retire only the example owner
worked.explanation: Use the owner identified by the example evidence, then inspect it again. This is not an assignment PID to copy.

worked.label: After repair
worked.value:
9000/tcp closed from both views
loopback 9001 owner unchanged
worked.explanation: The preserved current filter permits a conclusive closed response. Additional filtering is also acceptable after actual retirement.

worked.label: Preserve useful access
worked.explanation: A repair that ends a required owner or breaks a whole client range fails the task.

practice.title: Find the exposed owner
practice.action: In Server terminal run ss -lntp and pgrep -x previewd. Match wildcard 9000 to PID 110; keep loopback 9001 and PID 111.
practice.observe: The process name alone has two matches. Only the wildcard owner is the practice retirement target.

practice.title: Observe it from both positions
practice.action: In Observer terminal run nmap -n -Pn -sT -p 22,80,443,9000 192.0.2.10. Select Public and repeat.
practice.observe: 9000 is open from both views before retirement. A local-only socket is not exposed on the server address.

practice.title: End the right owner and verify
practice.action: In Server terminal run kill -TERM 110. Repeat both observer scans, inspect ss again, then Check example. Use the independent assignment evidence for its different owner IDs.
practice.observe: The wildcard listener disappears and required SSH/HTTPS access remains. STOP or a firewall-only concealment does not meet retirement.

requirements: Retire the owner of the unused wildcard TCP 9000 preview. A paused owner or a firewall-only concealment is insufficient.
Preserve the loopback-only preview on TCP 9001 and every approved owner, including SSH and HTTPS.
Keep SSH on TCP 22 reachable for Admin clients 10.20.0.0/24 and filtered for Public clients 10.30.0.0/24; HTTPS on 443 must work from both ranges.
TCP 9000 must no longer be open from either observer; closed or filtered is acceptable after its actual owner has ended.

goal: Repair an outside peer destination and supplied identity references, then verify both LAN directions without disabling identity checks.
context: A VPN joins two private networks across an outside network. Here you edit two virtual configuration fragments. The earlier routing and service-exposure lessons supply the request/reply and port foundations. These fragments demonstrate selected OpenVPN 2.6 settings; they are not complete deployable profiles and perform no real cryptography.

concepts.title: Separate outside, tunnel and LAN addresses
concepts.text: The topology shows each outside endpoint and local LAN. The client remote setting selects the server outside address and UDP port. The ifconfig pair names the tunnel endpoints: the other peer reverses the local and remote values. A LAN host is neither the outside endpoint nor a tunnel endpoint.

concepts.title: Check each identity reference for its own job
concepts.text: ca chooses a supplied authority; cert names this peer; key must have the same supplied pair ID as that certificate. remote-cert-tls asks for the other peer’s server/client purpose. verify-x509-name asks for its exact expected name. The virtual file table lists all supplied facts. Choosing a different file can repair a reference; removing verification cannot.

concepts.title: Keep draft, saved and applied settings distinct
concepts.text: Type in a profile editor, choose Save profile below that editor, then Apply profiles. Apply reads both saved fragments together. An unsupported directive reports its peer and line and keeps the previous applied pair. Supported but incorrect values can apply and still fail the identity/path checks. Test path investigates one supplied path; Check configuration grades the complete policy, including both directions and unrelated destinations.

worked.label: Example outside destination
worked.explanation: The demo-branch client contacts the studio outside endpoint. The initial client port differs from the studio port; tunnel addresses do not belong here.

worked.label: Example authority and own key
worked.explanation: The authority matches both supplied certificates. The client certificate and selected key must both name demo-branch-pair; the studio key is a different identity.

worked.label: Retain explicit peer verification
worked.explanation: The client expects the studio server identity. Keep the reciprocal client-purpose/name requests on the studio peer; these are supplied metadata comparisons, not a real TLS handshake.

worked.label: Expected result after Save and Apply
worked.explanation: Both directions should report outward and return routes passing. An unrelated destination stays outside this modeled VPN; that does not assert external connectivity.

practice.title: Read the studio profile
practice.action: Compare its port, authority, certificate and key with the supplied virtual identity files below the editors. Keep the correct studio settings.
practice.observe: The studio port is 1194; its certificate/key pair and explicit client-identity requests already agree.

practice.title: Repair demo-branch references
practice.action: In the demo-branch editor, compare remote with the studio outside endpoint/port. Match ca and key to the supplied certificate facts. Choose Save profile below that editor.
practice.observe: The saved label changes, but the new pair is not applied until you choose Apply profiles. Keep all other required settings.

practice.title: Apply and investigate both directions
practice.action: Choose Apply profiles, then Test path. Change From LAN to demo-branch and test the reverse path. Choose Check example. Try changing the saved key to the studio key, Apply and Check again; repair afterward.
practice.observe: Expected: both directions pass after repair; the mismatched own key causes a specific prerequisite failure. The actual result appears only after your action.

Preserve the assigned roles, explicit peer-name/purpose checks, reciprocal tunnel addresses and both full LAN route policies.
Save, apply and verify the virtual profiles; do not disable verification or redirect unrelated traffic through the VPN.

goal: Repair a site-to-site VPN’s complete outward and return routes while keeping unrelated destinations outside the tunnel.
context: First complete the peer-profile lesson: outside endpoints, identities and reciprocal tunnel addresses must agree before a LAN path can work. Here those peer settings are already correct. The faults concern which destinations each peer sends through its tunnel.

concepts.title: Read a route from its source side
concepts.text: A route names a destination network and dotted-decimal mask. On practice-hub, reaching the office requires a route for the office LAN. On practice-office, replying requires a route for the hub LAN. Fixing only the first peer does not create the return route on the other.

concepts.title: Cover the complete LAN, not one successful host
concepts.text: A /20 uses mask 255.255.240.0 and spans sixteen /24 blocks. The example hub LAN is 10.32.0.0–10.32.15.255; the example office LAN is 10.48.16.0–10.48.31.255. A /24 return route can make an early host work while missing later hosts. A default route goes too far and redirects unrelated addresses.

concepts.title: Diagnose before and after applying
concepts.text: Apply profiles first, then Test path and read whether the outward or return selection is missing. Use each entire supplied opposite LAN in its peer’s route. Save both changed profiles and Apply again. Check configuration evaluates complete destination intervals plus several host paths, including addresses beyond the first /24; equivalent split routes are accepted.

worked.label: Example outward selection on practice-hub
worked.explanation: This covers the entire opposite office /20. The initial adjacent /20 does not contain the supplied destination.

worked.label: Example return selection on practice-office
worked.explanation: The reply must reach all hub hosts, not only the first /24. This is the other peer’s destination route, not a duplicate of its own LAN.

worked.label: Expected two-way observation
worked.explanation: After both Save actions and Apply, the high-end ordinary hosts should have outward and return routes. Unrelated 203.0.113 destinations stay outside the VPN.

practice.title: Inspect the hub’s destination route
practice.action: Apply profiles before editing and Test path to see the starting failure. In practice-hub, compare its route with the office LAN. Repair the destination and choose Save profile.
practice.observe: An adjacent /20 is a different network. Saving this repair alone does not fix the return route on the other peer.

practice.title: Repair the office’s return coverage
practice.action: In practice-office, compare its route mask with the full hub /20. Save profile and Apply profiles. Keep the already correct identities, ports and tunnel addresses.
practice.observe: A /24 matches only the early hub hosts. A /20 includes the later host blocks without selecting unrelated networks.

practice.title: Test beyond the first /24
practice.action: Test a high-end pair from the worked example, then select the reverse From LAN and swap its source/destination. Check example. Try an unrelated destination such as 203.0.113.200.
practice.observe: Expected: high-end hosts pass both ways; the unrelated destination stays outside the VPN. A single successful sample does not prove the full policy.

requirements: Restore both directions between central LAN 172.20.16.0/20 and depot LAN 172.21.32.0/20.
Cover every ordinary host in both LANs, including hosts beyond the first /24.
Keep unrelated destinations outside the VPN.
Preserve the supplied peer identities, authority, transport and reciprocal tunnel addresses.
Save and apply the current profiles, investigate the modeled paths and check the complete configuration.

context: Builds on installed versus local RPM records, package version ordering and declared provides/requires. You will investigate fixed vendor facts, choose supplied archives and verify retained configuration. No host package manager or service is run.

concepts.title: Read the advisory before choosing a version
concepts.text: A security advisory identifies the affected product, release, package and the first vendor build containing a fix. A vendor can backport a security change into an older upstream version. Compare the full package version and release against the supplied advisory; do not assume the largest upstream number is the right package. These TRAINING notices and packages are fictional, not current real-world security advice.

concepts.title: Separate target release from package release
concepts.text: Training Enterprise Linux 8 is the target system release. In 1.0-4, 1.0 is the upstream version and 4 is the package release. The supplied origin table says which target system each archive belongs to. A 1.0-5 archive for system release 9 is not the stated release-8 fix.

concepts.title: Preserve deliberate site configuration
concepts.text: The current configuration contains site-specific settings. RPM marks it as %config(noreplace). When the archived default changes and local text differs from both defaults, this activity keeps the site file and stages the new default as .rpmnew. Inspect the site text before and after updating. A .rpmnew file is an incoming default to review, not proof that a running service has reloaded it.

concepts.title: Check the installed file as well as its version
concepts.text: A fixed version header does not repair damaged application files. Compare the actual ordinary file with the installed archive in the read-only inspector. Exact reinstall restores that archive’s ordinary payload; this activity preserves the intentional configuration text separately. This checks supplied file data, not a real executable or vulnerability.

concepts.title: Choose a useful alert source
concepts.text: Use the affected vendor’s advisory for product-specific fixed builds. CERT coordination notices can provide cross-vendor context and links to affected suppliers. A port scan alone does not establish a vulnerable or fixed version. This offline lab supplies fictional notices instead of subscribing to live feeds. Bugtraq is a historical alert-source name still listed in the current LPI objectives, not a promise of an active service.

goal: Repair a filter that detects denied logins without treating successful logins or unrelated messages as failures.
requirements: Match complete rejected-login records with a reported numeric IPv4 address for the supplied application.
Handle the changing usernames, decimal ports and addresses in every supplied sample; do not restrict the filter to one recorded user.
Leave accepted logins, unrelated applications, incomplete records and extra-text notices unmatched.
Save the repaired virtual filter and preserve every supplied log sample.

practice.title: Read the records beside the example filter
practice.action: Read the workshop log lines and the event word in the example editor. Which lines describe rejected logins, and which describe successful or unrelated events?
practice.observe: The starter’s accepted event word selects the wrong kind of login. The worked example shows how to describe a complete rejected record while allowing its fields to change.

practice.title: Repair and test the saved example
practice.action: Change the example event word from accepted to rejected. Save virtual filter, then Run command. Compare the actual labels beside each supplied line. Use Log sample to try the changed fields and lookalike events.
practice.observe: Expected: complete workshop rejected records match; accepted, incomplete, other-application and extra-text records stay unmatched. The command output and row labels show actual results after each run.

practice.title: Diagnose a deliberate mistake and retry
practice.action: Use Check example. Then change rejected back to accepted in the example filter, save and run again. Read its failure feedback, restore rejected, save and check again.
practice.observe: Successful logins become false positives and real failures are missed. Retrying uses the same preserved example; assignment work stays in its own editor.

worked.label: Complete separate example filter
worked.explanation: The example uses workshop messages and its own saved virtual file; this is not the assignment filter.

worked.label: Run the saved example
worked.explanation: Save virtual filter first. Actual output labels the selected sample after Run command.

worked.label: Useful detection
worked.explanation: Expected: Matched. This is a complete denied-login event with a changing username, address and port.

worked.label: Successful login
worked.explanation: Expected: Missed. A successful login is not a denied-login failure.

concepts.title: Read what the application reported
concepts.text: Each supplied log line is a piece of text. rejected means this application denied a login; accepted means it allowed one. user= names the attempted identity, from introduces the reported address, and port gives the recorded client port. A filter selects messages; it does not contact those addresses.

concepts.title: Describe changing text with a pattern
concepts.text: Ordinary words and spaces match themselves. [A-Za-z0-9_-] means one ASCII letter, digit, underscore or hyphen; the + after it means one or more. [0-9]+ means one or more decimal digits. These classes let one pattern handle changing names and ports instead of copying a single log line.

concepts.title: Require a complete record and its address
concepts.text: ^ marks the beginning and $ marks the end of a line. They keep an unrelated prefix or an extra trailing notice out of this activity’s complete-record format. <HOST> marks the reported numeric IPv4 address. It must be a complete required field here; a line without a recorded address cannot supply one.

concepts.title: Save the filter, then test the saved file
concepts.text: A filter file starts with [Definition] and gives failregex = followed by the pattern. Type in Filter editor and use Save virtual filter. Run command reads that saved text and the selected virtual log sample. Matched means selected as a failure; Missed means not selected. The numeric-only --usedns=no option is supported; no host file, network lookup, daemon or ban is involved.

context: Builds on reading supplied Linux logs and using a saved configuration file. The pattern characters needed here are taught below; no previous regular-expression experience is assumed.

goal: Keep real denied logins detectable while excluding only explicitly marked failed health checks.
requirements: Match complete denied-login records for the supplied application, including changing names, ports and numeric addresses.
Ignore denied records marked source=health; an interactive failure with the same username and address must still match.
Leave accepted logins, unrelated notices and incomplete or extra-text records unmatched.
Save the repaired virtual filter and preserve every supplied log sample.

practice.title: Inspect the false positives beside the editor
practice.action: Read the selected archive log sample and the example filter. Use Log sample to compare ordinary events with Health checks and real users sharing an identity. Identify the event word and source marker before editing.
practice.observe: The starter selects successful events and ignores a username. The supplied health and interactive lines show why those are separate mistakes.

practice.title: Save a precise filter and test its real results
practice.action: Restrict the example failure pattern to denied records, and make its ignore rule specific to denied source=health records. Save virtual filter, then Run command. Read each Matched, Ignored or Missed label beside the actual line.
practice.observe: Expected: genuine denied logins match, denied health checks are ignored, and successful logins remain unmatched. Actual results appear only after the test command runs.

practice.title: Try a broader exception and repair it
practice.action: After Check example passes, change the ignore rule to select the probe username regardless of source. Save and test the health-exception sample, then Check example. Restore the narrow source marker and check again.
practice.observe: The interactive probe failure is now hidden as well. The failed sample explains the lost detection; restoring the specific exception repairs it.

worked.label: Complete separate example filter
worked.value:
[Definition]
failregex = ^archive denied user=[A-Za-z0-9_-]+ from <HOST> port [0-9]+ source=[a-z]+$
ignoreregex = ^archive denied user=[A-Za-z0-9_-]+ from [0-9.]+ port [0-9]+ source=health$
worked.explanation: The example uses archive messages and its own saved virtual file; this is not the assignment filter.

worked.label: Run the saved example
worked.explanation: Save virtual filter first. Actual output labels the selected sample after Run command.

worked.label: Useful detection
worked.value: archive denied user=tariq from 203.0.113.42 port 53142 source=interactive
worked.explanation: Expected: Matched. This is a complete denied-login event with a changing username, address and port.

worked.label: Successful login
worked.value: archive accepted user=tariq from 203.0.113.42 port 53143 source=interactive
worked.explanation: Expected: Missed. A successful login is not a denied-login failure.

worked.label: Health exception
worked.value: archive denied user=probe from 203.0.113.42 port 100 source=health
worked.explanation: Expected: Ignored. Only the explicit denied source=health case is excluded; the interactive record remains detectable.

concepts.title: A match is evidence, not a verdict
concepts.text: A filter can select text that is harmless in context. This application records deliberate failed health checks with source=health. That marker identifies the exception; the username or address alone does not, because a real user may share both.

concepts.title: Separate failure detection from exceptions
concepts.text: failregex selects a denied-login record. ignoreregex selects a narrow exception before failures are counted. A health-check failure should be Ignored; a successful login should be Missed; a genuine interactive failure should be Matched.

concepts.title: Keep the whole event specific
concepts.text: Use the denied event word and the end of the complete record in the failure pattern. A pattern that selects any event word also selects successful logins. The ignore pattern should include both the denied event and the explicit source=health marker, rather than hiding every record from one user.

concepts.title: Test both sides after editing
concepts.text: Read the health-exception sample as well as the ordinary events. Compare the same identity in health and interactive records. A quiet filter that ignores everything is not useful. This offline test classifies supplied lines; it does not run a jail or ban an address.

goal: Repair a reversed rule header and verify its protocol, address, port and direction scope.
requirements: Alert only on supplied TCP records from 203.0.113.0/24 to 192.0.2.40 port 8088 in that direction.

Save the repaired virtual rule with a positive sid for this activity, and preserve all supplied records.

practice.title: Read the supplied pairs

practice.observe: The starter has the endpoint pairs reversed; its arrow selects the response instead of the request.

practice.title: Repair and replay the example

practice.observe: Expected: only scoped TCP requests with the uppercase SYNC literal alert. Actual decisions appear beside records after replay.

practice.action: Choose Check example. Then change -> to <>, save and replay Request and reverse direction. Read the false-positive feedback, restore ->, save and check again.
practice.observe: Expected: the reverse response also alerts. Its failed case identifies the unwanted detection; restoring -> excludes it.

worked.explanation: These are the example endpoints and marker, not the assignment solution.

worked.label: Matching example request
worked.explanation: Expected: Alert. The client network, receiving service and uppercase SYNC marker all match.

worked.label: Contrasting example record
worked.explanation: Expected: No alert. This response travels in the reverse direction; the -> rule selects requests only.

concepts.title: Read the header before the payload
concepts.text: An alert rule first selects a protocol and two endpoint pairs. Each pair is an address followed by a port. The -> arrow means source on the left, destination on the right. any accepts any value in that one position; it does not reverse the arrow. <> allows the complete pairs in either direction.

concepts.title: Describe a network and a marker
concepts.text: A numeric address selects one host. A CIDR such as 192.0.2.0/24 selects that network, including changing client addresses. content:"SYNC"; requires the literal text SYNC somewhere in the supplied payload. The marker is case-sensitive unless followed by ,nocase. It is not a regular expression.

concepts.title: Edit, save and replay
concepts.text: Type in Rule editor. Save virtual rule changes the simulated rule file. Replay record set tests that saved file against the selected supplied records and shows actual decisions. Check answers evaluates all record sets. An unsaved draft is preserved, but cannot keep a completed assignment successful. Options end with semicolons inside parentheses. sid identifies the rule; keep a positive ID in this activity. Snort itself permits omission, and recommends local rule IDs starting at 1000000.

concepts.title: Know what an alert establishes
concepts.text: An alert means the supported rule conditions matched a supplied record. It does not prove an attack succeeded. Snort is an intrusion-detection engine; Greenbone/OpenVAS scans for vulnerability findings. A scanner finding and an observed traffic match answer different questions. This activity runs neither tool: its decoded records omit packets, streams and service state.

concepts.title: Read the header before the payload
concepts.text: An alert rule first selects a protocol and two endpoint pairs. Each pair is an address followed by a port. The -> arrow means source on the left, destination on the right. any accepts any value in that one position; it does not reverse the arrow. <> allows the complete pairs in either direction.

concepts.title: Require both clues, with deliberate case handling
concepts.text: Multiple content options must all match the same supplied payload. Without relative modifiers, each literal can occur anywhere; their order in the payload need not match option order. content:"AUDIT",nocase; accepts AUDIT, audit or Audit. A separate content:"change=disable"; stays case-sensitive. A marker alone also selects harmless actions.

concepts.title: Keep a wider network scoped correctly
concepts.text: A /20 prefix leaves 12 host bits. For 172.20.16.0/20 the third octet spans 16–31 and the fourth spans 0–255. A client just before or after that interval is outside the header scope. This is address membership for rule matching, not a claim that every address is assignable to a workstation.
